The main feature we wanted from this was to pull the photos from our iPhone without having to sync all the time. Sometimes our phone gets filled so quickly with photos and videos that we can't take any more and we're not near our syncing computer. That's where this comes in handy.

In order to use it fully, you have to download the compatible app (which is free), connect the device, and let the app and device access your photos, contacts, and calendar. We have a few microSD cards lying around, and so far our brands (Kensington and SanDisk) worked fine, even though the packaging is adamant in having you buy their brand of cards. ;)

The app itself is pretty easy to use, but I'd rather have the main syncing buttons appear on the first page. When you open it up the app is split into three "pages" that you can swipe through to select. At the top are icons to select the app and card memory (though I'm not sure why you'd back up the phone to the app over the card), and then at the bottom you get features to sync to other apps. Those aren't why we got this product, so when you swipe right you get the buttons to sync the photos, contacts, and calendar. You can sync selected ones or sync them all to the card. We usually just select all, even if we know only pictures and videos have been added since the last sync; we just like to be cautious.
Syncing takes only a few minutes. To confirm that all the photos and videos have been synced, I removed the memory card and plugged it in to both my computer and an Android device. I was able to navigate the folders in the card without issue (that is, no restrictions as I thought there might've been since it was an Apple's synced history going into Windows and Google machines) and see all the photos, etc. You can also navigate the folders via the device in the iPhone, but the thumbnails sometimes take a while to load.
Initially I didn't think the videos were backed up, but that's because they didn't have that little play icon on them as other videos usually do. When I scoured carefully through the dates, however, I found them all, and no noticeable resolution loss. Perfect!

So far this is exactly what we wanted and it works just fine.

As a child one of my favorite things to do was to look at things under a microscope. I vividly remember gathering a water sample from a swamp near the house and looking at a sample and finding my first paramecium. It has been years since I have owned a microscope, but with this microscope I can see how things have advanced and changed. This one does not have the same magnification as that microscope I had as a child but it is a lot easier to use and I can still see things with it that I cannot see even with a good magnifying glass.

This unit looks more like a drill press than a microscope, in terms of the design. The scope itself fits on a metal shaft and two turning knobs make it easy to raise and lower the scope in relation to the base. The base has two clips for holding down your slides or paper or whatever else you want to look at through the scope. There is no eye-piece on the scope – the image is viewed on a computer screen instead and the connection is made via USB.

Included with the scope is a software CD and this must be installed to use the scope. Installation is quick and painless. I installed under Windows 10 64-bit and had no issues. After installation I launched the software immediately.

The software consists of a view/capture application and a supplemental application for saving your work. The main part of the view & capture app is a live window that shows what is visible through the scope. As the object or slide on the scope base is moved, the image updates in real time. I found it a little awkward to line things up just right at first but I finally did manage to get things in the viewer just as I wanted them.

I started with a gray piece of paper that I thought was solid gray, but I found that the gray is actually a micro dot pattern like magazine print. More interesting was the corner of a $5 bill showing not just the print pattern detail but the fine fibers in the paper. A penny, cat hair and a very close-up view of a microfiber cleaning cloth all proved to be interesting subjects. Attached to this review are some of those detailed images, my favorite being the penny. I have not yet gone to the culvert near the house to gather water samples.

The software allows for two different capture types – photo or video. I have only played with the photo capture so far but it it very straightforward – click the photo button, either on the application interface or on the USB cable where the light level can be adjusted and the image appears in a list on the right side of the application window. If you double click the image you can save the image to the hard drive, zoom in on it and do a few other operations.

Linked to a tablet instead of a computer, this is a great travel scope to take with you. It is well-suited for classroom use as well as for use in the office.

I like this microscope. It is very easy to use, it does a good job of magnification and images are nice and clear. It is very different than the microscope I used growing up, in ways that I like. It's so much easier viewing on a screen than looking through a viewer, making this more fun to use too.

Amazon rejected this review once because they accused of bad deed. Let me give some context. I am a private investigator and an independent journalist. Noting I did with this camera was illegal or nefarious therefore this review is not breaking any rules. I spent a lot of time using this product and this was my unbiased opinion and recommendation based on my experience with this device!

I was blown away by this camera’s versatility and its incredibly sturdy design. The instructions were well written and easy to follow. I tested this camera in some extreme conditions that it wasn't designed for and it worked very well. It held up in both high and low temperatures with no problems. I don’t advise trying this but, it was accidentally dropped into a water fountain. Luckily, I was able to recover it quickly, shut it off and remove the SD card. I let it dry for 24 hours expecting it to be dead, but both the camera and SD card were fine.

It was tested with 10 different brands and makes of 128Gb SDXC Micro SD cards. It worked with every brand card that I installed in it including Samsung, SanDisk, PNY, Gigastone, Kingston, Adata and Lexar brands. I tested it only with the Pro+, Extreme, Elite and/or Evo+ versions of SDXC Micro SD cards. The reason I tested it with so many different brands was to help you guys know for sure that whichever one you pick, that if I listed it here it worked fine. I am not recommending a brand just telling you which ones worked for me.

I loved the location of the Micro SD card slot directly above the USB connector which are protected by a cap. The audio recording could have had a little better range, but a better mic would be hard to fit inside the device. Being able to switch between audio and video recording was a huge bonus. It had exceptional battery life for the polymer Lithium 550mAH battery installed in it. I was able to get around 2 1/2 hours of 1080p video recording out of this battery. The audio recording doesn't use nearly as much charge so it'll last a lot longer. I recharged the camera over 200 times in the course of the month I tested it and didn't notice any battery degradation yet.
It recorded in both 720p and 1080p resolutions flawlessly. It did well in low light environments also. My only issue with this camera was the placement of the LED light. Its current location could unintentionally expose the device to the subject you are legally recording or interviewing. The LED should be somewhere out of sight. Even in its current location it would be difficult for the subject to notice due to the LED being dim. I believe it was designed to use a lower brightness LED for that very reason. The subject would have to be standing over you for them to notice it happened to blink for any reason i.e. low battery.

This was one of the best spy cameras I have ever used in its price range. It might seem a little plain on the outside, but it is supposed to. Overall this camera performed admirably for the month I tested prior to writing this review.

With my camera's side strap sticking out of one side (which I prefer to running it through the top hole because access is quicker), it's like a little mini-purse. The cutout in the top happens to be right over the USB cable port on my camera, so if I had to (but I probably won't), I could run the USB cable to it without removing the camera from its case. Another thing I could do if I wanted to is use that little hole to loop an ID tag or small ID/credit card holder through using one of those beaded lamp-pull type thingies. Little things mean a lot to me, and I have to say I just love the magnetic clasp underneath the low-key silverish AmazonBasics logo on the front of the case. The magnet is not so strong as to be annoyingly hard to pull apart, but it's strong enough to do the job without slipping. The little circular magnetic piece in the clasp has a small center button that fits into a recession in the other part of the clasp; when closing the cover, you hear a satisfying little click when you slide it into place, so you know it's snugly closed.

I was thinking when I got this (not paying great attention) that the holder "clip" on the back was actually a clip suitable for clipping to the edge of your pants or a coat pocket, but it's not. It's actually better than that, because we all know how quickly those clips break off our cell phones. This one closes with strong velcro so you can loop it through a belt loop or other strap or onto a belt. The part of the holder that does not have velcro on it is not quite an inch wide, though, so it wouldn't work as well with wider belts. With the camera in it, it would be too heavy (at least for me) to want to wear around your neck, but you could definitely put it on a lanyard if you wanted to—and then perhaps stick it in a breast pocket so it's not dangling. One nice thing about the velcro is that, even though it is sewn on very well, part of the piece that is sewn to the camera case actually lifts up as you pull the velcro apart. This should extend the life of the case because you're not pulling against case stitching when you're trying to get it apart. This is not wimpy velcro, so you have to tug a bit to get it open.

I wanted a set of speakers to use mainly for my Kindle Fire and MP3 player, but also as my computer speakers. Due to space constraints, a 2.0 system was my only option, since a subwoofer (regardless of the size) would be problematic.

So the search began. There were several speakers that sounded great, including the Creative Gigaworks, M Audio and Audioengine. However, they lacked the convenience features I wanted such as ease of connecting/disconnecting a tablet and volume control without having to reach out and touch the speaker.

The Bose Companion 20 initially caught my eye because of the control pod. That was a great solution to my problems since I could control the volume right on my desk plus have the ability to plug in/unplug a tablet very easily. The sound quality sealed the deal - everyone who hears these speakers think they are a 2.1 set due to the ample bass. But, the bass is not at the expense of clear mid and upper ranges.

I use these 60% for music and 40% for video, and for both applications, the sound quality has been just wonderful. I'm also impressed that they sound just as good with the volume dialed way down as they do at moderate or blast-out-the-walls loud.

The control pod is very well made. It has a nice weight to it and a non-skid backing so it stays put. The volume control works very smoothly with a solid feel. I'm especially fond of being able to turn the speakers on and off by just touching the control pod.

You can connect it to the PC and to an aux device (such as a tablet) and use both at the same time. That's important since I want to listen to music or a video from my Fire, but still want to hear a chime when an email arrives.

My complaints are that the control pod cable is a bit too short for my needs. It's about 5 foot long, which is ample if you have the speakers next to your PC, but I have my speakers on a shelf above my desk. I was able to arrange things to make it work, but another foot or two of cable (or the ability to purchase an extension) would have been nice. It's a custom cable, so an off-the-shelf extension is not possible.

My other complaint is the price. I was able to get a used pair for half of the regular price. I think these are a bit overpriced at the regular price. But, Bose hit a really unique niche - the ability to have great sound without any compromise in convenience. If you want both, there's a high cost for admission.

If the price is not an issue, these very much deserve a hard look if you're in the market for a great sounding pair of 2.0 speakers. Highly recommend.

Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones which have their strengths and weaknesses. I have a few pairs of nice non-ANC phones, some of which are excellent for studio work, but this is my first pair of true studio phones. After working with them, I am very pleased with them. They are comfortable to wear for long periods of time and they sound great with a very balanced sound profile.

These are over-the-ear phones, not on-ear, and I prefer that. They do not pinch or press my ears and I can wear them for several hours without them getting uncomfortable. The pads are soft and do not irritate as some phone pads sometimes can. The pads do not breathe, though, so after some time they do eventually get a bit warm.

If using these as Bluetooth phones, operation is simple – turn them on. They’re immediately ready to pair and my system discovered them and paired without incident. The Bluetooth range is good and I was able to get between 30’ and 50’ with walls in between before the sound began to stutter a little.

If you prefer to use them corded, that works too and these come with several audio cords with which to connect. Speaking of the cords: these do not use a standard audio cable with a standard connector on the phone side, so you can’t simply use any audio cable with them (though they will work with extension cables). Bear this in mind.

Volume can be controlled by touching the connector on the left side – flick up to increase volume, flick down to decrease.

The most important aspect of any headphones is the sound quality and these definitely deliver. The highs are sharp and crisp without being piercing. The midlevels are full and warm, and the base is strong without being overdriven. Most headphones anymore are tuned to overdrive the bass at the expense of the midrange making music sound hollow while pounding the listener to a headache. It is refreshing to listen to music that is properly balanced without needing an equalizer to get the sound right. I would not call these audiophile phones, but they’re better than many headphones I have used that cost much more.

If I could change one thing… I prefer a headphone set that clamps down on my head and fits snugly. These are not as snug as I’d like, but they are better than some I have used. When I turn my head and look down, they remain in place without slipping which is an issue with loose-fitting phones. Since these don’t slip, I’m satisfied.

I’m happy with these phones and based on my experience with them I am pleased to recommend them. They sound great and they are comfortable enough for extended use.

I bought the printer because it was affordable, and had lots of features. I wanted something with a duplex document feeder scanner, full duplex printing, color, and flatbed scanning. This seemed to have it all. As a scanner, it's pretty good if you manage to stay away from the HP software. As a printer, the quality is decent, but the ink situation is enough to make me never buy from HP again.

I'm sure HP read lots and lots of letters from angry customers complaining about their ink prices. Indeed, with other HP printers, it can be frustrating to be charged $35 when you run out of black ink. HP's solution to this can be seen with the 564 ink cartridge - the colors are $10 and the black is $12. Seems cheap!

Here's the awful truth: the black ink lasts about 30 - 50 pages. This is not an exaggeration. You need to replace the ink ALL THE TIME. The printer also has a bizarre habit of using ALL of the colors even when you're printing things that look black and white. So even if you're not printing very much in color at all, the printer will inexplicably run out of colors. Since the ink cartridges are so small, it seems like the printer CONSTANTLY has a low ink warning, and is CONSTANTLY stopping with out of ink errors. So even though you're only spending $10 - $12 on each cartridge, you're buying tons of them, and you need a huge stock for replenishment. This is HP's marketing department guiding the hand of their engineering department and delivering a crippled product. You will learn to hate this printer. It will constantly need your care and feeding, and you won't save any money on ink.

Here's a tip: in the print settings on your computer, you can tell it to use black ink only. That's a lifesafer.

First thing's first, it is important to understand what you are getting. This isn't a VR headset - you aren't going to be bringing these on a trip to play some beat saber. These are simply a screen that you can strap to your head.

Now that we have that out of the way, lets go into the things I love about these. Plugging these into a device is (usually) a breeze and you can get to consuming your content on a virtual screen in no time. The included blackout shade is a great addition, giving you the choice between maintaining situational awareness of your surroundings, or closing yourself off to the world and immersing yourself in the content.

I particularly like using these on a plane. It is great to be able to shut out everything that is going on around you and just watching content without your seatmates peeking over to see what you are watching. I do recommend using in-ear headphones since on or over ear types of headphones can get uncomfortable when combined with the glasses.

If you wear glasses, I suggest purchasing prescription lens inserts - it will really make your experience just that much better.

I think it is really smart that these are powered by whatever device they are plugged into. This allows the device to be less bulky and lighter; hence more comfortable for long term wear. The downside being, your device will consume power quicker. This can be mitigated with a wireless charger (since your glasses are plugged into your device).

Great Addition to Home Security System

First I should say there is no 100% perfect home security system. That is why I have a home security “solution” that incorporates several different, but tied together systems. I have a full Lorex Camera System, Smart Things Hub and a wired alarm system. But even with all that there was something missing. If I wasn’t home, all of the other items were only good after the fact. Meaning I could see who was at my door, or in my house after I got back home. Sure I could set alerts on those other devices, but when your phone chirps 10 alerts per hour, it just becomes white noise. These other systems had so many false positives I ultimately turned them off.

Pros: But the Ring Bell filled several voids in these other systems. One, the false positives are almost nonexistent due to the ability to mask the alert area of the camera. My existing security system may alert me, but then I had to log into the camera system to see what was going on. The time it takes to do that could make a real difference. The ability to answer and interact with someone who rings your bell from your couch or from at work is invaluable! The person ringing the bell has no idea where you are answering from. But the best part is being able to ignore solicitors and screen people before you answer. It’s as easy as answering a phone call and the live image is instantaneous. The fact that it integrates with my SmartThings hub is just icing on the cake.

I was able to install the Ring Bell Pro in about 15 minutes following the simple instructions. It is extremely well thought out. The video quality of the Ring Pro is excellent! It does not have a very wide angle and there is a slight fisheye distortion, but it should be more than sufficient for most applications. The mobile app is also very intuitive. As I mentioned, when you get an alert, you can immediately see who is at the door and you can choose to answer and speak, or just watch.

Cons: I was confused by the wall plate not having the mounting holes line up with the existing wall plate holes. This required drilling holes above and below the existing holes to mount the plate. I could see no reason for this.

The unit can easily be ripped off the wall with one hand. Because the main unit mounts onto a plastic wall cover, it would take about 2 seconds to remove and disable the unit. But at least you will get an alert and when you went to log in you would know something was wrong. However, the Ring Pro has a unique purchase protection that sates “If your Ring™ Video Doorbell is stolen at any time after your purchase, Bot Home Automation, Inc. will replace your Ring™ Video Doorbell at no charge to you”. That’s pretty impressive!

If you want to keep your Ring History, you have to sign up for their paid service. Otherwise you only see live views. Prices vary by plan, but they do offer one free month for new customers.

Overall: There is no perfect security system. Each one has its plusses and minuses. But the Ring Pro should be part of every home security solution. Also, if I had to choose only one component for a complete home security solution, this would be high up on my list.

It is a perfect fit for my Mac, and I don't even realize it's on it except for the fact that it works MUCH better than the rubberized grips on the bottom of my Mac to hold it firmly on my lap desk—it stays put even when the board is slanted at a 45-degree angle! I wish I had gotten this when I first got my Mac, because I do have a few scratches on it now that this case would have prevented. The fit is so tight, the only thing I don't like about it is that I do have a [[ASIN:B00D6A2Z2C palm rest protector]] on my Mac, and on one side it won't quite fit underneath the case's tab. I'll probably wind up taking a hair off the protector so I don't notice it so much, but I wouldn't have to because it looks like it will stay stuck.

I don't really know how the keyboard skin compares to others on the market, because I hate the things and won't use one. I can say that it does fit the keyboard well and provides cover from spills. I think you can see from my photos how it fits; also how the case fits. The one with my chiweenie Bingo in the picture was taken when I had my lap desk at a precipitous incline, and there was no sliding!

The screen protector has a top and bottom. I thought at first it was not going to fit right, but it's because I had it upside down. It has a protective film over it that you remove once you place it on the screen. I don't know yet if I'm going to use it, because we've got a lot of dog hair floating around and I'm not confident I could get it on without dog hair under it. That happened when I first put the hard shell case on, and I had to remove it and put it back on again.

One thing to note about this case: there are no installation instructions, and there is a definite right way and wrong way to put on both pieces. The lip on the bottom part goes in the front, and the open part is in the back where all your ports are. The top of the case has three tabs on one of the long sides and two tabs on the other. The three-tab side goes at the top of the screen. I don't think you can see these details in my photos. You really can't see that there is a case on it at all unless you look closely.

I'm still just knocked out at how well the grippers on the case grip my lap desk. I broke my last Mac by dumping it off into the floor—actually, Bingo did it. This case is great insurance, and the price is definitely right, even if you wind up only using the case. But with all three protective items, this set is a real bargain. I got this item free in exchange for my honest review, but had I known how great it was, I definitely would have bought it a long time ago.

I love my laptop. It is so handy and easy to type on, but one thing has a tendency to drive me crazy- the touchpad. Although I like some of the features on the touchpad, it has a tendency to make so many mistakes or tracking errors that I often want to throw it out the window.

When I was given an opportunity to review and rate the Logitech Wireless Marathon Mouse 750, I was skeptical, but willing to try it.

I do not do well with most mice. They hurt my wrists and make me so frustrated that I prefer using my desktop keyboard touchpad which is perfect- has been for over 10 years.

I was so frustrated with my touchpad on my laptop, however, that I decided to give it a try anyway. What I discovered was so exciting that I actually LOVE using a mouse with my laptop.

WHAT DOES THIS MOUSE COME WITH?
Although the mouse comes with a CD with drivers and program on it, I downloaded it from the Logitech site finding it to be more current. There are two AA batteries that come with it and they are easy to put in the mouse. There is also a short instruction sheet, and a tiny little USB wireless antenna that plugs into the laptop USB.

HOW WELL DOES THIS MOUSE WORK?
I am very impressed with this mouse. I use my Kindle case to run the mouse on, but it will work with many surfaces. Tracking is very accurate and can be adjusted through the program. Plugging in was easy and the mouse worked instantly with no problems. The ergonomic mouse is the most comfortable mouse I have used. There is an ON OFF button and a side button for going forward and backward on web pages.

I can not comment on battery longevity as I have only had it for a month. This is supposed to last for three years. Only time will tell.

All in all, despite the fact that it is an extra piece to stuff in my laptop case, I really like this mouse. It is very comfortable, easy to use, and excellent in tracking performance. The buttons work well and the center wheel will magnify or reduce the size of the screen- internet pages are esp handy this way. You press once, and then a magnifier comes up. Clicking the wheel one direction will enlarge, and the other direction would decrease the size. Clicking again locks it into place.

The center wheel will also scroll the page down incrementally, or really fast if you spin it, making it much easier to control the page views. Two buttons on the left hand side will forward or reverse pages on the browser very easily using the thumb. There is a little button just below the center wheel which I have not figured out yet.

There is a press point right where the thumb rests which reduces windows allowing you to pick the application you want to use- you click on the window you want to change to.

You can completely change the settings on your mouse any way you want to, however so that you can have it the way you like it.

FINAL COMMENTS
I really love this mouse- and I can not stand most mice for computers- they really get to me. This one is so comfortable and easy to use, it has changed my opinion of mice- at least this one.

This is something that you get more for the look rather than the sound quality (although the sound quality is pretty good as well). It’s one of the more novel looking small speakers I’ve seen, and well worth a 5 star rating.

I have some cognitive impairment and mobility challenges from lupus, and I was able to set up Fire TV really easily. The batteries go in the remote; the hdmi cable goes where it goes, and the power plugs in where it plugs in. The interface is simple and intuitive, and you can get everywhere with the home button, the directionals, back, and select. The only painful part for me/my hands was logging into my wireless network via the onscreen qwerty keyboard.

The screens are responsive with virtually no latency, thanks to the quad core processor and 2 gb ram. And video streaming is also very smooth. I have only been using this a day, but I haven't had it pause to buffer yet. I have a Chromecast in my son's room, a recent model Mac Mini in the living room, an older C2D Mac Mini in my room with Boxee on it, and a Raspberry Pi, and they all buffer at some point during just about every movie. I stayed in a vacation home with a Roku 2 last summer, and it was great, but it also had to buffer a lot. We also have three game consoles that have streaming video apps, and they buffer, too. I think the Fire's secret may be its wifi card. I am sure that, at some point, my ISP will find a way to slow it down.

So, yeah, I am giving the Fire TV four stars for doing exactly what I need it to do. I had come to Amazon to get another Chromecast, but I saw this and thought it would probably be better suited to what I need in my bedroom (I need my husband to be able to watch a tv show without my help - he is completely tech-challenged and cannot work the Dish remote - too many buttons).

The reason it doesn't get five stars is that there aren't yet enough content apps. There is a manga channel, a documentary channel, an art house channel, along with Crackle and Flixter and Plex (Plex is a for pay service that lets you stream your home content). There is plenty to watch if you are a Prime member (I am - and I appreciated having that already set up on my Fire TV - Thank you, Amazon!) I am also a Dish subscriber, with HBO and a Hopper. I have apps for those directly on some of my devices. I can get them on the internet on the tbs I have hooked up to computers. I can even blast them over to my Chromecast from my tablets. But they aren't on Fire TV, and none of my tablets will screencast to Fire TV. Soon as they are, this is a five star device for me.

I read in Entertainment Weekly that HBO and Amazon Prime have come to an understanding that will make lots and lots of HBO shows available through prime, which will also make them available through Fire TV. For the ones that are not, HBOGO will have an app for this. Between that news and my son's enjoyment of an eight dollar (as opposed to 40 to 60 dollars) platformed on this thing, I am adding a star.

My daughter and I do a lot of photography of jewelry. We have had a variety of tripods and camera aids. This kit seemed like a good one for us. I got it.

WHAT IS THIS KIT LIKE?
CASE
This has a hard case that zips around the edge. It has a pocket in it to hold things in place and a cupped side to allow for the tripod storage.

LENS BAGS
There are bags in here which fit small medium or large lenses. I don't have any lenses yet, but I do have a small light that fits in one.

CLEANING CLOTH
These come in a zip topped plastic bag. This is pretty nice and works well as is expected with microfiber cloth for cleaning glass.

QUICK RELEASE CAMERA STRAP
This comes in a nice package with good instructions in it. The idea is that this helps stabilize the camera when you are taking a lot of photos. You can not have to grip the camera so hard so your hand does not get tired too. If you accidentally slip your grip, it does not crash to the ground.

This had a learning curve to it, but I finally figured out how to use it for me where it was helpful.

LENS PAPER
This paper allows you to clean the lens off gently wet or dry. The wet means that you use the Altura cleaning solution for greasy heavier prints.

PUFFER CLEANER
This is a rubberized ball that when you squeeze it, there will be a blast of air that will blow things off of the lenses. This works quite well when I get a particle on the lens so I don't have to touch it.

BRUSH
This is when the dust won't blow off the lens or other glass you can gently brush it and then blow it away with the puffer cleaner.

EMPTY BOTTLE
This is for alcohol or lens cleaner.

TRIPOD
This is why I wanted this kit the most. It has an ingenious design to it. It folds up flat and quite small, yet when you take it apart and tilt it, you can stand it up for close photos, or use it in your hand. It has rubber on the bottom to keep it put, and it also has a rubberized grip if you want to hold it. The camera platform tilts, but it locks into place which I love. This is working great for us taking close up photos of some of the small jewelry we are photographing. It has come in really handy.

What I love is that we can pick it up and use it by hand if we need another angle than the table top one.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This kit is a nice kit. I got it mostly for the tripod, but the cleaning accessories and the wrist strap make it really nice. The puffer ball is one of those things that you don't realize you need until you have it.- at least for me. The case is protective and easy to travel with.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. I am happy with this kit. It has worked better for us than I expected. We will be using this a lot in the future too.

IMPORTANT ADVICE... do not thread the mini ball head onto anything too tightly. This stand is actually fine, it's the cheap ball head that has given me headaches. The ball head has a... I'm not sure what the technical term is for this kind of bolt, but lets call it a "dual bolt." 1/4 bolt is threaded inside a bigger bolt, I presume 1/2. I threaded a mini projector onto this thing, I guess a little too tight. When I unthreaded the projector, the 1/4 bolt was stuck, meaning it was unthreading WITH the projector. So the 1/4 bolt came off the 1/2 bolt. You would think that all it takes are some pliers, but surprisingly, pliers even with teeth, have a hard time gripping this bolt. I had to use my drill press vise to get it off.

To properly use that ball head, you want to thread it onto whatever device you're using, but don't thread it on too tight like me. Then tighten with the lower knob. You might think, this reviewer isn't using common sense. I don't think so at all. Anybody would like his/her electronics threaded securely. The amount of strength I used was reasonable. The issue lies in that inner 1/4 bolt not being secured enough inside that bigger bolt. But I fixed that. Once I was able to unthread the projector from the vise... with the 1/4 bolt now free, but secured by the vise, I then took the ball head body to the vise and threaded the bigger bolt onto the 1/4 bolt a "wee bit" tighter than the manufacturer did.

If you don't have drill press vise like I do, then you better be extra careful using this. 3-Stars.

This USB-C hub worked well with my Samsung Galaxy Tab S6. I didn't have any issues using it.

Pluses
1. Great build quality
2. Aluminum case
3. Braided USB-C cable
4. 3x USB-A ports, 1x SD & Micro SD ports and 1x 4k/60p HDMI port
5. Plug and play; no drivers needed

Minuses
1. No USB power pass-through to charge a mobile device while using the hub
2. The USB hub draws power from the device it's connected to, limiting the number of devices that can be connected & used at any given time

I was able to plug the USB hub directly to my Samsung Galaxy Tab S6's USB-C. I connected a 32GB flash drive, a 128GB MicroSD card and a HDMI cable to the hub. The hub was instantly recognized by the tablet & showed the drives connected to it. I could browse the contents of both drives using Samsung's My Files app. Once I connected the hub to my Vizio PX 4k HDTV, the tablet's display was mirrored to the TV. Movies, TV shows and streaming videos from popular websites all played back flawlessly.

There were 2 downsides found while using the hub. The first one was not being able to charge my tablet while using the hub. The second one deals with using an unpowered hub such as this with mobile devices that provide limited power to their USB port. While the flash drive & SD cards worked fine during my use, I can see where higher power draw input sources can fail. My tablet only provides so much power, so it can't provide enough power for sources like unpowered external hard drives.

At first glance the Asus VivoBook V551LA-DS17T appears to be a nice touch-screen UltraBook-class computer, but it is a few steps beyond a typical UltraBook. Combining features of UltraBook systems and multimedia/entertainment workstations, this computer is what new systems ought to be. There are a couple of design decisions I would change and it's by no means a high-end gaming rig, but Asus got the important things right.

There are two things that set this system apart from a normal UltraBook. First is the inclusion of a slimline CD/DVD R/W drive. I have seen no other UltraBooks out there that include one, so finding one in this system was a very pleasant surprise. Carrying an external CD/DVD drive around can be inconvenient (especially when traveling) so having a built-in drive is a huge plus. Asus managed to include this drive in the system while still keeping the system to roughly an inch thick. The other differentiating factor that makes this system different than other UltraBooks I have seen (and not in a positive way) is the weight. This is a particularly heavy system and will make toting it around a chore.

I booted up the system and configured it for use and immediately went about looking for the utility for making recovery/restore DVD media. After searching the file system and the installed program list with no success I finally resorted to calling technical support. I spoke to a charming young lady who was exceptionally helpful and got me on my way to creating a recovery USB drive. So, from that experience I can say that technical support is courteous and helpful. However, I never did figure out how to make DVD media, but at least I can restore the system now should I have a need to do so.

After power-on for the first time it performed a bunch of hands-off updates and when it finished and finally allowed interaction with the OS it was loaded with Windows 8.1; it wasn't obvious if the initial OS install was 8 or 8.1 but that is irrelevant - 8.1 is what is there when the user can finally begin exploring the system. I spent a little time digging through the list of installed applications and was pleased to see that Asus did not load this system up with excessive bloatware. There are several applications I do not need and I intend to remove them - MS Office and McAfee protection services being among them - but at least what is there is not unreasonable. Interestingly, most new systems I have used have come with 1-2 years of internet security protection, but this system comes with just 30 days.

One design decision that really surprised me is that this system does not include a solid-state drive (SSD). I understand the reason - it drives up cost - but to me having an SSD in this system would make it even faster and make the battery last longer. This is by no means a deal-breaker but bootup times are slower as a result.

Asus makes a big deal about the touch screen on this system and touts it as more sensitive than most other touch screens. Asus' claims appear to be well-founded as the other touch screen systems available to me are nowhere near as responsive. After spending a couple of hours working with this system I unplugged my trackball and I don't think I will need it again for this particular system. If you are buying this system for the ability to use the touch screen, you will be pleased.

Battery life so far is excellent. I charged the system up completely and spent a good three hours using it for web surfing and typing up documents and the battery still maintains more than half of its charge. I plan to load up my development environment and see how the battery holds up under load, and I expect that to make the battery drain faster, but for typical use (surfing the web, writing document and watching online videos) the battery seems to be very much in the game.

The graphics system is provided by the Intel chipset and it is acceptable for most uses. It's not high end graphics but it's not terrible either. Serious gamers will not appreciate this system whereas most casual gamers and people using the system for more business-types of functions will be more than satisfied. As an experiment I had my teenage son load up Minecraft (an online game that uses 1st-person perspective) and test the graphics. He noticed that while the game played well enough it is not quite as smooth as a system that has a dedicated graphics card.

Wi-Fi connection speed seems to be about average with other wireless-n devices on the network.

One thing that really startled me is the quality of the sound system. Asus says that this is the best configuration for embedded sound available and I found the sound quality coming from the embedded speakers to be more than acceptable. The speakers are on the bottom of the unit and are visible via two inch-long slits in the case. In spite of the small aperture, the output is very good, better than one would expect.

With the slimline DVD and the decent sound quality, paired with the i7 processor and 8GB RAM this system is well-suited for multimedia tasks such as video production and music creation. It has the horsepower to handle the renders and so far has performed well while working on either audio or video composition. As I mentioned above I expect these types of activities to take more battery than less strenuous tasks but I have not spent enough time with these types of applications on this system yet to determine just how much they will impact battery life.

The touch pad is a bit better than average and is placed well. One issue I have with most laptops is that I tend to tap the touch pad while typing and on occasion I can highlight and delete a whole section of text unintentionally. So far this has not been a problem with this system and I think it has a lot to do with the way the touch pad is positioned relative to the open space on the keyboard. Asus includes a very nice utility (accessible by a special key on the keyboard) that makes turning the touch pad on and off very simple, so it's easy to eliminate any issue with it if it's "in the way" while typing.

The power adapter is odd and I am not sure I like it. The shape requires a little planning as it is a square block pressed against the wall when it is plugged in. Most adapters typically have the brick in the middle. So, plugging this adapter in when working in a cramped space could potentially pose a challenge. Another observation - the adapter gets rather warm.

I do not like the way the hard drive is partitioned right out of the box. It appears that the drive was simply chopped into two roughly equal partitions, the D: drive labeled as "data". I would rather have one large drive, instead of two smaller ones. This is a personal preference though and I am sure most will be indifferent.

I decided to toss in a Linux LiveCD and boot it up to see how well supported the touch screen is with a current distribution. The system refused to boot from it initially; to get it to boot I had to turn off Secure Boot in the BIOS after which I was able to boot up from the DVD. My distribution of choice for this experiment was Mint 16 with the Cinnamon Desktop. I found that there is basic support in place for the screen, though only as a standard pointing device (a lot like using a Wacom tablet) and not as a swipe and gesture interface. There are other distributions out now that are geared more towards tablets; I will try one of those and see how well it works out. That said, the fact that the desktop at least recognizes the screen as a pointing device and properly responds to it is a good thing.

A few other technical details: The system has 3 USB ports (two of them USB 3.0 and one of them USB 2.0), an HDMI port, an Ethernet port (which is not a given anymore when it comes to notebook computers), an audio out and a SD card reader. Given a choice I would have liked to have a VGA or DVI port to put the display on a second screen but that's not something I have seen on the most recent systems.

Asus has put together a very nice UltraBook-like system in this notebook. It's a nice workhorse for most uses and the touch screen is absolutely wonderful. The system's a bit hefty though and might prove to be cumbersome for those on the go, and the graphics system is not at serious gaming level, but the system is a solid performer and provides the best features of an UltraBook and a multimedia workstations in one place.

First of all, the signal quality is great over my 300' of CAT5e cable going from my entertainment system in front of my room to my projector around the back (cable goes behind walls and snakes around furnishings to get where it needs to go). It is fast and responsive, and the lag seems minimal if any. I love that it can also be used as a pass through, and that it only requires power on ONE side! My old HDMI extender required a power adapter on both the tx and rx side, but this can actually send power over the network cable (PoE) so that the other side does not need its own adapter. Now THAT's awesome!
This is one of the primary reasons I was interested in this, as there are two times I use such an adapter: When I use my projector instead of my TV for movies, and when moving a camera around at an event that I want to send a live feed back to a screen or streaming box for. Currently I have to supply power at both ends of the network cable, but I imagined ONLY needing power on the receiver, and having THAT power the transmitter. For example, in the case of the camera, I could have the screen receiving the signal send power to the transmitter by the camera using PoE and be somewhat more free of tethered power on that side. Also, when using the projector, I could turn on the outlet controlling the projector via remote and have it power on the transmitter behind the TV as well. Less wires and outlet spaces where already difficult / congested is good! THE PROBLEM, however, is that this thing misses its potential by only sending power from the TRANSMITTER! In other words, I can send power from the tx with PoE to the rx side, but the RECEIVER can't power the transmitter! It only goes the same direction as the HDMI signal. This, to me, was disappointing as that's the side I wanted to save from having more wires to plug in. Not the receiving side. That side is never an issue to supply power.
So I was a little upset about that. But otherwise, it is a solid product that seems to do what it claims to, and so far seems more reliable than my previous setup. If it could send power using EITHER side, it would be perfect! So close this time!
You definitely get your moneys worth with this one. If you’re on fence, go for it. So far my family and I have been enjoying this little projector which is perfect for our current place.

I live in a rural area and find myself in areas with no cell service frequently.  Radios like these can be a lifesaver if you get separated from your group and can't make a cell phone call.  I plan to leave one radio home for my spouse while I go hiking away from the cabin.  This radio has a few functions that are important to have.  First you can set your channel number and be sure to make it the same on each radio.  You can find a channel that sounds the best or just pick a number where you don't hear any other radio traffic (people talking).  In addition to the main channel numbers there are 0-121 tone codes you can select.  This code in addition to the channel number provides more confidentiality to your calls.  The channel and tone code it is set at out of the box is 01 and 01.  You can set the volume.  If you don't want to have to press the PTT (push to talk) button you can set it to Vox and you can talk without pushing a button.  You can still only have one person talking at once but lets say you were doing something where your hands weren't available, like rock climbing or kayaking, you could still respond to someone calling you are start talking and others will hear you.  You should also be aware that each channel may or may not be capable of transmitting under hi power.  For maximum power, use channels 1-7 or 15-22.  To get the most range, be sure that you are using high power mode on the channels that allow it.  If you are unclear what channel someone else is using you can put it into scan mode and it will cycle through the 22 channels until it finds a signal. Lastly you can get weather channels on this so if you are uncertain about incoming weather you can go to an active weather channel and hear the latest forecast for the area.  You can also setup weather alerts so an alarm will sound should a weather emergency be forecasted.  In summary, for the money, you get a lot out of these 4 radios and they will make any trip safer if you use them.

Looks like I have the privilege of being the first person to review the BA M25 speakers. I picked up a pair of these on Christmas Eve and have been playing them constantly over the past 2 weeks. My focus has been on 2 channel stereo recordings instead of movies. My set up is through an older Denon AVR 610 receiver that I have had for almost 20 years. I was initially impressed with the smooth, balanced feel of these speakers. Good mid range, nice high end, but not too bright, and a very strong bass response. The M25s defy their size in producing bass tones. Give them some break in time before making a final assessment. These speakers excel at producing music performed on real instruments. The do a great job on jazz, blues and acoustic folk styles of music. Vocals come across nicely as well.
Boz Scaggs "But Beautiful" CD of standards sounds great. Upright bass, piano and vocals make you feel like you are in a small jazz club. Diana Krall "Live in Paris" also plays very well. Nice piano, guitar & vocal reproduction. Jorma Kaukonen's "Blue Country Heart" CD showcases some great finger style acoustic guitar. Very natural acoustic guitar tones. Linda Ronstadt's "Winter Light" CD has some of the most powerful vocals you will ever hear and the M25s reproduce Linda's voice and backing instrumentation extremely well. The sound is never strained or harsh. Initially, I was a bit more apprehensive on some CDs with lots of bass. They sounded like they were trying to overcompensate on bass, but this has evened out over the past week. Eric Clapton's "Pilgrim" CD has come serious bottom end and the M25s produce very deep, tight bass response. Peter Gabriel "So" is a similar story. Deep, tight bass response that does not bottom out. Paul Rogers "Muddy Waters Blues" is a treat on the M25s. The opening track features some acoustic delta blues guitar, followed by a chorus of female backup singers and later some nice Strat blues guitar tones. It all sounds great on these speakers.
The look and finish on the speakers is impressive also. They are finished in a polished black exterior with a leatherette finish on the top, back & bottom. They look like a piece of fine furniture that would fit into a modern style of home décor. These speakers are very expensive though. I got a demo pair at less than half of the $399 per speaker list price. I don't think I would have bought them at full price. I have been listening to Boston Acoustics speakers for over 20 years. I still own a pair of A60s and a pair of A120s that have served me well over the years. The M25s have replaced the A120s as my primary speakers in my living room due to their sonic capabilities and their stylistic good looks.

Update 6/24/14 - After listening to these speakers for 6 months, I continue to be even more impressed by the Boston M25s. I bought these thinking they will do until I can find better. While there are better speakers out there, I have concluded, after many demo sessions, that I would need to spend at least $1500-$1800 or more to get some form of improvement over the M25s. Short of stepping up to KEF R300 @ $1800, B&W CM5 @ $1500 or Aperion Verus Towers, the M25s deliver the goods with very balanced & neutral sound, great detail in the upper register and sold bass. Highly recommended.

I use active noise canceling (ANC) headphones all the time and prefer them to normal headphones as I tend to work in noisy environments and I’ve found that with ANC engaged I can play music at lower volumes. I like Sony headphones so I was excited to try these ANC ear buds. They’re a bit unusual in a few ways but they work well and are worth their asking price.

These are truly wireless and have no physical connection between them. Power them both on and they find one another. They pair via Bluetooth to a phone, tablet or PC, and the connection is stable up to about 40’ around corners. This is a good start.

There are several modes to these when it comes to the ANC function and each has its uses. I usually just use full ANC without any of the ambient sound modes turned on as it gives the best music experience. One of the two ambient modes is optimized for speech and voice, the other for more generalized noise. Neither completely cut off noise canceling, but rather they allow different bands of outside noise to come through. In full ANC mode, these are good noise cancellers, though not as aggressive as some others like Bose.

These have proven to be comfortable, and they have the little wings on each bud for keeping them in place in your ear. I used them while working in the yard and never once did I have a problem with slipping or falling out, even though I have the wrong size silicone insert on one of them.

The sound is very good but I would stop short of calling it outstanding. The bass is heavier than I like though not so bad that it gives me a headache unless I pump the volume up too much. The midrange is warm and full, and the highs are bright and crisp without being piercing. The sound can be adjusted a bit in the app that you can download, as it has an equalizer of sorts that lets you tweak the levels or choose a preset.

Ah, the app… This is the primary downside of these. The method to adjust these is either an Android or iOS app, not a physical piece of hardware and there is no Windows equivalent (for those who want to use these with a PC). The app is a little clunky though fairly self-explanatory and it does do what it’s supposed to do. Given a choice between an app or an additional piece of hardware, I would choose the hardware.

These charge up in the carrying case, which has leads that connect to each bud. Pay attention when you put these in the case – it is possible to reverse them, and while it hurts nothing the charging doesn’t work well… The case has some sort of battery in it and it charges the buds without being plugged in itself, though it does require occasional charging. Charging is fast – I charged them from empty to full in about an hour. One thing that could be improved, though: the buds can be popped in the charger while still powered on, and the act of charging them does not make them cut off. So, you can end up with dead buds and a dead charger too.

These are decent wireless sport buds that have good sound and good ANC functions. They’re comfortable and not overpriced. There are a couple of areas for improvement, particularly in charging but also in the app control, that would make these even better.

When it comes to hands free devices, I am pretty particular about what I need to have handy. I like to have ear pieces like this handy when I am shopping or out doing errands should I need to receive important business calls. I also have to be available due to health issues of family members. Let's see how this one measures up.

WHAT IS THIS EARPIECE LIKE?
This hands-free earpiece is black. That does make it harder to find in a pocket of a purse or carry case. The outside of the entire unit is black.

LIGHTS
There is a green battery light on the outside and a blue bluetooth light on the outside when you turn it on. When you turn it off, the battery light turns to red so you know that is what you are doing with it. I LOVE this feature.

EAR BUD
The ear bud is only one size. There are three ear covers in this set. Two of them have an ear circle in them which allows you to wear it with or without the ear loop that hooks over the entire ear. One of them has no ear circle (the kind that fits into your hear cartilage).

EAR HOOK
There is one ear hook connected to this ear piece and then there is an extra in case you break that one. This fits around the outside of the ear hooking it into place for added security.

Mini USB
The charging plug on the outside is pretty uniform.

CORD
It comes with a 12 inch cord that goes from USB to mini USB for charging. You will need to have a receptacle to plug that into.

INSTRUCTION BOOKLET
Instruction book is minimal. This is a basic set which I LOVE. It is pretty straight forward. You turn on the phone, turn on the ear piece and they pair. Then to turn up volume, you press one side of the bar, down is the other side and muting is both at once. To hang up press outiside of earpiece.

BATTERY TIME
This thing stays charged a LONG time. I rarely have to recharge it, although I do not use it daily. It also holds a charge when not used for a long time as long as it it not left on endlessly.

RECEPTION/MICROPHONE
Here is where my review gets difficult. The first few times I used this, the caller at the other end complained because the sound was so bad. I was even told that the old handsfree speaker in my car was better and that was like a tin echo chamber.

I was all set to write my review, after all, it was pretty cut and dried. Then for some reason I could not write my review, and I had to use the earpiece to call someone again. WOW, the comments:

"I am so glad you are not using your ear piece, that thing was awful. Your voice has never sounded so clear."

"WOW, your phone is so CLEAR. I can not hear anything around you. Where ARE you?"

That second comment, I was shopping in a loud area. Now I had a dilemma. It was like I had two different earpieces! People were commenting on how wonderful it was now, but previously, these SAME PEOPLE could not stand it before. Nothing had changed. Same phone, same earpiece, same people.

So, I tested this quite a bit and the more positive feedback outweighed the negative, so I will say that this is a fantastic OMG marvelous earpiece sometimes and other times it is not as good.

STREAMING MUSIC
This is a decent earpiece for streaming music or programming on the phone, but I tend to use it more for temporary phone answering when I am not in my car.

COMFORT
This is not as comfortable as other earpieces I have had. I still prefer my older plantronics ear piece as it is so comfortable I don't notice it is in my ear after a while. This one is a bit too large. I actually prefer to wear it without the rubber cushion on it if I have to use it for any length of time. The ear hook helps it stay on pretty well. Once in a while I will use the rubber cushion and it is not too bad.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a solid performer as a hands free earpiece. It has potential to deliver fantastic phone calls much of the time, and once in a while not as nice, but it still works. For comfort, I have had better, but this is not too bad. It has extra pieces which I love, and the colored lights on it are fantastic.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is a nice solid hands free ear piece. Despite a period of time when I was not so sure, longer term testing brought out its good points and solid performance. I would get this again.

I've had several Amazon Basics' items since the line was introduced. Most have been quite good. Unfortunately this tripod wasn't one of them.

The feel is cheap and plastic-y. I wasn't expecting bearings in the pan-head but the plastic on plastic mechanisms are terrible.

I tested this item with my Kodak Z990 digital camera. It weighs approx. 21 oz. with batteries.

The camera mount has a good rubber pad for your camera to sit on and the tightening screw has a butterfly head so no screwdriver or coins are needed to attach/detach the mount from the camera. The mount attaches to the tripod with a spring-loaded release arm. There is actually very little contact area on the tripod itself (only two corners) holding the mount in place, also the release arm does NOT have a safety catch.

Pan Functionality - Fully tightened down I can still, with not much effort, swing the head from left to right. Fully loosened the motion is heavy and awkward easily upsetting the tripod's position. Tightening this knob fully actually interferes with the...

Tilt Functionality - The action is not much better here. You can lock the tilt angle into place and it does stay there. There's just as much plastic on plastic drag when in motion. The arm is generously long and comfortable to grip. The side-tilt mechanism goes reasonably easily from flat to 90°. It does not lock in place well.

Leg Functionality - The legs extend and retract with mild effort. They lock into place firmly. With just the larger leg section extended the tripod is fairly sturdy. Extending the smaller leg sections dramatically increases wobble. There is a weight/gear hook for added stabilization but it is plastic and feels easily broken. The swiveling rubber feet are innovative but only held on by friction and can easily become detached. The center stabilizer locks and unlocks easily with only a quarter turn and holds in place well. There is a serviceable carry handle attached to the leg mount section.

The tripod has two bubble levels. The first, a small button level is at the top of one of the leg mounts. The second, a tube level, is just under and inch long and is under and partially obscured by the camera mount. With a camera attached it becomes useless.

The center section extends and lowers via a crank mechanisms and locks in place with a plastic collar. There is no positive safety lock. Loosen the collar and your camera comes down rapidly on its own. Extending your camera this way will only increase the instability of this tripod.

The included carry bag reflects the quality of it's tripod. Its material is unpadded and thin. It has no extra pockets and the half-inch nylon shoulder strap is also unpadded making it rather uncomfortable to carry.

In conclusion... I wouldn't recommend this tripod even as a starter for someone just getting into photography it will only add frustration to the experience. Spend a little more and get a far better tripod or spend a little less and get something of equal quality.

I bought these primarily to use as studio monitors. I have or have had a number of high end cans over the years, Grado, Beyerdynamic, Sennheiser, Etymotic Research, etc.. however for recording purposes I have always preferred my AudioTechnica ATH-M40 due to their sealed design and extremely neutral response compared to most of the aforementioned cans which 'color' the sound in one way or another.

I've had the M40 monitors since they first came out in the early 90's and they were really starting to fall apart so I decided to look for a replacement. I was somewhat surprised by all of the praise for these Denon cans considering that last time I paid attention to the headphone scene Denon wasn't even making headphones. However, after looking at the response curves and reading all the glowing reviews from knowledgeable users on these and the D5000 series I decided to give these a shot as my new studio monitors.

Overall, I would say they live up to the hype. This is one of the modems that's on Comcast's recommended list for my cable system here in California. When the cable guy showed up to install my Internet service, he checked it out and said "It will work fine." After about an hour of pulling wires around my house, he hooked things up to the modem and I had very high speed Internet service. Pretty sweet.

I chose this model because its upload and download specs are well above what my cable Internet service needs, and because it has advanced features like IPv6. So I'm assuming they got the basic stuff right as well. Other reviewers have said this model runs hot, but I haven't observed that. I have it in my utility room which is in the basement where it's pretty cool to start with.

The lights on the front of the unit show what's going on, which is mostly useful as it boots up. They work well, and are also attractive to look at -- they had a good designer for that. The unit has only 3 connection ports on the back, one for power, one for the incoming cable, and one Ethernet RJ-45 out. If you want to hook up more than a single computer, you'll need to connect this single Ethernet port to a router, or wireless router. I have the cable modem connected into a 5-port NetGear switch downstairs, which is connected to an 8-port NetGear switch upstairs, which is then connected to my Linksys wireless router. My computers then use the IP addresses that the wireless router provides. (It won't work to plug additional computers into the switch that I connected directly to the cable modem because the cable company provides only one IP address. It's the wireless router that hands out additional IP addresses. Each computer that you're using requires its own IP address.) The wireless connection works well for my 2 computers and my Roku box for Netflix. (And the bandwidth available to Netflix is amazing. It spends virtually no time at all buffering before it starts streaming HD video.)

Oh, and of course I had to reboot everything (including the modem and the wireless router) for the new modem to be recognized. For now, I'm keeping my old DSL service as a backup Internet service. Not sure when I might decide to give that up.

This Cat8 is thicker than some due to the shielding within and additional insulation. This cable is made to withstand and holdup to exterior environments for the long term. The connector bases are reinforced at each end of the wire which really help hold all of the wires in place even if you have to bend and twist it to fit it within the plug. The connector plug itself is gold plated which is the ultimate standard in connectivity.

This Cat8 Ethernet Cable is 75’ long which makes it absolutely ideal for using it to directly plug your TV or gaming system into your router - even if located in a different room. So many of us stream programs and movies via our TV and there is no comparison in speed between a WiFi connection and a wired connection. For gamers, it is absolutely the way to go - do away with all lag caused by your WiFi by connecting directly to your router.

You will not find a better exterior grade Cat8 Ethernet Cable - this is really a top of the line cable that you’ll love.

Let me begin by saying that I am not gifted in the arena of art. I am more technically oriented and as such I use tablets in different ways than most people. For that reason, this is likely going to be a very different review than that of most others on here.

I use pen tablets for handwriting and as general pointing devices as I find them to be more comfortable than mice and trackballs. I started experimenting with tablets a couple of years ago with a Bamboo small, which worked well but was just too small for me. I then compared a Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch to an Intuos4 and it took no time at all to determine that for me, the Intuos4 was a much better choice. With the release of the Intuos5 I jumped at the chance to compare it to the Intuos4, and so far I like it but I have found a couple of things about it that are, in my opinion, less than ideal.

I am using an Intuos5 on a Core i7-based laptop with 8 GB RAM and Windows 7 64-bit.

The very first thing - installation. Installation was about as painless as could be. I plugged in the tablet, installed the drivers and I was able to start using my tablet immediately without any issue. That's a big plus right off the bat. I have had trouble with installs in the past, in particular with the Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch, so having a smooth install is a great relief.

There is one thing about the install that troubles me, though. This tablet is capable of left- or right-handed use, so by simply rotating the tablet it is easy for anyone to use it. However, unlike the Intuos4 the Intuos5 only has a USB plug on one side, and it's the edge that always faces away from the computer. This means that the cord will always run above or below the tablet when plugged in unless it's plugged in to a USB hub of some sort. Perhaps that is not a big deal to some, but to me it is a minor irritant. The included USB cable is long enough, though, that I can hang most of it off the far edge of my desk. I suppose it's a good thing that my desk faces the wall.

I immediately grabbed the pen and started writing, and what I have found is that the Intuos5 seems to be a little more sensitive than the Intuos4, which means I can write a little more softly and still get what I want from it. Wacom did a good job of adjusting the sensitivity to the pen and subsequently turning off the touch feature. With my Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch the pen had to be very, very close to the surface of the tablet before touch was disabled, and even then the tablet kept trying to zoom on me as I wrote. Not so with the Intuos5 - the sensitivity to the pen seems to be good up to about an inch from the surface, which is fine for my purposes.

The surface of the Intuos5 does seem to be a little rougher than that of the Intuos4, so expect the nibs to wear more quickly. Though it has more texture it still feels very natural to me and I have no issue with writing on the surface. That said, why make it rougher so that it eats the nibs faster?

While the buttons along the side are configurable, I don't mess with them. I do use the scroll ring though and it works well. It is sensitive to light touch and so far has given me no trouble at all.

For a good graphics test I brought up Corel Painter and did a little doodling. The tablet and Painter work together quite well. Painter was able to determine at what angle I held the pen and it allowed me to make nice strokes and then reverse the pen to erase without any hassle. I really have not tried to push the tablet through all of Painter's features (which would do a great job of showcasing what the tablet can do) but I did enough to convince myself that the Intuos5 is a strong tool for the really artistic individual.

The Intuos4 has a small, no-frills 3-button mouse where the Intuos5 has touch features that make it work like a giant laptop touchpad. This comes down to personal preference. I never use the mouse on my Intuos4 but the touch features on the Intuos5 are very handy and convenient. Others may find the removal of the mouse to be a deal-breaker.

So far, the handwriting recognition seems to be about equivalent to that with the Intuos4. I have had to adjust my writing habits because of my using tablets for this, so a lot of the retraining took place long before the Intuos5 came. The recognition software does a reasonable job of reading my handwriting but it still makes mistakes and requires more patience.

The Intuos5 is a really nice pen tablet. It is comfortable, it is sensitive and it has two modes for accepting input. I question why Wacom placed the USB port on the outside edge of the tablet, and I also wonder why the surface is more rough than the Intuos4, but of all the current tablet offerings on the market right now this one is the best. It's not perfect, but it does try hard. I'm satisfied.

I have worked with a number of trackballs, my most successful being a Logitech M570 which served me well for years. I finally wore it out and after some research I purchased the Logitech MX Ergo to replace it. I have had it about three days, and it has already proven to be exactly what I had hoped and more. It’s not perfect but it’s close.

I was attracted to the fact that it works both as a wireless mouse with a USB receiver as well as a Bluetooth mouse. I have two computers on my desk, one being a Windows 10 system and the other being a Linux (Arch-based) system. My old trackball worked with both though I had to move the receiver between the systems, so I went with the assumption that this one would also work with both.

I connected the trackball to my Windows system via Bluetooth and it has been flawless in operation. It connects without intervention and it works exactly as expected - all buttons work as they should and the operation is very smooth and predictable.

I plugged the USB receiver into the Linux machine, pushed the channel button on the trackball and it immediately started working on the Linux machine, even though it was still paired to the Windows system via Bluetooth. It works exactly as it should and I have had absolutely no issues with the trackball on my Linux installation. So now, I can switch back and forth between the two systems with the push of the channel button and without having to connect or disconnect anything. It simply works, and the switch-over is fast. The take-away for me is that I no longer need two mice on the desk.

I friend came over with his MacBook and there was no issue at all with connecting the trackball via USB. We did not try connecting via Bluetooth.

The trackball has a metal plate on the bottom that is held in place with magnets, and depending on how the plate is attached the trackball can be tilted to ease wrist strain. The plate serves another purpose too - it adds a lot of weight to the trackball. Even without the plate, the trackball is hefty and has some mass to it, but the plate just makes it even more so. For me that’s a positive; others may dislike the added weight.

One of the things I have missed has been a tilting scroll wheel. This trackball has one and I have been enjoying getting used to that feature again.

One thing I did notice is that there is no CD/DVD in the package for loading drivers. This isn’t a big deal, and it’s easy enough to get the drivers from the net. That said, the trackball just seems to work when you attach it, without any issue. For me it has absolutely been plug-and-play, on every system I have tried.

If I could change one thing - I would have made this trackball a little bigger. I have big hands and I struggle to find a trackball that’s an absolute perfect fit. This one is close. For the large majority of people it’s going to be spot on.

I am very happy with this trackball and have no issue with recommending it. It works great, connects easily, when connected to two different systems it switches at the press of a button, it has a bit of heft to it and the tilt is adjustable for wrist comfort. It’s really all I could ask for.

First off, for those of you buying this product expecting the e-ink experience, you are wrong. This isn't an e-ink screen, if that is what you are looking for, go with (a) the original nook, (b) the kindle, or (c) any of the other e-ink dedicated e-readers on the market.

This iteration of the nook is marketed towards certain select categories of readers:
-The Magazine reader
-Students with text books that have graphics
-Childrens' books with lots of pictures
-Comic book readers

If you notice, these are categories of readers that benefit from the ability of the reader to handle color graphics, which is something e-ink can't yet do!

PRICE
For the price, you are getting an android tablet with limited functionality, though, with some technical knowledge, it is possible to unlock this device to be able to fully take advantage of the android market (though it may void your warranty, so do it at your own risk). Similarly sized android tablets go for prices starting at double the price of the nook color, but they come with full functionality. Another device this has been compared to is the iPad- which runs at about twice the price as well for the very base model. On the price point, you are definitely getting a decent deal, though, you are sacrificing some of the functionality for the the reduced cost.

Also note, you are not getting 3G access or any other cellular service to access the market- unlike the original nook, that came with the free mobile access to be able to make purchases from the nook market on the go. The likely reason for the lack of mobile access is due to the fact that this device runs a lot faster and features a full web browser- this increases the speed and easy of the user to access web content- which would be undesirable to any phone service that hosts access because it would reduce the service that their paying customers get. Instead of mobile data service, users have the option of accessing the BN market and the full internet through wireless. With today's cell phone technology, many phones are able to be set up as wireless hotspots that users can use to get access on the go- when they are away from their home network. Overall, this isn't a big deal to me, but I am sure some original nook users depend on that free mobile service to get access to the BN market, so this would be a draw back for you for sure.

WEIGHT
Honestly, this device does run a little on the heavy side, however, I do believe that it is slightly lighter than it's predecessor. Still, for the e-reader market, it is heavy. For the tablet market, it is a little more reasonable. The weight is a sacrifice, but as long as you aren't trying to read while laying on your back, you should be ok.

USER FRIENDLINESS AND EXTRA FEATURES
I find this device to be quite simple almost immediately. Every function that I have looked for has been where I expect it to be and everything has worked smoothly for me. The page controls while you read work great, and I love that they now give you the option to tap to turn the page rather than having to swipe like you did with the last version of the nook.

The full web is pretty easy to use once you get used to typing on a touch screen keyboard (which is always annoying).

This device also integrates with your facebook, twitter, and google accounts. This is great for the avid readers that want to be plugged into their social media.

Another feature that is nice to have on the reader is Pandora- it is a nice added bonus to have internet radio available on the reader.

One thing I wish this device had was access to android market, but I guess you can't have everything.

OVERALL
I like this tablet. I think it was a good buy and I would buy another one if this one broke. For the price, you are getting an underpowered tablet, but it still has access to the full internet- which you can use multiple windows in. It is primarily a reader, which makes me wish it were as easy on the eyes as e-ink, but for the market it is being geared towards, you can't really complain about that!
