This is a tablet running a real operating system (Windows 10) hooked up to a small keyboard with a trackpad. And it's all right.

It's thicker and heavier but smaller than my 11 inch MacBook Air, which makes it more convenient in some respects and less convenient in others. The MacBook Air is a used 2012 model with a Core i5 and 4gb ram. It's snappy, but it didn't come with an SD slot, and used it cost about a hundred more than this. The quad core atom processor on the transformer book is pretty fast for a tablet, but it is definitely a lightweight compared to a core i5. Or even an i3.

My iPad Air runs iOS. Way less versatile than Windows 10 in terms of doing work-a-day things, having a browser respond the way you're used to having it respond, etc., but it's still pretty good. However, the keyboard experience is something of a pain, especially since there's no trackpad and you have to touch the tablet face to do the mouse-like things. And using the mail program is harder on the iPad than it is on a mac laptop or on the transformer book.

The transformer book is noticeably slower than either of the other devices, but I was able to do everything I set out to do on it. The Office apps are good and integrate seamlessly with the other Office installations on my other stuff. The screen is as nice as or nicer than my iPad Air. I had a MeMo for a year, and I loved the screen on that. This is very similar - excellent resolution, nice and bright, a bit wider aspect than what the iPad Air has.

The sound is about as good as one would expect. Which is to say, meh. But that's what headphones are for.

Cortano makes it easy to get set up. I asked it to find the apps I wanted. When I want something from the control panel, I ask for that. Since this is my first time with Windows 10, having the assistant helps a lot.

There do seem to be some battery issues. Charging takes a long time. There was an issue with the MeMos, as well, that I sort of resolved by fully cycling the battery a couple of times.

All things considered, I like this tablet/transformer book quite a bit. My only significant issue with it is weight. For my purposes, the ultralight notebook or the regular tablet will meet my needs on any given day. However, if you like your PC desktop and need, essentially, a shuttle craft, though. this is a pretty good compromise machine. It's a decent enough tablet. You can do business stuff, check email, surf the web, and watch movies. You won't be transcoding video or playing resource intense games, but this ultimately is a nice tablet with a keyboard. Not a desktop substitute. Maybe not even a laptop substitute, depending on your needs. But definitely a nice tablet.

UPDATE WITH USAGE ISSUES:

I was getting really annoyed with battery life/charging issues. My iPad Air will stand by for a couple of weeks, no problem, whereas this thing dies if I leave it off the charger a couple of days. It also needs its OEM charger if you intend to charge it within a few hours time, as opposed to overnight and then some. I was able to solve some of this by running task manager and disabling some of the high impact background apps (Microsoft OneDrive is a big offender). And, similar to my other Asus tablet, the battery charging problem seems to improve with conditioning. On the positive side, the more I use this, the better I like it.

Pros:
(1) It does the job. It's roomy -- in fact, it's really big. There's room for a really big graphics card without taking out any drive cages.
(2) Comes with four quiet fans (2 intakes in front, one large intake on the side, one exhaust on the back), and room to add more on the top.
(3) Having a couple of usb3 ports and audio/mike ports in the front is very convenient. Having the power supply at the bottom (in the back) also worked well for me.
(4) All the bits come apart and back together without too much trouble.

Cons:
(1) I had a lot of trouble getting my EVGA power supply to install, because the screw holes didn't line up nicely. Finally managed it by using a combination of power and adapting to what the case gave me.
(2) The 5.25 drive bays go in the conventional way, with the backs near the mobo for easy connections. But the 2.5/3.5 drive bays go in sideways, which might seem convenient at first, but now you have their connectors on the other side of the box -- so you're threading your power and sata cables around, and creating a bulge of cables etc. And that extra wiring room that the case promises? It doesn't extend all the way to the front, apparently the artists overcame the engineers (or they fought and the users lost). This arrangement also means that it's harder to share your sata power cables, depending on what you're trying to do with your setup.
(3) As others have pointed out, those nice intake fans aren't standard, they would be hard to replace individually. I'd have to replace all of them with standard case fans, I think.
(4) I wasn't as impressed with the cable management as many others were -- while it was useful to be able to run some wires on the back, that also made some of the shorter ones trickier to connect. Also, I find it easiest to place the box down on the side to work on the inside. Having to flip it over or keep it standing vertical wasn't my idea of convenience during assembly, and it made things really tricky when I wanted to add another hdd.

Neutral:
(1) An inexpensive mini-speaker (for POST beeps) would have been a good idea to include with the box.

All in all, I'm not unhappy enough to curse it, but I'm also far from recommending it. I'd look around more the next time, so 3* seems about right.

What a great thing, proper high-res PoE cameras like this one. I learned a while back not to care if the brand was generic, because all these things are from the same 4 or 5 OEMs. You can search for which pretty easily, although some of the really new "brands" like this one may not show up.

Regardless, this had the minimum specs (and also basically the maximum available) I wanted for my new home's camera setup, and it is also white, to blend in with the fascia boards it is mounted on. I got it up high enough into the recession on my porch roof that you can't see it from the sidewalk - at least if you're my height - but it can see you. And you have to be discreet in a nice neighborhood: I don't think people want to feel like cameras are a necessity. But you never know. And good theives would be scoping your property out ahead of time, so in my mind a purposefully discreet camera would say, "there are lots of security features here you probably don't know about".

Anyway, it works with my off-branded NVR, which I believe to be a Uniview OEM. I have it so the cables go into a hole in the fascia and the camera covers the hole (I was able to make a generous sized hole, thankfully, due to the large mounting plate (not too large, but basically the diameter of the camera). I really needed that larger hole to pull my cables (this is a very old house, so getting the cables run inside columns and underground and all hidden was really a feat).

It has what I'm not gathering is standard equipment on a good PoE camera - 3 cable ends - one for RJ-45, one for external power if you're not using PoE, and one for a reset button which I hope I won't need since it'd be a bit of a pain to get to.

If you can't hide your cables completely, you can also run them out the side of the baseplate. The camera is essentially infinitely adjustable with very large range. This seems basically the same standard design as all my old analog cameras from my last system on my last house.

I believe you can get this to show up on an app all by itself if you don't use an NVR, which is an awesome feature if you only have one camera or a few by the same brand. I'm also sure I can get this set up with my QNAP NAS if I wanted to, but when I played around with that on my last camera, I wasn't super-impressed (plus, I'm not about to pay for additional licenses on this stystem that is going to be augmented many times). Since I knew I was going to use the NVR, I just went right to it with this camera.

The NVR way sort of automatically makes a VLAN on your network so your cameras aren't taking up IP addresses and getting in your way. You can also set it up so it takes a regular IP address on your regular network and your NVR sees it and records over the network. There's less traffic eating up your other connections if you go straight to the NVR, though. Personally, I don't need a lot of IoT IP addresses obfuscating my network when I'm trying to track down a new device or other computer. But the variety and versatility of these setups is unmatched compared to DVR systems (although those are perhaps unmatched in their simplicity...but you can make the NVR thing as simple as you want to as well).

Anyway, I love the camera. Love the security. Love being able to see if I have a package. Love being able to see what cars are in my driveway. Love having great newage features on an old house.

We have a couple of other pairs of binoculars; one cost $300 and the other cost $100. This set is far cheaper that our others and you get what you pay for. On the plus side, I have a larger face and I have no problem focusing these binoculars despite what some other reviewers say. However, despite the binoculars having adjustable eye cups, they are not adjustable enough for me to focus while wearing eye glasses. I have to take my glasses off then adjust the eye cups all the way out to get a clear image.

In bright sunlight, these binoculars give me a reasonably colorful and clear but not especially sharp image. There is some distortion and chromatic aberration, even in the center of the image. In lower light conditions, like around sunset when the wild animals I want to watch are more active, these binoculars give me dim image with poor detail. All compact binoculars degrade quickly in lower light conditions, but cheaper ones like this especially so.

The field of view is advertised as 342 feet at 1000 yards. That number is printed on the front of the binoculars. However, in use the field of view is much smaller than our Nikon 10x25 binoculars that also advertise as 342 feet field of view. These Pronite binoculars are semi-sharp and clear over a much smaller portion of the field of view than our Nikon as well.

In summary, you get what you pay for. These binoculars are near the cheaper end of binoculars that I would consider usable. They are somewhat usable, especially if you don't need great clarity. These binoculars can help you figure out which way a road or trail heads through the valley ahead. They may not be able to distinguish one species of bird from another if you are looking at the shape and colors of the bird.

I needed a simple dock station to copy some hard disks. The All in 1 HDD Docking System fitted my needs nicely. I was able to insert an old Maxtor IDE drive in the first slot and a brand new SATA SSD in the second slot.

I had hoped to test the one-button copy feature so I powered it up and tried to follow the directions. Both drives were recognized, however I could not get the docking system to perform a drive copy. This could be due to either a brand new, unformatted SSD or due to the use of the Linux EXT2 file system (not FAT or NTFS). If I have a chance I will test copying between two FAT file systems.

With both the Maxtor and SSD plugged in, I added an SD card. I could mount the card and read the files from it, or copy files from it to either of the hard disks or to my system disk!

I tried using both a CF card and an SD card at the same time. However, I was not able to successfully access both at the same time. When I removed the SD card, I could read the CF card.

The device came with a short manual which was written in broken English. It was marginally useful and largely discussed how to use the PC Clone EX program that came with the docking device.

The docking system includes a USB hub. To test it, I plugged a Seagate USB hard disk into the USB port on the front. I was able to copy files from my camera's CF card to the Seagate USB drive. As a final test, I plugged a Maple Mini embedded ARM processor into the other port on the USB hub and uploaded an Arduino-compatible sketch. The USB hub works great!

Even a 2.5Amp charger won't really feed enough juice to charge all 8 rapidly, and most of my chargers / laptops / etc are feeding more like 0.5amp anyway. Those are much slower.

However, if you do heavy workloads like video editing, file transfers, etc,. where you are regularly moving large (15GB+) files around this is NOT the drive for you. If you are a “heavy” user I highly recommend the 860 Pro. It can keep up those high R/W speeds without slowing down after ~15GB. It will maintain full speed throughout the duration of whatever you are doing.

With that said this is a great drive for light/moderate workloads (gaming, web browsing, small work files, etc.,) and it is at a price that gives you excellent value and quality for your money.

I would’ve happily paid a couple dollars more for it and it wouldn’t have cost Samsung that much so they could’ve made a little bit of extra profit by adding it.

I still recommend this drive though and would buy it or the 860 Evo again if I needed more storage.

I polish metal specimens for aerospace testing so I know how to polish out scratches in plastics. This device might have accomplished that - if it had functioned. But the cheap construction plastic gears hidden inside did not seem to engage and so the disk did not turn. Also, the reversing switch did not work, in fact, it would just lock it if I tried to go counterclockwise. My kids even tried and agreed it was just broke when it arrived. (kids know these things, old guys not so much)

1- it didn't work and appeared to be non-repairable - a complete waste of $30.
2- the poorly written instructions and pictures were sized for ant-people to read.
3- They had spent way too much attention on [silly] appearance and not performance.
4- The product was ridiculously hard to extricate from the packaging which was wasteful with no apparent recycle symbols either.
5-IF I had gotten it to work, I would have needed more than a square inch of the buffing cloth they included. The blue non-woven cloth included had succumbed to degradation in the package and had holes and weak spots in it. Apparently it was degraded by the packaging plasticizes. And it was just way too small for a polishing or buffing job.
6- Apparently the marketers, designers or tech development team did not understand that keeping a wet polishing compound on the disc is the secret - so apparently they did not know they could have just made a tray on the disk holding the CD, to contain liquid and help users out. I feel like it was just designed to look like a gee whiz thing and get your money, not really concerned about whether or not it really worked. Save your money. Instead, buy polishing rags and buffing compound from outfits that do this sort of thing for a living. You will very likely be happy and for a much longer period of time.
Polishing plastic is not that hard, but it is NOT EASY either, because it takes a lot of patience and some properly applied buffing compound and elbow grease. IT TAKES A LITTLE TIME no matter how you do it. This device is trying to make you think it is physically and temporally easy. No magic machine exists that can polish without some work. We use polishing machines where I work, and it takes a LOT of time and effort, even when mechanized.

I think that maybe the product COULD have worked, but I doubt if the company leader-persons who oversaw the packaging and function decisions that dragged it's quality and capability down are accountable for their poor decisions. It definitely does not work as delivered. Look elsewhere when you need to restore and polish a scratched disk.

I am an audiophile who is determined to get great sound without spending large amounts of money.  It is esy to get world class sound if you are willing to spend over $5,000.  I will never do that, however.  In the 1970's, I worked part time in two high end audio stores -- hence I know what good sound is and is not.  I was interested in the Motion 4's because they are Martin Logan speakers and Martin Logan has been a leader in producing remarkable speakers for decades.  And I was interested because of the technology employed in the Motion 4's. I got a pair of the Motion 4 speakers about one week ago after auditioning them three times at my local Best Buy. In the store, they sounded far superior to any other speaker even close to their price range.  Once I got them home, they sounded even better as I hooked them up to a Denon 3805 receiver.  I got the 3805 used for $200 after doing much research on receiver performance vis a vis 4 ohm speakers -- which the Motion 4's are.  This is a big deal -- matching you amp to your speakers -- since there are many amps that simply fall apart sonically under 4 ohm speaker loads.  Many receivers won't even rate their output into 4 ohm loads because of their embarassing performance. This particular Denon receiver, however is a throwback in terms of build quality and handles 4 ohm loads exceedingly well. The Motion 4's are not big speakers but they will fill an average sized listening room quite nicely. There is not much low end but that did not surprise me and it wasn't needed since I have a subwoofer. The midrange and the high end, however, are nothing short of glorious.  They are spacious and very open and incredibly detailed. I absolutely was hearing more and better sounds than I have heard in years. The folded tweeter -- a smaller version of the incredible Heil Air Motion transformer of 30 years ago -- clearly is amazing. Any high frequency -- cymbals, pianos, acoustic and electric guitars, etc -- simply come to life with a sense of immediacy and aural acceleration lacking in any other speaker near its price range and size.  The only possible reason anyone would find these speakers lacking is if you installed them in a very large room that they couldn't possibly fill OR if you hooked them up to an amp that could not handle 4 ohm loads -- and beware, there are a lot of amps out there that have this problem.  Otherwise, buy the Motion 4's with confidence.

I am so very pleased with these headphones. I was expecting them to sound pretty good given the Sennheiser lineage, but they really set me back on my heels with the sound quality, comfort, and overall design.

Let's start with the easy one - how they look. To my eye, they are very nicely styled. Classic-looking rather than flashy. I especially like how the headband is not excessively padded -- it does not stick out when you wear them. Very elegant overall. Everything looks and feels high quality.

They also hit the mark regarding comfort. I usually have a 1 hour limit when it comes to over-the-ear headphones, in that after an hour of wearing them I've reached my limit of tolerance. These, however, felt wonderful. They are light enough that I hardly noticed the weight. More importantly, the ear cups fit me just right. Cushy enough to seal out ambient noise but not at the expense of having my ears feel like they were trapped in a vice. They felt just as good well into hour 2 as they did in the first 15 minutes. I found the headband also very comfortable for long stretches without getting "sweaty head" as I get with other headphones.

But it's the sound that counts. To my ear, these `phones deliver in spades. I started off with some Stanley Clarke. Wonderful -- ample bass but not at the expense of hearing every string being plucked. I listened to School Days a couple of times in a row, just amazed at how good it sounded. The same for Florence and the Machine -- solid, deep bass but not overwhelming.

Next up was Metric to see how vocals come through. Again, superb. I was finally able to figure out some of the lyrics on Synthetica that never came through clear enough on my ear buds. Regina Spektor was also an absolute pleasure to listen to and have all facets of her unique vocal styling come through so clearly.

I also tried them for movie watching on my Fire, and again was very pleased. Dialog was clean and pronounced; explosions were, well, explosive.

The noise isolation is quite good. These are not noise cancelling headphones, so some ambient noise will leak in, but it keeps out everything other than the most significant ambient sounds.

I really can't fault these on any criterion. They look great, feel great, and sound great. Granted, the price is not so great, but good quality costs. If you're a demanding headphone user, these are worth the money charged. Highly recommend.

This weird little tripod is a useful addition to the gear of any amateur or hobby photographer with a DSLR and the inspiration to take breath-taking and/or unusual photographs. (I'm using it with a Nikon D7000)

Pros:

1. Light and portable. If you don't have a side pocket on your camera bag, just wrap it around a strap or loop.
2. Flexible. As advertised, the legs can be bent into loops and angles for getting shots from weird angles. It can also be wrapped around posts, tree branches, bench rails etc.
3. Convenient. An easy way to get shots requiring a stable camera almost level with ledges or sideways attached to a tree. However, you can only shoot in landscape format unless you get the accessory BH1 ball head. Naturally, with its little legs, you'll be pretty close to the ground if there's nothing available for wrapping around, but you'll be sure to get great camera angles from a worm's eye view.

Cons:

1. Attaching your camera to the tripod is a bit of a pain, requiring a coin (any currency) or a strong fingernail. A better bet is to get the accessory Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level and attach the quick release clip to your camera beforehand.
2. You need to practice with it a bit to get the stability right, and if you have the legs in an unbalanced position, or on a smooth surface, you can get sagging and camera movement.
3. Trying to get the camera level without the ball head can be quite challenging, and you may well miss the shot. (Of course you can always do the straightening with software, but it's better to get it right the first time.)
4. Can't shoot in portrait format unless you get the ball head.
5. Hard to get the legs back straight with all the segments in line.

Note: It comes with a 1/4-to-3/8-inch adapter attached to the mounting screw, so you have to remove this to attach the camera or accessory ball head.

Recommended (with the [[ASIN:B002CVU4G0 Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level for Joby GP3 SLR-Zoom Gorillapods]]) for photo walks, theme parks or general walk-abouts where that prize-winning shot may be just a Gorillapod away.

But then the remote did not seem to work. Fine, I'll just use the controls on the player, right? WRONG. The only option on the player is the play/pause button. So if your DVD has a menu that starts with the cursor over play, that's fine. But if you need to navigate the menus at all, you're out of luck without the remote working. There is no D-pad or any other obvious way to get the cursor to move.
But then I thankfully read another review here that described not getting the remote to work unless it was in direct line-of-sight with the TOP of the player (as if mounted to a wall in the picture- basically it isn't just that it CAN be wall mounted, it is designed to ONLY work properly in that angle!). Well folks, it does work if only in that exact scenario, which is kind of boggling. If this gets used in a classroom or senior center, the experience will not be intuitive without being told you have to hold the remote in a very specific orientation for it to work. I've never seen an IR remote that was so picky... usually if you point a remote at something nearby the sensor, it will still pick it up. But I guess the placement of the sensor here makes it very narrow, and to me that seems like an odd design flaw.

3 stars because it DOES work once you figure out how, but it is really not intuitive out of the box to expect others to use.

It had no problems working with my Alienware M17xR4 with AGA, The AGA has an ASUS Rog Strix 1080 Ti in it with 2 27" Monitors and a 55" TV attached to it. I was able to add a fourth monitor using the DP on the USB hub, but the 4th monitor also worked through the video card as well. It took a little load off the graphics card but seemed to slow down the system a bit. It's kind of like using the internal monitor on the laptop when docked. Data transfer rates were higher then expected even when using multiple ports at once. This is also the first USB C hub that I have found that allowed a second USB C hub to be installed on a different USB C port. Not sure if it's designed that way or just luck though. Usually both are not detected only one, but for some reason I am able to connect both and that's how it should be considering that was the goal of USB in the first place.

Overall this is one of the best hubs I have owned to date. It adds a lot of functionality for a good price. The Micro-SD and SD card readers are easy to access and use. It's very user friendly and required no real setup even in my advanced environment. That kind of shocked me to be honest. It even works with virtual machines when configured. I've been using a Keurig machine for several years -- I currently own 2 of them. But I've always had an ethical issue with all the little plastic cups that get tossed into the environment. To that end, I've tried and used several different varieties of reusable K-cups, and had finally settled on the Ekobrew cups.

I was offered an opportunity to try this set, and decided to do a side-by-side comparison. The results were interesting. These Brewooze cups perform just as good as the more expensive Ekobrew cups.

I tried several different coffees and several different grinds. As with all reusable cups, you have to be careful how fine/coarse the grind is. Too coarse, and you get weaker coffee; too fine, and you get either overflow and/or sludge. I found that a medium-fine grind worked best for both cup brands. This way, I get the right strength and almost no powdery sludge in the bottom of the cup. One advantage of the Brewooze over the Ekobrew: I was able to use LESS coffee in the cup to get the right brew strength. With the Ekobrew, I needed to fill the cup; with the Brewooze, I filled it about 2/3 full to get the same flavor/strength.

As with all reusable K-cups, you need to take care when you seal them prior to use. These are no trouble to seal correctly -- you can easily see if there are gaps and do an extra "squeeze." Inserting them into the machine takes a bit of attention, too -- otherwise, you can pierce the cup. There are arrows on the lid that show which direction, so that shouldn't be a problem.

This set comes with 20 paper filters plus a replacement charcoal filter for the Keurig filter wand. I didn't see much advantage to the paper filters except possibly ease of cleaning. The coffee was weaker, and using a finer grind didn't seem to help. And it still resulted in some grinds getting "around" the paper filter and onto the mesh, so I still had to clean the cup. It's not a big deal, really -- the cups are easy to rinse clean after use. So I won't be using the paper filters, but you may find them useful.

I'm a little surprised at how nicely these performed, given the price. You get 3 cups (brown, medium tan, and light tan color -- the photo makes them look orange, but they're more of a tan/brown), so if you want to assign a color to different family members, there you go. Since I usually brew 2 cups into a large mug, I just fill 2 of them with the same coffee and run them one after the other in the morning.

kI have to say I was impressed. I didn't expect these to perform as well as they did. Definitely comparable to the Ek​​​​obrew so far -- the only question I have is durability, and only time will tell. I've been using these for about 4 days, and after the initial side-by-side test (when I brewed about 12 cups total), I've been brewing 2-3 cups every morning, rotating them, cleaning after each use, and so far, no signs of any wear problems. If I notice a serious issue, I'll update this review.

The UPRIGHT SMART WEARABLE POSTURE TRAINER is an "anti-slouch" posture trainer that really works! I discarded my [[ASIN:B00N9P8GMW Lumo Lift]] after a week or so, because my sitting posture is pretty good, and I rarely slouched badly enough to trigger the Lumo Lift. In contrast, the Upright buzzes me whenever I start to relax my posture even partway to a full slouch.

The Upright needs to be pasted to your back with gentle adhesive pads (60 included), rather than pinned to your clothing (like the Lumo Lift), but the greater sensitivity makes the extra effort worthwhile. Packets of one-time-use adhesive pads are available from the Upright web site for about $15.

You can wear the Upright between your shoulder blades if you're going to be standing, walking, and sitting; or at the small of your back if you're an Upright novice or generally sitting. As long as it's turned on, the Upright works even without the accompanying app (Android or iOS) that tracks your training progress. The Upright app uses Bluetooth to connect with the wearable Upright.

The app walks you through the simple setup, which mostly involves (1) finding the proper spot for placement on your back, and (2) calibrating the device so that it can detect a slouch. Once it's calibrated, the device will gently buzz you whenever you sink into a slouch--which inevitably happens as your muscles tire from holding a single position--so that you can straighten up. (There is no sound. The product page video that demonstrates the buzz is kind of amusing.)

When you create an account (free), the app collects information about your height, weight, and age, and then generates a daily posture training program that is personalized for you. The training program begins with your wearing the device for a few minutes, and then for longer and longer sessions. At the end of a session, the app gives you a score, based on how long you held your upright posture. (Mine was only 86%, because I intentionally slouched to test the buzz.)

The Upright arrives fully charged. The app tells you how much charge is remaining in your Upright. When you're charging the device in the supplied charging dock, a solid red light tells you that it's properly connected and charging.

Arlo is not perfect, but it is wicked close.

What's Great: You can put it anywhere within range of the link/router. The alerts are reliable, if a little slow on the uptake. The picture is good. Set up was simple and worked the first time. A reasonable amount of cloud storage is free, and it's easy to download whatever you want to save. The cameras are easy to move around to wherever you need them, and you don't have to set them up again.

What's Okay: A person who walks fast can get through a room almost faster than Arlo can start recording. Now, it's still much faster than an old Belkin Netcam HD, which sends pictures of where the motion WAS. Before the picture. And the D-Link 930L, which is a fine monitor cam, but has never been able to send a snap or a clip, no matter how many times it has been set up to do that. However, both of those cameras have audio and stream reasonably good images via their apps (the Belkin video resolution is way better than the Dlink). That makes them okay monitors next to smart security sensors - if the sensor alerts, you can look to see what tripped it and listen to see what's going on. Arlo will - most of the time - catch whatever set it off and let you know within seconds. And it's free, not an extra $$$ feature.

What Could Be Better: The link thing is enormous. It could be a little less expensive. And it would be WONDERFUL if it integrated with Z-Wave or Smart Things. The plan here is to station the Arlo cams near other devices that send push notifications - Nest Alarms, Smanos smart sensors, etc.

How It Compares: Beats the Canary I couldn't get to activate. Way better than the other netcams in the house. Love it. Just added another camera.

I bought this so I could play Blu-Ray movies on my computer or my laptop.

Interestingly enough, the drive itself seems to be recognized by Windows, and Windows can actually see the files on the discs, so the drive seems to work in that respect. However, the drive comes bundled with an older version of CyberLink's media playing software (PowerDVD 12), which is supposed to be able to play Blu-Ray discs.

However, the software just doesn't want to play Blu-Ray movies. I popped in "The Equalizer" and it showed me the thumbnail icon for it, but when I tried to play, it just took me back to the home screen of the PowerDVD 12 player. I tried updating the software with no luck, and I tried it on a different computer that is almost brand-new, and got the same results. I even installed CyberLink's "Advisor" tool that analyzes your system to see if there are any items that could cause issues with playing such content, and it told me everything passed.

From what I've read, it sounds like you need to constantly upgrade to newer versions of PowerDVD (up to version 15 now, which is an extra $99 upgrade fee) in order to play newer movies.

So while this might be a good drive for data-driven usage of Blu-Ray discs, just be aware that the packaged software is just too old to be useful nowadays. You'll need to account for another $99 upgrade charge to watch more recently-released movies unless you already have a newer version of that software.

As of today, if you can find a version of PowerDVD that is version 13 or 14, the upgrade fee to version 15 is $49, I think, so the included version is just one version too old.

It's unfortunate, since the drive itself seems like a really nice piece of hardware. It's very convenient in terms of being able to be plugged in, it's very small, and seemed very quiet, too.

I have waited a while to review this because I got it for my daughter who was very interested to have it, but after a while, she lost interest so it was back to me. Let's take a look.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?

EAR BUD JACK

MUSIC SEQUENCE
That is another odd feature of this player. This will play in order when I have albums in it and so far they play in alphabetical order which is rather strange. RECORDING BUTTON
This has some storage on it, so you can record with the little red recording button. That can come in handy if you need it, but I don't use it much. It works.

SPEAKER
This has its own little speaker on it which is handy for using the auto alarm function if you are camping or something and don't want to use your phone for that.

AUTO ALARM FUNCTION
This will wake you up if you want it to.

FM RADIO
This works pretty good, but again, the jack is toast, which is part of the antenna grounding the signal, so in my case, it is good but not WOW.

INSTRUCTIONS
This really is frustrating. This should have extensive instructions in it. This thing is really frustrating despite it being almost user friendly in some ways. In others it is downright frustrating.

BATTERY LIFE
The battery life on this is great. If not in use for a long period, it will keep the charge nicely, a feature I appreciate.

TOUCHY TOUCH SCREEN
This bottom half with the touch screen is very touchy. If I have it in my pocket and it hits my body just right, it will change to another song. Sometimes it will go to another direction if I put my hand in my pocket which is frustrating. That part is also difficult.

BLUETOOTH
This is a great feature. I had no problems hooking this up to my bluetooth headphones at all. It was easy and stayed connected, but I am at home when I use this and not around other wireless items, so I am not sure how well this would work when around other devices.

WHO MIGHT LIKE THIS?
If you are in need of some music and don't want your phone handy and feel like it does not matter what songs you hear in what order, then this might be a good mindless device for running, or working around cleaning, etc. It also might be nice for a young person who is not supposed to be using their phone and you want to give them something else to play music with.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For the price, the music quality is fantastic, the bluetooth connection is also very easy and one of the best I have used. As for other things like the music order, lack of instructions, and super touchy controls, this takes the fun out of using it.

MY RATING
I am between 3 and 4 stars for this. I am going with FOUR STARS. It is BARELY four stars though. The bluetooth and music quality are excellent. The screen is also decent too. The price is right. However, the other frustrations and lack of instructions frustrate me a bit. I am sure there are ways to put the music on there, but I just don't have the time to mess with it. Kids would probably have a lot of fun messing with this and making it do all sorts of amazing things.

Very nice high quality item, but you're sort of left in the wind to figure things out yourself. Here are some things to note, so you don't encounter the same issues as I did.

-The app to download is called PRINT MASTER. You'll naturally want to download Phomemo app, but you'll soon realize it won't connect with your printer. Then you'll notice there is a specific Phomemo 110 app, so you download that as well. But after installing this app, a pop up says "we are discontinuing this app, please download PRINT MASTER." There, I saved you from the run-around I encountered. LOL!

-You are given a starter roll of labels, but to use the templates in the Print Master app, you'll need to choose the proper dimension. It would be nice if this info was given in the manual, but the manual doesn't even mention the free roll. Everything is in mm, but I happened to have a mm ruler and measured the labels to be 40x30mm.

-Lastly, the most important advice you need to know is you need to turn on AUTOMATIC. You might ask AUTOMATIC what? My reply is.. EXACTLY. LOL! You see, once you go to print your label. There is a setting called AUTOMATIC. There is no explanation as to what this means. The default is WHITE, which is OFF. What it means is where it will stop after it prints your label. If it's OFF, it will NOT stop. It will continue spitting out blank labels. I saw a YT reviewer who had this issue, and I didn't think anything of it, until it happened to me. LOL! You need to turn this to GRAY, which is ON. It will then automatically stop after it prints your label. Why in the world is the default set to continuously print blanks? We all tend to use default settings because we trust the manufacture knows what's best for us. I mean why would you turn something on if you don't know what it does? So I can see why many make this mistake. But now you know. Turn it on! Even if you need multiple copies, for example 5 copies. You still need to turn it on, so that it will stop after 5 labels. I would love for someone experience with these things, or the seller, to comment below what that setting is for, and why is the default off?

The Asus has a sleek look with its silver brushed metal lid and slightly rounded sides. Between this and it being JUST under 5 lbs, it makes for an easy transport if you want a laptop to carry around.

The touchscreen has a sleek design with a black outline around the active screen that frames the look of the screen nicely. If you put pressure on the top of the laptop lid it does not affect the screen at all which tells of the durability of the laptop casing. The touchscreen has very nice vibrant display graphics that allows it to be seen easily from various angles without too much glare.

The visuals of the screen are great, which make for impressive video viewing. Picture is great and graphics are very crisp whether it is a Powerpoint still picture on display or a movie. The audio is great, too. While not a gaming pc, this is a nice one for video/audio usage.

It is a very thin and elegant design. The DVD multi recorder fits nicely along the side panels along with three USB ports, a microphone jack, SD slot, network slot and HDMI port.

The grooved out design around the touch pad is a small detail that has a nice impact on the overall look of the keyboard and touchpad (the touchpad is a bit of a different design with the 'clicks', but honestly, at this point with various keyboards for various devices, I'm used to things being different and just roll with it. But FYI to buyer). Keyboard is nicely laid out with light/'chiclet' touch keys and touchpad is sensitive without being too touchy. Considering that I also have a Asus Ultrabook S500-CA with a twitchy as heck touchpad OOB, this is a welcome relief.

Battery life appears to be great as well. I had the machine in hibernate for approx. 6 hours after machine was fully charged and the battery was not even down past ½ charge after all that time. And while in use, it does last about 6 hours. Considering the size and weight, that's pretty good.

Now for some negatives (or at least not so greats).
Fan vent is on the bottom which can be seen as a negative to anyone that works with the laptop sitting on their lap. I would imagine that the fan would be blocked in this instance and would not function properly and possibly allow machine to overheat? Gonna need a cooler for this one while using it for any length of time.

No SSD at all?

It barely comes in under 5lbs. As stated, I also have a ASUS Ultrabook S500CA, which is a 15" screen and weighs less. It also doesn't have a DVD drive, so.... You're definitely adding weight here for that and a few other options (and losing USB and other ports).

No full Microsoft Office Suite/software (you'll have to pay to get more than a trial version or use something else). Just making that clear. - edited as before I had stated 'Windows'. Sorry for any confusion.

All in all, this is a responsive laptop with impressive visual and audio that can be useful to an everyday user. It probably has some drawbacks to someone needing serious processing (no SSD), but for a lot of users, this one is good. I like ASUS, I find them to be reliable laptops, their designs tend to be good, and this ultrabook is no exception.

For everyday use, I'd give this 4.5 -5 stars. Anything else, take off a star or two.

If you've been using a "free" router provided by your ISP, this Linksys router will give you some interesting additional features not found in the freebies. A guest mode lets you create a separate network with a separate password and access to the internet, but not to other devices on your network. A USB port lets you connect a hard driver or printer that can be accessed by any device on your network. Parental controls let you limit access based on time of day or web address.

There are supposedly performance optimizations based on media prioritization and beam forming, but I have no way to test whether those actually work or not. I had no problems with connectivity and performance, though my home is not really large. Media prioritization supposedly allows you to give higher priority to selected devices on your network, which could be useful if for example you want to allocate a lot of bandwidth to streaming video and less to other uses.

Setup and configuration is always an issue with network devices. Make sure you access is using a generic DNS setup or you will confuse the setup process. Once I figured that out, the setup went smoothly. The setup makes you create a Linksys account to manage your router remotely. Network control is nice since you can login from anywhere to manipulate your router settings; but if someone hacks into the Linksys server, you could be in trouble. There is an option to disable network access in the settings.

The main issue I have with this device is that the configuration software is too simple. Simplicity is good for people with only basic computer skills, but it also leaves out a lot of things that more advanced uses will want to do. For example, the guest SSID is your main SSID with "-guest" appended; there is no way to create a custom SSID for guests. Also, the USB port sometimes work for me and sometimes not. Rebooting usually got it to work, but that is a big hassle. This is a cheap way to store music and videos on a central hard drive, then play them on any computer on your network.

I bought these on impulse because 1) they were Klipsch, 2) they were "noise isolating" and 3) they were on sale. $30. Sorry to say they aren't worth half that.

They are NOT noise canceling. They are noise "isolating" because they are the ear bud design that seals into the ear canal, like millions of other ear buds. Nothing special. Any descent set of silicon earbuds will do the same noise isolation.

I knew in 30 seconds these earbuds lacked any low end. No bass at all. The specs say they go down to 12 Hz. Hah. No way. The music is simply not full and rich. The highs are excellent, but with no bass, the music is really thin.

I'm amazed how many reviews say how nice the music is. My throwaway Creative earbuds are much fuller and more sensitive.

With the S3's I have to turn the volume up more and there's still no bass. I would consider this somewhat dangerous. You crank up the volume to get more bass and you burn your ears out with the excessive treble.

I tried all three sizes of earbuds, too, just to see if it was a sealing problem. But no matter which size earbud I tried, the music sucked.

I tried all the EQ settings on my iPhone 4. None added any noticeable bass. Maybe it's an impedance mismatch

This concerns me about other things Klipsch.

I did like the way you can turn them upside down and drape the wires over you ears to hold them in place for running, but I didn't actually try them before putting them away. Might work. Might not. My initial feeling with any of the bud sizes is that they tended to fall out of my ears.

Strangely, the buds that came with an old Creative MP3 player are far superior.

If I had paid the full $49 for these things I would be really upset.

I picked this router up at another online retailer as soon as I spotted it was on sale. I had my eye on the Tenda 1800/1801 routers for a while before that though, as these seem to be the only decent Gigabit / AC routers that are directly compatible with Tomato right out of the box, that don't break the bank!

My router is essentially the same thing as the much more expensive ASUS RT-AC66U, but with less memory. Having less memory on a router is not really the same thing as less memory on a computer. In other words, most people (including myself) will not notice the difference.

Hardware Look and Feel:
This Tenda sports the basic router design, and includes wall mounting screw holes that are 6” apart, and 3 movable antennas that are easy to install. There is lots of good ventilation on the sides and bottom, and a glossy white top. Altogether, the router seems will made, and doesn't feel cheap at all. Glad to say that it doesn't have a gimmicky cylindrical shape, or a stupid upright design, with an even more stupid non-adjustable plastic stand. I don’t mind at all that I can't take selfies next to my neat looking stylish black router to post on Facebook; Boring routers are just plain under-rated!

Stock Firmware:
I spent about 5-minutes poking around in the stock firmware before flashing to Tomato. To me the stock firmware seemed like an unpolished version of Asus firmware. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but why settle for stock when there is a specific version of the very stable, configurable, and admired Tomato USB written just for routers just like this! Enter Shibby K26RT-AC...

Tomato Flashing Process:
No feverish searching the internet for firmware “that will work” with your router, simply go to the Shibby download page, find the latest version for your router, download the compressed file, and unzip it.
Then unplug your WAN cable, open your routers firmware page, go to tools, upgrade, navigate to the folder your just unzipped, select the .TRX file, click upgrade, and wait about 10 minutes. Once it is done, you might want to do a factory reset in Tomato to clear the RAM.

That’s it people, no messing around with cumbersome flash utilities, no 30/30/30 resets in restore mode while holding your nose and saying the alphabet backwards in Pig Latin while crossing your fingers that you won’t brick your router. This one is as simple as it gets!

I've had the pleasure of using and reviewing a lot of different mini PCs, so I have a pretty good baseline of what they should be capable of. This is definitely upper level for the price.
Generally, you should expect these to be somewhere around a budget laptop in performance, but I'm happy to say that this one actually exceeded my expectations! The 11th Gen Celeron actually outperforms a lot of laptop level processors, and is faster than almost all of my other mini PCs I've tried! Combined with the 16GB of DDR4, Windows 11 feels like more a breeze than it has any right to be at this size and price point!

This thing will zip through most basic computing tasks, or stream video like a champ. Don't expect much GPU performance, but if retro gaming is your thing, this is more than enough- in fact, a great deal faster and more powerful than most of the stuff out there people use for that task (Raspberry Pi, etc). The only thing I'm disappointed about, is the lack of USB-C. I mean, to be fair a lot of the mini PCs on the market inexplicably omit it as well, but it just seems like once we're on 11th Gen CPUs and Windows 11, why on earth are we still skimping on the most versatile connection port in existence currently?
It is so close to being perfect, but if you want a small footprint HTPC or digital signage setup, or just a way to turn any existing TV into a more-than-capable PC, this is a hard value to beat!

USB hubs are one of those computer extras that don't get a lot of attention or thought until one runs out of ports. When needed, though, a hub can greatly expand the USB capabilities of a system. This particular hub is one that comes with its own power supply, which is in my opinion better for most uses.

This is an unassuming little device, about the size of a small harmonica and about as solid. Its small size allows it to take up a small amount of desk space, tucking easily behind a monitor or case (or, if being used with a laptop, behind the whole system). In my specific situation I have it plugged into a laptop with an external monitor attached to it so I have the hub just at the base of the external monitor where it is out of thew way but still easily accessible.

In use, it works as it should. My one real test for the hub was to connect up an external USB hard drive, which does not work well with my other USB hub (coincidentally, also a Belkin product). When I attached the hard drive, the system immediately saw it and assigned a drive letter to it, just as if I connected it directly. This is how a hub should handle such a drive and I was pleased when there was no issue.

The one complaint I have with this hub is that the power cord is not snug. When the hub is moved while attached it is very easy to disconnect it from the power supply. My workaround was to use a twist tie to attach the power cord to the USB cable that attaches the hub to the system, after which I can move the hub without any difficulty.

This is a decent USB hub that works as it is supposed to work. Other than the less-than-secure plug for power I have no complaints.

Has 1/8" spring steel rods with 8mm ends that fit normal speedrings well. The other end of the rods have smaller ends if your ring has smaller holes.

The nature of softboxes is that you can get the rods into the holes on the speedring fairly easily but getting the rods out to break the box down is a real pain. The [[ASIN:B00093GGMY Calumet Quickring Speedring]] folds in half and locks. I believe the Calumet ring will do the trick. Undo the lock and all the tension will relax. Chimera makes a quick-release ring too, but it's $87 for the ring alone.

The Philips GoGear Raga is the first exposure I have had to Philips' line of mp3 players and I was unsure of what I should expect of it. The price is comparable to other mp3 players of similar capacity so I expected it to be in the ballpark with them. For the most part I was correct, though there are a few things about which one should be aware when using this particular offering. It's a good product, but it has its quirks.

Setting up the Raga is easy. In the package is a USB cable that allows one to connect to a PC (packaging does not indicate if MacOS supports the Raga), and upon connecting Philips Songbird downloads and installs automatically. The installation is painless and does not take long, and a few clicks of the mouse along the way and the software loads up.

The first thing I tried to do was load music into the Raga, and once I got the music into Songbird the Raga disappeared from the available devices list. I am not sure what happened. I unplugged it and shut down Songbird, plugged the Raga back in and everything was as it should be, so I dragged 67 songs to the Raga for transfer. I saw two problems. First, the user has to know to drag and drop - there is no "transfer to..." option that I could find in any of the menus. The bigger problem, though, is that the transfer speed is abysmal and it took close to 2 minutes to transfer 67 songs that average 5MB in size. With my old iPod and with my ZuneHD, transfer speeds are appreciably faster. This doesn't make the Raga a piece of junk, of course, as the problem may be Songbird itself, but the transfer speed is something of which to be aware, especially if transferring large amounts of music.

Navigating to the newly transferred music is simple. For that matter, navigating the Raga is simple, period. Anyone with even slight familiarity with music players will have no problem finding and playing music on the Raga.

For comparison, I matched the Raga against my ZuneHD for playback. Of course, the Zune HD produced a more natural and clear sound, but only slightly. For the difference in price, I would have expected the ZuneHD to REALLY outperform the Raga, but this was not the case. In fact, when playing with the built in equalizers in both, I was able to get the Raga to get very close to the ZuneHD for sound quality. The difference was more pronounced with higher end ANC headphones, but this is unlikely to matter to the large majority of users.

The Raga has a tiny screen (the package says it's 1" diagonally) so this is not the kind of player one would want if frequently messing with settings and searching through. That said, the Raga is designed as a player to be worn with the included arm band, suitable for using at the gym. The ear buds that come with it have over-the-ear hooks to help keep them in place.

Considering the price and size, Philips has put together a very nice music player that will suit active users very well. It has some idiosyncrasies, in particular the transfer speeds, but it really is a capable player.

This LEATHER LAPTOP MESSENGER BAG FOR MEN (by Leather Centric) is made of real leather--animal hide, NOT the man-made “pleather” stuff that’s often marketed on Amazon as “real leather” or “genuine leather”. That’s a big plus, but the bag itself has a lot of minuses.

First, the bag’s styling is so old-fashioned, it makes the bag look cheap. You have to really love the 1950s “retro” look, to like the overall appearance. The bag definitely looks handmade, but it also looks crudely rustic.

Second, although the bag has lots of zippered compartments (inside and outside), it is only 3” deep. It has no expansion gussets, so the total capacity is one laptop or one very thick sheaf of documents. Internal zipper compartments are relatively useless if a bag can’t expand to hold the things added to the compartments.

Third, the bag is difficult to open. It opens with two metal clasps--these are hidden beneath the purely decorative buckled front straps. You have to pull up on both clasps at once to lift the flap, and you can’t do this easily without laying the bag flat on one side, or holding it on your lap. The leather flap itself is very stiff (at least when the bag is new), and this adds to the opening difficulty.

Fourth, the bag has no locking mechanism. Not that it is easy to open (see previous paragraph).

Fifth, the brass fittings must tarnish very easily, because the bag arrives with every single exposed brass piece wrapped tightly in thin plastic wrap. It takes something very sharp to cut the plastic, and you must be careful not to scratch the fittings. (I succeeded in removing the wrappings without damaging the bag, but I punctured my left wrist with an Olfa knife in the process.)

The bag is reasonably priced (about $90 on Amazon). It comes with a snap-on shoulder carrying strap, and has a sturdy, permanently attached satchel handle. The handle is very comfortable. The bag leather is already distressed, so you needn’t worry about scratches. This is a truly rugged laptop bag.

Just got this and started playing with it, but first a little background.

I also have two 5 Blacks and a 7 Black. I drive a truck (truck, not peekup) and use these to record my trips and the traffic around me. I record several hours of video every day. With a minor amount of effort, these work much better than typical dashcams. I use them without batteries inside the cab, with USB-C cables powering them. They tend to overheat with the batteries installed when mounted inside the windshield. The 5s still overheat sometimes without the battery. The 7 seldom does. They're often in the sun for hours at a time, so this isn't really a fault. It's not what they're designed to do. The 7 stays connected to the app much better than the 5s do. It's just a much more capable camera all around.

The Hero 7 Black TimeWarp and stabilization are first rate. The first video I took using it on my Jeep, a friend thought I'd bought a gyro-stabilized mount. It's that good. I assume the 8 is at least as good. I expect it to be better.

I've also owned a cheaper "Action Camera". It actually handled the heat better, until the battery swelled up and destroyed the camera. If you're looking for a toy, those are fine. If you want something that lasts, GoPro, with all its faults, is just about all there is. Nothing else does what they do while taking a substantial amount of abuse.

There is a dive case with external battery available from Suptig (on Amazon) for the 5, 6, and 7, but not for the 8. I use this case for the 5s when I mount them outside the truck. I use a Panavise mount with tethers outside the truck. The Panavise mount is heavy enough to hold the heavy battery with the camera mounted on it. I've also used this setup on my Jeep, but not as much as I'd like. There are dive cases for the 8, but not with external batteries that I've found.

The main feature of the 8 that I was drawn to was the ability to switch from TimeWarp to Realtime and back while recording. Unfortunately, this control isn't available on the app, only on the camera screen. I'll just have to mount the 8 where I can tap the screen easily while driving. Not optimum, but not a deal killer.

The app could be a lot better, but GoPro insists on using it for marketing. The app is useful, but I've already bought four GoPros. The cameras sold themselves. The app lacks a lot of features I'd like to see on it, though it is much better now than when I was given my first GoPro 4. The 4 still works fine, by the way, and I still use it where I'm afraid I might lose the camera, such as under the Jeep.

The battery door and charge port on the Hero 8 Black are completely different from the Hero 5 Black and Hero 7 Black. If you plan to use the camera for long periods without the battery, you'll need to get a battery door designed to allow connecting USB while closed. I've ordered one. Just search for "Hero 8 battery door." The alternative is to leave the battery door open, or off. I really don't like that choice. Either way, the camera isn't waterproof without the original door in place and closed.

I can't recommend any of the GoPro 6 series, because for a bit more you can get a 7, and for a bit less, you can get a 5 Black. I bought the 8 instead of another 7 because the price dropped to within $40 of the 7, and there are several improvements. Before you buy any of them, do some research into what each can and cannot do. There are various video modes on each. The older models drop in price every time a new model comes out.

I've always thought photo frames are gimmicky, but FeelCare has changed my mind. The difference in using these versus turning a tablet into a photo frame is that it SIMPLY WORKS as it should. Getting a tablet to be a photo frame is quite involved and requires more maintenance. Also, this item actually looks like a picture frame! When you fire it up, it's actually running Android, a stripped down version that focuses just on being a photo player. The Frameo app allows you to beam photos to it easily. You can designate sleep hours for the frame so that it's not always on 24/7. I have mine asleep from 1 am to 8 am. Techies will turn old tablets into photo frames, but I think the main market here is for older people who are not techies. Great for parents and grandparents, but we'll be using it too and we're not quite grandparents yet.

Here are some outside the box ideas...

A joke on your friends:
--------------------------
Imagine your buddy come over to your house and looking at all the frames on your mantle. Smack dab in the center is a picture of his grandparents, or perhaps, his mom? LOL! He'll be like, "What the... why do you have a picture of my mom?" LOL! To do this joke, you need the frame to have only a few photos that's because it doesn't know how to display just 1 photo all day. It has to be in Slideshow mode 24/7. But you can select photos to hide. So if you have 5 photos, you can easily hide 4 of it, then it will only show 1 photo all day. If you have 200 photos, you would have to select 199 to hide. The joke is probably not worth that hassle. LOL! To pull it off, you also need to lower the brightness so that it matches the brightness of the regular surrounding pictures. And of course, hide the wires as best you can.

Card Magic Trick:
-------------------
I do card magic, and immediately I thought of a use for this frame. Have your spectator choose a card, then read his mind, then point him to the photo frame and say, "is that your card?" If you do Magic, you'll figure out plenty of ways to pull off this trick. This frame is pretty neat! 5 Stars!

UPDATE (2/21/19): So far, my clock is working well. I did buy a second clock, and succeeded in pairing it with my 1st Gen Echo Show. If you make a pairing mistake, you can press the clock's pairing button 5 times to unpair the clock and start over. Oddly, when the Show was correctly paired, the light turned solid orange. The Echo Show is hard to pair because it isn't completely integrated with the Alexa app when it comes to setting up a wall clock. However, for me, having two clocks, with visual timer displays paired to different Echo devices, was worth all the Setup hassles.

This ECHO WALL CLOCK does two things that I really want. First, it keeps accurate time by using an Internet connection (through an Echo device) instead of a radio signal (which can malfunction in bad weather or at Daylight Savings Time changes). Second, it gives a bright visual display of the time remaining on all the timers currently set with my first-generation Echo. (Yes, it simultaneously displays the time left on multiple timers.)

If my clock continues to work without requiring frequent Bluetooth re-pairing (as other reviewers have reported), I will order a second clock to pair with my Echo Show. The visual time-left display is very useful when I’m timing exercises or post-exercise ice treatments.

The instructions warn you NOT to try to move the clock hands. (Other reviewers warn that touching the hands will break the clock, or cause it to tell slightly inaccurate time forever if you succeed in replacing the hands.) It’s too bad that the clock does NOT have a plastic cover over the face--dusting it is going to be a problem. I put mine on a wall, to protect it as much as possible from dust, and from accidentally being knocked over.

SETUP PROBLEMS: Out of the box, the clock paired effortlessly with my Echo Show (using the option of asking the Show to set up the clock). However, I ran into a lot of difficulty when I tried to pair it with a second device (a first-generation Echo). The instructions do NOT make it clear that the clock PAIRS WITH ONLY ONE ECHO DEVICE.

Probably because I failed to start the second Setup attempt by using the Alexa app to un-pair the clock from the Show, the second attempt failed. It ended with a green light that has no defined meaning in the paper or online setup instructions. Worse, the clock no longer worked with the Show. Still worse, the clock did NOT appear as a device in the Alexa app; and the app did NOT display the clock as a Connected or Bluetooth device under the Show settings.

Eventually I found the clock under the settings for the Echo (subject of my second, failed Setup attempt). I was able to unpair it, delete it, and start Setup again. At long last, the clock paired with the Echo, and began working again (with the first-generation Echo).

However, I failed in all attempts to use the Show to set up the clock again. Those attempts always concluded with a red error light or with that mysterious green light. At some point, I had to remove the batteries and replace them so that the pairing button on the clock would work. Naturally I now dread having to pair the clock again with any Echo device, should the Bluetooth connection malfunction.

SUMMARY: The concept of the Wall Clock is great. I love my clock now, and really do intend to buy a second one, if the clock that I now have continues to work normally. However, I hope that later generations of the Echo Wall Clock will have a covered clock face, and that later versions of the Setup software will have much better integration with the Alexa app.

I have a good tangle of cables in my home office for a variety of devices that require a micro-USB cable. Most of these cables are very nondescript and I have no idea who made them, though there are a couple of them that have manufacturer names printed on the plugs on the end. Most are plain black and are mostly indistinguishable from one another. These cables from Magic-T are absolutely the most easily identifiable cables on the desk and it has made it very easy to assign cables to every device on the desk. But, there is more to these cables than just pretty colors.

The most obvious advantage of this cable set is the colors. Each of these cables is a different color and none of them are black or gray - there’s blue, pink, orange and green. And, even more important than the color is the fact that they are insulated in nylon weave, not plastic coating, which in my experience holds up a bit better under stress and the result is a more reliable cable.

The plugs on both ends are metal shielding with a plastic base, sufficient to give these strength for the connections. The cables have been inserted in the bases and attached within, not attached to the plug base, but those connections are very tight and seem to be solid so I am not concerned about them pulling loose.

Each cable is about six and a half feet in length which is much more convenient for me than the regular 3' cables.

These cables are capable of high-speed charging so if you have a device and a charger that are both capable of high-speed charging then these cables will work well for you. I used one for my tablet and a high-speed USB charger and the tablet did charge faster than when using a lower-grade cable.

I want to mention the pricing. As I write this, the price on this set of four cables is about $9. That’s about $2.25 per cable, and the cables are of good quality. The price can change of course, but at the current price this is an absolute bargain.

There’s something else I need to mention. The manufacturer offers a 12-month warranty on these cables, and to me that’s just amazing. For a cable that costs less than $2.50 per individual cable the manufacturer thinks enough of their product to back it with a 12-month warranty. I doubt I would ever need to use the warranty for one of these, but it’s reassuring to know the manufacturer believes in their products.

It is hard to find fault with these cables. They are made well, they are easily identifiable and they are very inexpensive. This is a fine set at a great price.

I bought the 24" 1440 model for one reason: Pixel density.

I'm not a gamer. For me it's all about legible screen fonts for easy reading. And pixels per inch is where it's at. The higher the pixel density, the clearer the type looks. Fonts on a larger monitor with a lower density won't look as clear as a smaller one with a higher number of pixels per inch.

The density on the 24" model (2560 x 1440 resolution) is a little over 120 pixels per inch (ppi). A Kindle Paperwhite pixel density is 300 ppi. So if this monitor is a bit over twice the distance from you as a Kindle Paperwhite, the density and clarity will look about the same.

There is one thing I do want to mention: brightness. Wow this thing is bright. In the early days of LCD and LED monitors, brightness and color accuracy were issues. The brightness issue has certainly been solved, and maybe too well. I have mine set on just "5" on the on-board brightness setting. Occasionally I have dialed it down to "0" and it's still readable.

This isn't a good first telescope, if the intent is to introduce and encourage someone to pursue the hobby of astronomy further. The images were fuzzy and distorted and varied in focus across the field of view. Any reflector telescope, even this small one, requires the mirrors to be precisely aligned (collimated) to get sharp images. Out of the box, the two mirrors were not aligned well. I did take it apart. I unscrewed the primary mirror holder from the bottom and drilled out larger diameter holes so that I could adjust the positioning of primary mirror I reseated the secondary mirror (below the eyepiece) which was not level. The 3 existing screws in the secondary mirror can be adjusted to adjust the alignment of the secondary mirror. After some manual collimation, the image is now much better. Stars no longer look like fuzzy balls. But this process isn't easily done in this telescope, nor is it described in the included instructions. If what you're looking for is a complete backup utility, that's reasonably easy to use, this one might suit your purpose.

Installation, update, and activation are easy, similar to other Symantec programs. (This one also uses Live Update.) I do have an objection to the fact that Symantec never does a full uninstall -- they leave around stuff in the registry, as well as LiveUpdate, and it requires extra work (and some technical skill) to remove everything. I take off one star for that.

The setup is quite simple, especially if you follow their procedures. A full system backup is recommended, and the program will nag you about your system being "at risk" if you don't set up the full backup. You can in addition set up backup jobs for selectively backing up some of your files and folders. So for instance you might want to do nightly backup of your key folders, and weekly or monthly backup of the full system.

I would recommend that you use a network disk (NAS) for your backup -- there are many not-too-expensive products available, and I've been quite happy with the Buffalo products.

You can also use this program to do remote management of other computers on your network, but be aware that each computer needs its own license for the program.

One thing I don't like is that the backup files are not copies, they are in a compressed format. For daily backups I prefer to be able to make normal copies of files, so that I can go quickly to the backup folder and find a backup copy I might want. This optimizes my time and convenience over computer time and disk space, and this is how it should be. Or at least, this should at least be an option.

I take off another star for the nagging about full system backup, and the unavailability of a simple file backup or file sync (backup by copying selected files/folders directly from one disk to another).

But overall a solid program that does what it says, and does it competently. Just make sure what you want is what it wants to do. :-)

MY HISTORY WITH THIS PRODUCT:
I've owned this headset for almost a full year. Technically, I've had two of them, since the boom mic snapped off the first one and had it replaced. I use these every day, for multiple hours and a variety of uses (VoIP calls, gaming, music, and movies).

PROS:
The audio quality, when it is working, is good. The bass in 7.1 mode is great, and the overall surround sound is pretty convincing. They are comfortable and rechargeable via USB.

CONS:
The biggest problem here is the wireless connection. Both headsets I owned suffered from this same problem - they would frequently just restart or lose the signal and reconnect. The process takes about 3-5 seconds each time, and sometimes you get multiple restarts in a row. It doesn't sound too bad until it happens when you're watching a movie and you have to quickly pause or rewind a bit because you suddenly couldn't hear anything they were saying (which also completely pulls you out of the movie), or when it drops out in the middle of a phone conversation, or drops out at the worst possible moment in a game... It happens probably two dozen times a day, if not more. At first, I didn't care too much about it, but the first time you have it drop out 3 times in a matter of a single minute, it's simply maddening. Imagine going randomly deaf for several seconds throughout every day of your life, and you'll get a sense of what it's like.

If I could simply plug the cable in and it would use the USB cable to transmit the audio instead of wireless, that would be perfect, but when it's plugged in, it simply charges the internal battery - you still get audio interruptions all the time. The interruptions will also reset the "mute" status on the mic, which can be troublesome if you're intentionally muted on a conference call and suddenly your mic is on and people hear you eating lunch.

Second problem is that the power button is a bit flaky. If the headset is plugged in via USB and powered off, sometimes it will not power on unless you unplug the headset and THEN power it on (and then you can plug it back in to continue charging). I thought it was a defect in my first headset until the same thing happened with the second one.

A minor third problem is that the boom mic is a little flimsy on the construction. I am careful with my toys, but it still cracked and finally snapped off one day when I was lowering the mic to use it, and that was only a few months into owning it.

OVERALL:
If they would fix the wireless, I would rate this 4 stars in a heartbeat. If they fixed the power button, it would go up to 5. That said, the G35 seems to be the G930 but wired, and cheaper. The number of times that I've wanted to really make good use of the wireless (go to another room and keep the audio going) is far less frequent than the dozens upon dozens of times that the audio cuts out, so it's just an unacceptable point for me, since that is what this headset is about.

Ok, so I have to admit at first I was wondering why someone would spend this much on a Bluetooth headset that isn't a feature-rich entertainment one like those from Sony or a major fad brand like Beats, both of which I have some experience with. But this, no... this is actually something different. This is a serious tool for serious use with serious built quality and seriously useful features. Seriously.
For example, the telescoping mouthpiece means you'll get unparalleled mic quality compared to headsets that pick the mic up by your ears (looking at YOU, airpods!), both in clarity and isolation from background noise. You can also physically bend it out of the way, or use the button on the mic itself to mute. Try doing that with airpods. Then there's the button based features. Shortcuts and touch-sensitive buttons are cool on aesthetic devices, but the physical controls on this are an ergonomic user experience DREAM. Everything is easy to access and control, no apps or press-and-hold or counting LED blinks, etc. Sort of makes me miss the old days of phones with physical switches and buttons. When you want your equipment to get serious, this is the sort of user experience you expect. Then there's the charging rack. OMG I love that, I can store it on my desk and it's charging automagically. Pick it up and put it on, ready to go. Never needs to be charged because it's been charging in between uses. Finally, I'm really impressed with the USB dongle option. You see, the one thing I really dislike about wireless headphones is that you usually need to pair it with a device, then unpair it to switch to another device. For example, using my Sony headphones on my phone and tablet, if my wife wants to borrow them for a zoom meeting, I need to pair with her device but then also unpair with mine so that it doesn't keep trying to reconnect to it. Sometimes we just give up and use a wired headset to avoid that mess. Non-bluetooth wireless headsets have a dongle, which makes it easy to swap what you are connected to (no unpairing needed, just move the dongle) but then you can't connect to devices without a USB port like a phone. This is the best of both- you can pair it with your phone, but ALSO use the USB to quickly connect with your desktop or laptop without going through the process of pairing and unpairing. This is the kind of usability and professional quality I would expect from a brand like Plantronics, and all the while it works well as a stereo headset for music/gaming/etc as well. Very comfortable to wear for long hours, I'd highly recommend it for serious users.

I just unpackaged and started using the Amazon Fire TV. Right off I had to do a small update which didn't take long at all. Next there is a neat video that shows you how to use the device.
