What's missing from this is the Amazon Music of which I have quite a few albums. I hope we get to see music in some future update. That's kind of a glaring omission in my opion. One star knocked off for that right there.

One cool feature I noted right off the bat is that the device already knows me. I didn't have to log in or do anything.

The watchlist

So I went straight to my watchlist to confirm that it indeed already knows me. It does. And I went to a recent season of shows I am watching where the first two episodes have been watched and the third has not. There is a white bar at the bottom of those watched and missing from the one that is yet to be watched. So I'll guess that is my progress bar as well. Nice touch.

Voice feature

This feature is slightly confusing to me right off. What you do is hold the mic button down until you hear a tone, then continue to hold it down as you speak your question or title search. When you are done talking, only then do you release the button. I kept letting it go as soon as I heard the tone, which causes it to attempt to process the question. So the feature is a little odd, but once you get used to that oddity it works quite well.

I asked it, "what's new this week" and got three suggestions. I further asked it questions like, show me my watchlist which offered me two methods, "watch list" and "watchlist". Neither of which showed me my actual watchlist. Clearly the audio search isn't yet fully aware of navigation.

Purchasing a TV show

Photos

Looks like they have an iOS and Android app that lets you share photos with Amazon Cloud Drive and thus have them available on this device. I'll have to try that out. I'll skip it for now.

Apps

This looks good for now. NetFlix and Pandora are here as well as Hulu. I use all three of those so that's good.

Games

There are good looking games here. I didn't buy the game controller as I own a console already, but I might rethink that.

YouTube

I didn't see YouTube, so I did a voice search and an app popped up. Once the app downloaded and installed, I had to visit an activation page of YouTube to connect it to the device. Very simple and now I have YouTube on here.

NetFlix

Netflix didn't have a simple activate system. I had to punch in my email and password via the remote. Boo! In this era of complex passwords, activation should become a standard function on TV based media devices.

Navigation

The navigation is quite smooth. I guess thanks to some good specs under the hood. This device doesn't feel sluggish at all. Getting to your watch this is as fast as hitting 'home' and then moving up or down from wherever you left off. I can do it in a second. There is also a nice back button so you can navigate backwards. All device should do this. Works perfectly.

Fast Forward

When you are watching a movie, you can fast forward and see a small picture window that gives you a visual preview of the fast forward event. It's really well done. I can quickly find where I want to be and drop off there.

I use laptops at home instead of tower systems, but I still prefer a stand-alone keyboard for most things. I have had very good success with Microsoft peripherals in the past so I had high expectations for this keyboard. So far, it works well enough but I have encountered a couple of snags that make it less than perfect.

This is a slim and efficiently designed keyboard and it is slightly wider than my 15.6” laptop. It’s the right size for me and I am happy with the dimensions when it comes to fitting it in my work space. No complaints there.

Set-up is a little on the tricky side. I tried to set it up for Bluetooth use without following the instructions first and got nowhere. It does not appear in the list of available devices so it could not be paired right off the bat, though my system does handle the Bluetooth standard. The instructions say to connect it via USB first, then turn it on and follow the set-up when Windows detects it. However, the instructions do not say that you must use the cable that came with the keyboard; I used a different one and failed, though the keyboard did work as a USB keyboard with that 3rd-party cable connected.

I’ll answer the very obvious question right now – I was able to get it working under Linux as a USB keyboard, but not as a Bluetooth keyboard. I am not sure if the problem is with the Bluetooth receiver in the system I tested or if the keyboard is just not compatible at all. I have an iPhone as well and it did not see the keyboard in the list of available devices. This is not a failure or a shortcoming of the keyboard – it operates very much in accordance with how it has been marketed, so getting it to work under Linux with Bluetooth would have been just a bonus. Interestingly, it says it can be set up to work under the Windows Phone platform which has been discontinued...

When I set it up under Windows 10, it did not go as the documentation said it would go. I did get the toast notification and I clicked as directed. It set everything up and said it was ready to go. It never allowed me to set up the fingerprint configuration and I have been unable to find any setting within Windows to allow me to revisit. So, I have a fingerprint reader that I can’t configure. Considering that this is being used in a home with a private computer with password protection this really isn’t a show-stopper but it would have been nice to mess with this technology.

In operation the keyboard is very responsive and so far I have been pleased with it except for one thing that I cannot seem to reconfigure. I prefer to have the function keys operate as function keys by default, instead of media keys. Without being able to find a keyboard configuration setting in the OS anywhere I have no way to reverse the default operation, which is to require pressing the Function key prior to hitting F1 – F12 to get them to default as function keys instead of media keys.

I do like this keyboard and it works well for my needs. The set-up isn’t bullet-proof though, and there are some behaviors it would be nice to change or reconfigure.

I received this as a free review sample. This is not a zoom type telescope. You can adjust focus for your objective (the 52mm end) as well as the eye lens (the 16mm end), but you will not be able to zoom in. Think of this as a mono scope that can bring a far object into sharp focus.

Another thing to note is the field of vision is less than the 18 degrees marked on the body. It's about half that, and the night and day marking does not imply that this is a night vision scope. You will still need an external light source in low level lighting conditions. For example, moonlight will work, but in total darkness you will not be able to see a thing.

For me this is very useful for a hobby of mine, which is reptile spotting. Where I live there is an abundance of species, especially turtles and snakes, but we also have alligators and many interesting lizards. I prefer observing gators from a distance, and when walking down trails in parks (and there are many in my area) it's nice to be able to sit in a stationary point and scan for gators on banks as well as swimming. Same for various snakes, both land and water.

What I love about this scope is it's rugged. There are no lens caps, but the nylon case that comes with it makes it ideal for outdoors activities in harsh environments. It's outer material appears to be rubber, and I have dropped mine a few times without damaging it.

When you do bring an object into focus it's sharp and crystal clear. The field of vision may seem narrow, but you can actually take in a lot of details by slow scanning. It may take a little time to get accustomed to viewing wide fields of vision with it, but once you do, it's easy to use.

I selected the Meade 20225 TerrStar telescope as my youngest son is often asking me where to find certain constellations in the sky and has always been interested in celestial events. I thought this telescope might be a good entry level scope with which to foster his interest. While it does work, I would hesitate to recommend it, mainly on the basis of its build quality but also for its usability.

My son decided to assemble it himself and it was done by the time I got home from work. He had no issues putting it together and he managed to get it assembled correctly without any assistance. In short, it's easy to put together. However, his very first comment to me was that it was very cheaply made, and it did not take long to determine what he meant. The whole assembled unit is slightly wobbly and a little unstable though it does not feel like it will tip over without a little help - I would be more concerned about it breaking outright. There is much more lightweight plastic than metal and there are numerous opportunities to break components which all feel cheaply made.

One of the packing decisions made was to put the lenses in the carry bag which is folded up in the box. So, until we realized this we thought the lenses were not included in the package. While this is not a major problem - all the parts are there - it does show a lack of understanding of the consumer who is likely to call the support line first before searching the carry bag.

We took the telescope outside and started looking for objects in the sky, and we discovered a serious issue. Once we find something to view, the scope's positional setting is so loose that even the very slightest bump either knocks the object from view or causes the scope to shake which makes viewing impossible. At a minimum the scope itself should be mounted tightly and should move only with deliberate effort. I have found no way to tighten this up which is very unfortunate.

I have trouble recommending this telescope. It's very cheaply made and this shows all through the product from assembly to use. Research other options before selecting this telescope.

If you have a single band router like we do, it will not detect the wireless network or connect wirelessly. If our neighborhood is any indication, this extender won't work with most home routers. Out of the ten or so visible wireless networks in our area, the extender only detected one or two. The two it detected were two of the weaker signals, but I assume were dual band signals the extender would work with.

After several frustrating attempts to get it connected wirelessly, I spent about an hour with customer support before being informed of this limitation on the extender. The product listing says "compatible with all Wi-Fi routers," and it may be compatible with all routers if set up as a wired extender, but apparently it isn't compatible with all as a wirelessly connected extender. If you want wireless connection to your router, check your router's capability and make sure it is a dual-band router before ordering.

As I mentioned, I did get it set up as a wire-connected extender using an ethernet cable. And it works well for that. It puts a good strong WiFi signal all over our house and much of the yard. I'm giving it four stars for that.

Yes, this is a good hard drive that works just fine. No, I didn't waste my time with the preinstalled bloatware.

Just want to give you some details about the interface (something I would have wanted to know):

Although USB 3.0 is meant to be fully backward compatible, there are still some reported issues with some devices such as the Wii. I haven't heard about any with standard PCs, though.

The saving grace is the ability to change the connecting device to an old USB 2.0 cable. The problem is, it costs $20 for the privilege. That's pretty steep for going backward.

The fact is, these hard drives have a standard SATA connector on back just like any other hard drive, except that they manage to make themselves semi-proprietary by having the connector both recessed and more to the middle. I suspect that it is more to the middle only because the hard drive is a little larger than a 2.5" hard drive stuck in an external case. This keeps you from using a hard drive dock. The fact that it is recessed keeps you from using a hard drive bridge. Of course I understand the reason for the company trying to make this proprietary, but I don't have to be happy about it. I'd respect them more if they gave me more options that didn't involve going to them for replacement parts every time I need them.

Even so, the highest capacity external hard drives are almost always cheaper than an internal hard drive of the same size (especially after you buy a case as well), so this is not a bad pick if you are fully aware of your current needs and have considered future needs.

I have used and tested more Ethernet cables than I can remember and there is no question, all Ethernet cables are not created equally.

This Cat8 is designed to be thin, but don’t let that fool you into thinking that it lacks capacity - within the thin package contains the needed shielding and wires for super fast transfer speeds. The connector bases are reinforced at each end of the wire which really help hold all of the wires in place even if you have to bend and twist it to fit it within the plug. The connector plug itself is gold plated which is the ultimate standard in connectivity.

I used this 10’ cable to run from my router to my NAS - a primary connection where speed and a reliable relay is critical - and I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

You will not find a better Ethernet Cable - this is really a top of the line cable that you’ll love. This is a purchase that you’ll never regret.

I am having a love hate relationship w/these ear buds.

What I like about these ear buds was first the price...these are much more affordable than some other name brand blue tooth earbuds, but the performance also explains the price differences.

The sound: These do sound really good.

Noise Cancelling: Very good for earbuds, maybe even a little too good. I run w/these and still want to be able to hear road noise.

Fit: These fit me very well and stay put while running. To me this is probably the best part. I have not had good luck w/earbuds staying put while running or lifting hard. These do that. I find myself checking them often, out of habit, and they are tightly in place.

Battery Life: I've not had an occasion where the batteries have run dead. I use them, put them back in their case and they are ready for my next workout.
Telephone calls: Works well while making and taking phone calls.

The not so good:

The functions: Too many. On/Off, pair, pause, really are the only things I need.

Pairing: I can only get these to pair to one item. If I pair to my phone, I cannot pair to my watch. The first time out of the case they automatically paired to my phone. When I tried to also pair them to my watch, following the very complicated pairing sequence of button pushing, I could not get it to pair. I had to completely unpair these from my phone to get them to pair to my watch. Then I could not get the earbuds to pair back to my phone.

I also get a lot of static and drop off while in these. It's not on common for one of the ears to lose sound while out running or walking. I also get a static sound pretty frequently which requires me to pause and restart playing music.

In the end, I do not think I would buy these again unless they come out w/a better version. If they could make earbuds with this fit and work like some others, they would be perfect. Until then I'll use these until they die and probably not replace them w/more SkullCandy earbuds unless some improvements are made.

Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a reasonably priced MP3 player from Philips Electronics. Small and with a good deal of memory, this MP3 player offers enough of the basic features to satisfy casual MP3 users' needs.

Let's talk about the good points first. This MP3 player is a good value and it has a long battery life. A full charge can last the better part of a day so it is ready when you need it. The compact size and durable construction are also plusses with this MP3 player. It takes up very little space and the metal construction is made to last. I like the menu navigation as well and found it very intuitive.

Most important to an MP3 player is sound quality and in this area, my feelings are mixed. My MP3 player experience is limited, so I have little to which I can compare. But based on other MP3 players, the sound quality with this Phillips device is a little below average. I was also very disappointed with the Full Sound option. This is supposed to improve the sound quality, but I could barely tell any difference. It has a little too much bass for my tastes, but others might find it acceptable.

Probably my greatest complaint with this Philips MP3 player is the included ear buds. They are the type that hugs the ear, but they do not contain a foam cushion and thus are not very comfortable or very good at blocking outside noise. The good thing, of course, is that an accessory like this can be replaced, which I recommend doing if you purchase this product.

MP3 players are nice and Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a good MP3 player, especially for the price. There are certainly better MP3 players out there, but this is a good one for beginners or those with basic needs. I'm torn with my overall rating because of the division between the pros and cons. So, I will award this device with a middle rating of three stars and a modest recommendation.

My main TV - and thus my comparison point - is a Sony Bravia Z series from 2009. Here are some things I think are outstanding about the Samsung. I'll try to only talk about things that aren't mentioned constantly:

1) I dislike the overly contemporary look of most high-end Samsung TVs, and therefore don't usually consider them for purchase. This, however, is a classic looking TV that won't look old next year and doesn't draw attention to itself at the expense of everything else.

2) Sony - and most other companies - no longer make a high end 32" model, which is stupid. My main TV is most likely to have a local computer nearby. It's the kitchen and the bedroom where I need the SMART features most. For that reason, this TV actually has very little competition.

3) USB ports. These are outstanding, especially if your network is too slow for streaming (or if you don't have a port nearby and your wireless is slow). Where my older Sony only plays some pictures off USB - and way too slow to actually want to use that feature, this newer Samsung can play almost all my media files locally or use a wireless mouse/keyboard. I have one USB port filled with a Logitech receiver, which allows me to use a mouse and keyboard I have stashed under the bed. Haven't actually bothered to use those yet (except for testing), but it's nice to know I could turn them up and use them without having to mess with any options. In the other USB port, I have a micro-SD card reader about the same size that always has 32GB of TV series that I can watch in a pinch, say if they put on some reality crap instead of a decent show that I was expecting over the air. Neither USB device can be seen except from the side. It reads the files on the micro-SD card directly from the source menu and as quickly as Windows Explorer.

4) DLNA. As much as I love that micro-SD card USB reader, you really don't even need it because the DLNA features are pretty mature. The fact that it reads .mkv files so easily, and you can control integrated subtitles and audio tracks so easily is amazing. My other TV requires transcoding for anything but MPEG, which really bogs down the processor on my laptop. I really recommend Wild Media Server because it works so well with both this and my Sony, and can easily spit 720p to both TVs (different shows) simultaneously. I couldn't get Serviio or Mezzmo to work as well. Samsung apparently has some freeware available that you might want to try as well.

All that said, despite the high contrast ratio, I don't feel like the picture is quite as good as my older Sony (which I believe only has a CR of 100,000:1), even after a lot of playing around. As you'd expect from its small size, it does play SD (and lower) very nicely on its screen without pixelization (Comment for 32" ONLY!). Even so, I love this TV for the bedroom, and felt the price was reasonable. It may get moved to replace the TV in the kitchen one day, and it will be great there, as well.

Also, I would prefer a browser with adjustable transparency over the TV, as the PIP version has the sound and picture cutting out sometimes. Even so, I would absolutely recommend this TV if you're looking for a 32"er.

Oh, but one more thing: I just had some apps "pushed" on me, like the cell phone companies do to your smart phone. If this continues, I'll be lowering my rating. I did not buy a TV to have a bunch of useless crap sold to me. A warning to you, Samsung.

The display on the both lights up which input you've selected (A or B), you simply click the button in or out to alternate.  Easy to use, great product.

THE GOOD:
--------------
* 4 HDMI port in, 4 USB link ports, 1 HDMI port out.
* You can share up to 4 usb accessories
* 1 usb calculator included.
* 4 hdmi cables included.
* 4 usb link cables included.

THE BAD:
------------
* Case seems to be metal, but it's a little light. Doesn't feel has sturdy and robust as the Avstar.
* You're getting a lot in this bundle, but there is a reason for that... this is a very basic kvm switch.
* No usb 3.0 or 3.1. The usb ports on this switch are 1.1 and 2.0. If you don't need 3.0, then you should be happy with this switch.
* No mic port.
* No audio ports.
* Included calculator is a gimmick to create value, but it's pointless and lightweight plastic, very cheap.

Depending on what your needs are, you might want to check out the Avstar kvm switch that I recently reviewed. That one is $10 less, but it is more future proof, and more of a premium product. That one has 3 usb ports to share but they are 3.0 and 3.1. The Avstar also has an optical audio port, a stereo audio port and a mic port. The Avstar also has a remote control to switch inputs. So it is a better kvm switch overall, but it does not include any hdmi or usb link cables. Here is an Amazon link to that switch: https://www.amazon.com/review/RR34E657C5MOF/ref=cm_cr_srp_d_rdp_perm?ie=UTF8&ASIN=B09D6Y2CFL

USE CASE SCENARIO:
--------------------------
* Why would you need a KVM switch? You can share a single set of keyboard, mouse, speakers for multiple pcs. You can use your same PC monitor to view the Fire Stick, play PS5, Xbox, etc. There is no need to hook up different speakers, as long as you hook up your main speaker to the optical or stereo ports.

I was ready to give this switch 5 stars because of all the cables provided, but now that I've used both switches, I understand why the Avstar didn't include any cables. The Avstar is a higher end product, so they're keeping the cost down by not providing any cables. I use the Avstar with my higher end pc, and I'm using this Basicolor switch for master bedroom pc that has lower needs. I'll rate this switch 4-Stars as well.

I got excited to see one of these small portable LED style ones that actually had a decent native resolution (most of them can accept 1080p, but are in reality only 800x600 resolution, or sometimes worse... 640x480!). This one is actually capable of displaying 720p of real dot resolution, which should make it at least as sharp as my Viewsonic and other traditional HD projectors. Ok, perhaps I'm spoiled, but I'm comparing this to our Viewsonic 720p projector that, to be fair cost me 3-4x as much.
And for the most part, it DOES work, however there are some caveats to its use. First of all, it doesn't seem as sharp as my 720p projector, even though it should have the requisite amount of dots. It's OK, its definitely better than the cheap 600p projectors, but something just isn't quite there when comparing side by side. It also doesn't get all that bright, but I suppose that's expected from the LED tech being used. You'll need black out shades or use it only during the night. Then there's the color- it isn't great. It works, but it has a cheap color reproduction that looks kind of flat and lifeless. Dark scenes sort of all blend together and become nearly impossible to see. It lacks the vibrancy of even an inexpensive television from decades ago. It gets the job done, but hardly the "theater experience" if you've been waiting to see that latest action/vfx film the way it was intended. It will look better on your TV at home, the only thing this has going for it is the large projection experience. For example, if you just want to give your kids a backyard movie night and don't care that the color and detail won't be as great as your indoor system, it will do the job on the cheap. I personally would not give up my mid-range projector for this one.
One thing that I found particularly annoying is that rather than the optical zoom and focus dials found on usual projectors, there is only a focus and tilt dial. No zoom. That means you have to physically move the projector closer or further to get it to reach the correct size you are shooting for. That actually got in the way of using it in a couple of specific places my other projectors can be used at optimal sizes.
That's not to say it gets everything wrong- I DO like that it is small and light and can even be turned on it's back to aim at the ceiling. That's something my big projector can't do, due to the airflow and cable management sticking out the rear. It also has a standard 1/4" 20 threaded tripod mounting point, so you can place this onto a tripod and get maximum mounting freedom. That will come in handy as I've always wanted to watch a movie in bed on the ceiling. But otherwise, don't think this projector will be as good as the other mid-rangers out there. This is still very much a low end projector. You'll have to spend at least 2-3x as much to get a decent home theater style experience, and much more if you want a high end one that will handle FHD/4k to get the real deal. This is more of a specialty use item.

This is not a true coconut water, but a drink that contains coconut water, nata de coco (a gel made from fermented coconut water), and flavoring among the ingredients. I love it because it's refreshing, especially on humid days, and uses real sugar instead of substitutes that I try to avoid.

Each eight ounce serving contains 70 calories with 18 grams of carbs (16 of which are from sugars). Contrast that with the same serving of Classic Coke, which comes in at 95 calories and 26.4 grams of carbs (all of which are from sugars) and this wins from a nutritional perspective. This drink is much lighter than most sodas and I have personally found it to be good for suppressing my appetite as well.

While it does quench thirst, it does not have the sodium content to be ideal for rehydration. Gatorade, for example, contains roughly 100mg of sodium for the same serving size, which is significantly more than the 15mg this drink contains. Moreover, this drink is missing potassium, which is also recommended for rehydration. I am mentioning this because there are coconut waters that are formulated for rehydration, but this one is more of a beverage.

The main ingredient is mineral water, followed by nata de coco, organic cane sugar, coconut water, calcium lactate, citric acid, sodium citrate, gellan gum and grapefruid seed extract.

Bottom line for me: I consume about sixteen ounces of this per day, and during exceptionally hot and humid days about twice that. Although this is no substitute for a rehydration drink, it does quench my thirst and the sugar gives me a boost without causing cramps in my fingers and toes like a soda does.

As a general rule, I hate hands-free handsets.

I hate it when I begin speaking with someone, and I think they're agreeing with everything I say, and then it turns out they're actually talking to someone else using their dratted ear extension with the flashing blue light.

I hate the fact that my ears are the wrong size and shape for the majority of headsets.

I hate it when my untrained (clumsy) fingers hit the wrong part of the headset when I'm simply trying to stop it from falling to its death from a height of just over 5 feet, and I either redial the last number or hang up on the one person who hates being hung up on.

Plus, they're UGLY, and don't accessorise well with any wardrobe!!

HOWEVER,

I hate it even more when I have to pull over and park to take or make a call.

And I especially hate it if I DON'T pull over, and then get busted by the only policeman on the entire empty highway who has insomnia and a full book of blank tickets waiting to be filled in.

SO,

Hands free it shall be -
But ONLY when I'm driving.

That said, this device fits most of my basic needs, and throws in some convenient extras. The EASYGO Headset was indeed very easy to set up and even easier to use. Sound quality was good and the spoken connection status and audio volume adjuster are useful features.

The headset is also relatively small and stylish (as hands-free headsets go) without any flashing lights or buttons that attract unwanted attention (or cause an attack of photosensitive epilepsy, or signal the letters N-E-R-D in morse code.)

The most impressive feature of this headset has to be the long battery life, which is great because the miserly charger cord is so awkward to use that you don't want to have to use it more often than necessary. Besides, as I only use it in the car, it lasts me several trips, depending on how often and how long I prattle.

Admittedly it is more comfortable to use than I expected. The extra ear hook prevents suicidal leaps from ear to earth, and it doesn't weigh my head down on one side.

In summary, for a simple headset, it delivers.

I have been interested in a device that can find hidden cameras for a while as we do tend to travel periodically. This device seemed like a good one and I wanted to try it out before I travel again. It seems like a pretty neat device that works fairly well, but it is hamstrung by very poor documentation.

This does more than just find hidden cameras. It is able to pick up Wi-fi signals, wireless phone signals and more. The sensitivity is very much like working with a metal detector - turn it up too high and it becomes nothing more than a sight and sound show; turned too low and it hardly sees anything.

With the unit turned on and set to a reasonable initial detection level I set about looking for devices in my home office. I have several Wi-fi connected devices and I usually have my smartphone there too, and I messed with this detector until I found the level where it was able to find everything. I did not try going near the router which is in another room but I imagine that one would require another sensitivity adjustment.

Most of the functions are self-explanatory, but some took a little trial and error to figure out. This is where good documentation would come in handy, and unfortunately the documentation with this device is poor. It's sufficient to identify the different functions of the device and where to find different components, but the actual descriptions and explanations of the functions are written in very poorly translated English.

The fan on my eight year-old QNAP TS-669 Pro's power supply finally began to fail recently, producing an unpleasant tone at odd intervals. After checking up the specs of the PS online, I found that the fan was replaceable - and fairly easily too, so I picked up a Noctua not only for the PS but two more for the QNAP itself. Double-checked the specs, and since the voltage matched, and the amperage of the prior fan was higher than this one, I figured I was set.

Accurately, it seems. Install was dead simple. I did have to clip the wire off the old fan and solder it onto this one's - though the Noctua comes with several tie-ins you can use for this purpose, I wanted a cleaner install. After the install, it fired up perfectly, and it was so quiet I had to use a flashlight to make sure it was spinning at all. I'll know better in the summer, but so far I'm pretty happy with the outcome.

I've replaced all my computer fans with Noctua's, with the interest in minimizing noise, and they have proven consistently reliable, so I would recommend them to others looking for fans for a similar application.

Smart watches have gotten more popular with the release of the Apple watch. They tend to have a standard set of functions, such as access to instant messaging, email, time, alarms and a lot more, typically tied to your phone. Not all smart watches are alike, though, and offer different sets of functions, better connectivity and other various differences from one another. This particular smart watch offers the mainline set of functions, setting itself apart through the user interface which is more polished and clean than most others with which I have worked. That said, I have a couple of quibbles with it, leaving room for a little improvement.

This is a standard-sized watch with a rubber wristband that can actually fit a larger wrist like mine. I have trouble finding watches and watch bands that fit me, so the fact that this one fits me is a pleasant surprise.

Powering it on, the user is immediately greeted with a complex and fairly complete visual menu system with tiles for every function available to the user. This is a standard presentation for a smartwatch, but this one looks a bit more polished and clean than the others I have seen. Switching to other menu screens just requires a swipe gesture, as to be expected. I have big hands, and this means that, for me, using a stylus makes working with this watch a lot easier. This is not the fault of the watch but a reality of working with a small device.

My first issue with this watch came when I paired it to my phone. The date and time on the watch were off, so I expected that it would grab the time from my iPhone when I paired it. It did not. Instead, I had to dig for the clock application and manually set the time. I dislike this and think that having it set itself when it is paired is much more accurate and cuts effort on the part of the user. For Android users, there is an application to allow for syncing up the time, date and more, but iOS users are out of luck for now. To the manufacturer's credit this is made clear on the product listing so this is not a surprise. Regardless, I am of the opinion that the watch should fetch the time, not rely on being sent the time. In the grand scheme of things, though, this is an annoyance, not a deal breaker.

There is a fairly comprehensive list of functions provided by this watch in addition to time/date and phone answer. Through the menus the user has access to call logs and function, Bluetooth functions, a remote finder function, a pedometer, a sleep monitor, a reminder function to get up and move on occasion, calendar and clock functions, audio functions, video functions and a few more.

One of the interesting functions that this watch offers is a camera. So, I tried to use it and it complained that there was no memory card available. Reading through the limited documentation included, I was unable to find anything about a memory card. I finally noticed that the back of the watch has a small groove where it can be popped off, and when I removed the back I found the battery which is removable (replaceable - another pleasant surprise). Under the battery is a slot for a micro SD card.

Adding a memory card comes with a big catch. It requires removing the battery to get at the holder which in turn clears the clock and resets it to midnight 01-01-2015. So, adding the memory card requires me to set the time again. And again if I remove the card.

Although I think the time sync functions of this watch are lacking, it is otherwise a good smartwatch. The interface is professional and polished and the whole provides access to a large number of useful functions. It's priced well too. Overall, this is a solid offering worth a look if you are wanting a smartwatch.

I have an LG TV 47" so I thought another LG product might be the best course of action (of course the money involved had to do with this decision), so I went to my local Best Buy to get a glimpse of what is out there. Besides this LG sound bar they had quite a few choices. I quick referenced them to their reviews and came to the conclusion that most sound bars are just about at the same level in terms of overall performance. I did see a Bowers and Wilkins?, priced around $2200, which is way more expensive than the tv itself (but was taught that audio is supposed to be the greater investment for the true tv viewer), and this sound bar frankly was fantastic, truly a thing to behold. But $2200 Buckaroos are a long way from $300 and I did get the tv at a great bargain price, so cheap instead of expensive became the call of war.
For what I got this soundbar does everything I wanted done. It was very easy to install through the optical option, and even though the first unit I purchased had troubles pairing with the subwoofer and was returned immediately, the second was the charm and now it works very nicely with the added plus that it certainly did not require a Kamikaze investment. Works very well and it adds a great sound capability to the living room in our home which was the intended site. Some shows are better than others but even the subwoofer does its magic and is a lot of fun to crank it up once in a while, specially for the internet type movie sites (like Netflix, Amazon, Vudu, etc.) that come with the smart tv and required some sort of subscription. Their sound, specially amazon and netflix, was way below average and even at maximum volume on the tv it was very sad. I could hear it but one of the members of the tribe is a little more than a little hard of hearing and was always having trouble (probably the main reason why I decided on a sound bar in the first place).
Needless to say this soundbar delivered what was expected of the product and now my living room is one loud area and when the subwoofer is doing its thing you can feel it kind of in the furniture itself, like some of the controllers in PS3 with the added vibration. Minor thing but rather invigorating, for the whole room now sounds like a mini theater without having had to add several speakers coupled with tedious connections, which certainly I am not qualified or inclined to want to do myself. I just put the sound bar in the same table in which the television rest and the subwoofer about 6 feet away and voila! Just waiting for the neighbors to reassure me as to the loudness, kind of like its baptism when they finally complain (makes you feel a little bit proud that you are putting enough noise to draw the attention of nearby houses, silly but what can you do sometimes?), so for now I am very happy with the purchase and glad that when necessary I have the equipment to raise the noise way higher than it was capable before. 4 very solid Stars!

The plugs have a protective rubber boot guard that protects the clip on the plug - this becomes very important when snaking the cable through walls and tight spaces. Prior to doing this I wrap the boot and plug with a small piece of electrical tape to make sure I don’t unintentionally snag anything.

I love the white PVC shielding on this cable - not only is it durable and will help the cable withstand damage but it can be run along a wall and then painted to match the wall color.

I used this 100 foot cable to run between my router to a PoE switch that branches to several power and transmit data to and from one zone of my security cameras - a primary connection where speed and a reliable relay is critical - and I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

I didnt know which to try. So many! I didnt know what would fit. There are some really small looking ones and some that look bulky, some that are nearly same in appearance as a standard mouse, and some that have a deeper cut out where hand rests. Very confusing. So I just spent some time reading through various reviews of a wide assortment of ergonomical mice.

While I think some of it is trial and error for getting the right fit, I think I happened upon a really good fit and feel with my first try. I really have nothing to compare it to, but so far I am really quite pleased.

--I dont have small hands, but they aren't exactly big either. Size can be in length and width. I have quite small fingers, but wide palms (3.75"). So typically a size "large" in gloves, but the ends of the fingers always dangle quite a bit. Hope that gives impression going forward with my review:

--My hand easily grasps the width of this mouse. Feels very comfortable. My pointer finger just reaches the scroll wheel. I dont need to reach for it; my finger pad sits directly on top of apex of the wheel.

--Press of left or right side is easy and comfortable. Plenty of length to accommodate even the smallest of fingers. Yet plenty of spare room for fingers longer than mine.

-- Not a loud click, but I can feel the click. I personally find that satisfying. Gentle yet makes me feel my action.

--Scrolling is smooth.
--No stuttering or jerkiness
--Instant connect when I first got this, and no problems since

--Impressed with how natural it feels. Didnt realize how much the wrist and forearm twist to use a standard mouse. With this, the mouse and arm are in a natural alignment

--Charging is quick and easy. Comes with cord for charging. I charge it directly through use of my laptop. It can be used as a corded mouse with ease. Can store dongle in the mouse if need be. Has on/off switch. When in the ON position, it will go to sleep when computer shuts down (or after x amount of time when not used), and wake up along with computer. Typical for rechargeable mouse. If this is anything like any other rechargeable mouse I have had, it should hold a charge for a very long time.

--Haven't used this for gaming yet as I have it for use on my laptop, but may try it out on my gaming PC. If I like it, I will just buy another. I think it will work out. This is just so comfortable and easy to use.

Take a little getting used to, yet at same time feels really natural. Good grip, good responsiveness, all around good experience in the short time I have had it. Your experience may vary in terms of fit, but I think the quality is evident. I will update if I have anything else worth sharing :)

EDIT/UPDATE: Seriously love this mouse, and this company is great. They are VERY RESPONSIVE and helpful when I inquired about an issue I had. WOW really good customer service. Rare these days, thank you. Truly, 5 STARS ALL AROUND.

I found myself needing to teach from home, like most US teachers, because of covid-19. Using zoom and whiteboard software locally, I would attempt to maintain some of the same methods I use in class, but also knew I'd need to do a lot more "showing" for that low ratio of students showing up for conferences sessions. Another teacher loaned hers to me to test for a few minutes. It did the job, so I decided to get one myself.
I really only use Windows for games that won't install/run in linux. My distance teaching wasn't going to be from Windows if I could help it.
This worked right out of the box. It didn't have all the functions, but it worked as a mouse would. It meant I could write (doing math work) in the whiteboard software without trying to do it with a mouse or fumble equations in real time with an equation editor or giving too much away using Geogebra.
I'm also a lefty, so that proved annoying quickly. It defaults to right handed mode, and the body that holds the electronics gets in the way. So I HAD to find drivers. Thankfully at Github (search Linux driver for Veikk-brand digitizers ) there is a driver. Installing was not too bad (had to compile myself - and had to find a fix for something getting in the compile way, search ""FATAL: Module veikk not found in directory" and a potential fix" at github).
Viola! The touch sensitivity works just fine and I can rotate the orientation, by manually editing parameters in /sys/module/veikk/parameters
Great, but then I had to find the GUI, because it kept resetting my orientation setting any time I rebooted. Search "Configuration tool for the VEIKK Linux driver" at github for the gui installer. It gave me hassles to install, but somehow I got it installed. Idon't use it much, but somehow it also keeps my orientation setting correct on reboots, and that's what I cared most about. I could change button configs and the sensitivity curve, but I'm not there yet.
Openboard (foss whiteboard) actually works with the touch sensitivity, but Activinspire doesn't. No big deal. Gimp doesn't until you set it to in device settings. Krita didn't need to be told what to do and works wonderfully.

My complaints:
The PITA driver installation isn't one really. They don't officially support linux - THAT is worthy of a complaint though. For those using linux, I'm going to guess, still, many are used to dealing with this.
The placement of the USB cord is annoying when in lefty (108 deg orientation), as the cord comes in your direction.
The drawing surface isn't huge, but that's a given. The challenge is that the sensitive area goes very close to the edge, making it hard to draw on the edges if you are not using this on a regular flat surface. I'm using it on my lap, most of the time.
The pen is also thick! 7/16" or 11mm diameter. Not super comfy. My hands aren't small. It makes using the buttons a little less than optimal, but I don't use them much yet anyway. I'm sure as I do more art with it than math, I'll want to customize that. I have an older wacom stylus I'll try to locate and see if it magically works. It was a far better fit.
All said and done, I do recommend this. I might even buy one of the larger ones.

Sony's Handycam line of video recorders has been a solid choice for years, and with the introduction of the HDR-PJ430V Handycam Sony has brought another excellent recorder to the market. It produces excellent quality video, it takes good still shots and it has some features I have never seen in other camcorders.

This is a very small, compact and lightweight camcorder, roughly the size of a box of butter sticks. Out of curiosity I put the camcorder with the battery installed on the kitchen scale and it weighed in at under 14 oz. The small size and very light weight make this camcorder very easy to hold in one hand without fatigue. This is very good news for people who either do not have a tripod or would rather hold the camera for all of their work.

At first power on, the user gets to select all of the necessary first-time settings - date and time, language and other preferences. This is all done on the touch-screen LCD. My last camcorder did not have a touch screen so I was minorly surprised by this feature. It also revealed the one and only issue I have had with this camera so far - the touch screen is slightly unresponsive compared to other devices I have used that offer the technology, and I find myself having to be very deliberate about accessing the screen's features.

Once the first-time defaults are set, this camcorder is ready to start recording. Without too much thought about what I was doing I pointed the camera at a target and started recording. As I panned the room, the camera made the necessary adjustments for light and dark, making a huge adjustment as I passed the screen of my computer and adjusting back to normal lighting as I passed it. This is a normal camcorder feature and it seems to handle the light differences very easily.

The zoom is above average. From about 40' away the camera can be zoomed in enough to read small lettering on a box. This is great for recording when the subject is at an appreciable distance.

The camcorder also seems to do a very good job of auto-focusing, which it does as light conditions change. Setting the camera close to a wall and shining a light around it, you can actually see it making focal adjustments on the screen and settling on a good balance of light and focus.

Video quality is, in a word, outstanding. Videos I have taken have come out exceedingly clear and bright without a lot of graininess that I have gotten with lesser camcorders. Even zoomed in all the way, image quality remains very good. Sound is also very clear and crisp.

Where this camcorder excels over any other camera I have used, though, is in the image stability (anti-shake or anti-jitter, if you prefer). Sony makes a big deal about their stability component and it works as well as advertised. Turning the camera around so that the lens is facing the user, one can jiggle the camera and actually see the lens being adjusted as the camera moves. It moves very much like an eyeball which honestly is a little creepy but it works very well. If holding the camera instead of using a tripod, video will definitely come out better as a result of this feature.

This is not just a camcorder, though. It also takes still shots. I like that this camera can be used as a still-shot camera, and though the user can make a few adjustments to make the image come out better, most of the settings are automatic. I have had better success with dedicated still-shot cameras, personally, though I have managed to render some good photos with the Handycam as well. The camcorder definitely does a better job than the typical smartphone when it comes to taking photos... It is very convenient to have a single device doing the work of two.

Probably the most interesting feature of this camcorder is the built-in projector. I had low expectations of this feature until I actually tried it. Projecting roughly 30' down a dark hallway, the projector built into the camcorder lit up the wall with bright, clear images that looked great. As I moved farther from the wall image quality diminished as expected and it got better as I got closer, but this feature really does work nicely. It does not work well enough to give a professional presentation, of course, but it is fine for entertaining small groups and for quick playback right after shooting. Be aware, however, that the projector runs through all available images and movies in one sweep without taking a pause between.

The software that installs when the camcorder is plugged into a computer is called PlayMemories Home, and it is actually a decent application for managing the content on the camera. It has more features than one would expect from the software that comes with a device. It allows for importing/exporting media, making basic edits on media (such as quick color adjustments and trimming/cropping), putting together slide shows, creating CD/DVD media, share online with several social media sites and a lot more. Most included software packages (at least, the ones I have seen) provide for much more basic handling of media.

I can clearly hear this one two rooms away indoors and even outdoors in areas with high ambient noise this can cut through and project sound.

Sound quality is neutral, and I mean that in a good way. While there is some bias towards the mid range frequencies it does not 'color' the sound of music being streamed to it. To be honest, this is not going to crank out heavy bass, so if you listen to bass-centric music you may be disappointed. On the other hand, the highs and lows are practically seamless, with a slight emphasis towards the mid range, so if you listen to jazz, blues or some forms of rock and Americana this speaker will probably please you.

One review discussed bluetooth range issues so I specifically tested that. Even two rooms away, which normally causes drops in quality, I was able to get crystal clear streaming with no drops in the music quality streamed from a Samsung Note 3. The distance is approximately twenty feet, but definitely not line of sight, so I am happy with that aspect.

While the product specs claim six hours of music, you can realistically expect somewhere between four and four and a half hours if you have the volume cranked. If you drop it to about a quarter - perfect for near listening up to two or three meters - you will get the claimed play time.

So, let me start off by saying, this isn't the best quality webcam on the market. But for the price, no one is expecting it to be. And it is FAR from the worst! During the Covid Pandemic, all the regular brand name webcams were sold out so I found myself trying out a bunch of these no-name brands from Amazon. The last one I tried actually had a much harsher fisheye effect in the corners, as well as over-saturated color. This one seems far less cartoony and more realistic in color reproduction, as well as being somewhat more rectilinear (photo speak for straight lines being straight, not as much curved distortion). There is a bit of fisheye curve on the edges, but it is very usable and didn't make my ceiling look concave like my last one I tried. See attached images for examples of the room's wall distortion. It's there if you are looking for it, but not terrible when you're looking at a subject. The microphone is just meh. I have a desktop mic and the sound out of that was MUCH better, especially because you can get it closer to your face than the camera. But the fact that this HAS a mic is a good option in a pinch. I would just strongly recommend an external mic if you want people to hear you clearly. Also something I didn't know before trying this:
It is MANUAL focus! That means it won't follow and focus on you automatically, you have to twist the lens until you're sharp in the view. It actually isn't that hard to nail focus, the depth of focus is pretty deep so once you've set it for your standard sitting distance, you likely won't have to change it ever again unless you walk away from the camera. A fun side effect, however is that the focus lens gear lets you push it to EXTREME MACRO distances! So you can do insane closeups of things if you want to, for example, put a webcam on an ant farm maybe? I tried it out on my desktop speaker, and in one picture you can see the relative size of it compared to my desk and then the closeup you can see the detail of the scratched plastic where it says Harmon / Kardon. Ha, if nothing else this shows me I should probably get new desktop speakers too! These are beat up when up close! A fun and versatile camera for a good price. If you need autofocus tracking, this might not be for you though.

SanDisk has come out with an extension to their array of MP3 players, beyond the Clip and the View. Their new mp3 player, the Sansa Fuze, is definitely geared towards casual someone who just wants a basic, functional, and well-put together media device for their pocket.

The Sansa Fuze may look like a tiny device at first, but this thing packs some serious features. It has the ability to playback music, video, photos, FM radio, as well as audiobooks. The features for the Sansa Fuze are very impressive to say the least, as it also features a microSD card slot to add extra storage space, content, etc.

The first feature we will focus on is the one which will likely get the most use, the audio aspect. The music menu is organized with artist, album, song, genre, etc. There is also a recently added section which shows the most recent songs added onto the device, as well as a top rated section.

The album menu allows you to see album icons as you are scrolling through the various albums. There is also the ability to form a playlist directly on the player.

The sound quality is very well-done. If you have a great set of headphones you will not be disappointed in the least bit.

The video aspect is definitely not the highlight of the Sansa Fuze. Part of this is due to the low power of the device, and partly due to the screen itself. The supplied Sansa Media Converter does make it easy to convert movies into a format for the device though. A typical movie will take up a little under, or over 1GB. The video looks respectable, but can get a bit choppy at times. One very cool feature about the video is the ability to add a bookmark while watching it.

The photo viewer is very standard as you can view photos from the internal memory of a microSD card. You can set up a slide show with time intervals, and add music as well. The images looked quite sharp.

The FM radio feature is done extremely well on the Sansa Fuze. You get some great reception and the auto program feature picks out crystal clear radio stations. It also has the ability to record radio in WAV format.

This works with voice recording as well thanks to a microphone located right below the microSD slot.

Podcasts and audiobooks are pretty self-explanatory, but one issue with the audiobooks is the lack of a bookmark feature.

The overall user interface for the Sansa Fuze is put together nicely, set up in such a way that a first-time user could pick up this device and feel right at home with it. You have a scroll wheel as well as a home button and a middle click wheel. The scroll wheel can also be clicked up and down, which can make things a bit confusing at times. Overall though, beyond a few hiccups with organizational aspects of the UI, this is one easy device to use.

Getting media onto the Sansa Fuze is extremely simple as you can use any desktop media player to create playlists and such, easily syncing them to the device. It also supports drag and drop without the need for any software. We used Windows Media Player as well as a few other media players to test this all out, and syncing was as simple as can be.

The quality of the device itself is top-notch, as the screen can put out some great contrast and vibrant colors in spots. The screen is extremely clear and does a nice job with photo presentations. Battery life is equally as impressive, as I have been getting around 20 hours on each battery charge thus far. Video playback came in at around 6 hours on a charge.

The package comes with a proprietary USB cable and a pair of earbuds, pretty basic.

Also shipping with the Sansa Fuze is a great bonus, a microSD card which comes with DRM-free music from more than 50 new and emerging artists. This is a great way to immediately test out the music capabilities of the Sansa Fuze, and also adds value to the entire package. Music videos, images, and more are also included on the microSD card.

Overall SanDisk has done a great job with the Sansa Fuze.

I purchased this HDMI Capture USB device to record a Windows desktop session. What I noticed is that the passthrough video quality is very bad. What is clear text coming out of the computer becomes blurry by the time it gets to the TV. What this means is that you can't keep this device plugged in permanently to record when necessary. You'd have to settle for plugging it in only when recording. Perhaps for gaming devices that have larger text and buttons, it wouldn't be a big problem.

This device can also be used to live stream by plugging it in to the USB port on your PC. A few problems here:
-- This is only USB 2.0
-- The USB port is also used as the power supply for the device. This means that if your PC doesn't provide enough power through its USB port (especially if you have an external drive plugged in to the device), you won't be able to use this function. They did not include those two-headed dongles to provide additional power.
-- The drivers are bad. I was able to get OBS to preview the device only after a lot of changing inputs around. VLC will not work with it.

What I do like about it is that while the passthrough quality is pretty bad, the resulting recording isn't. You can certainly tell that it is a recording, probably due to the video compression but all of the text from the 1080p desktop is readable.

I also like the fact that you can record directly to a USB drive with scheduled recording capabilities. The UI of the built-in software is straight out of VHS days but it does the basics of what you need. The convenience of being able to press record on the remote to start your capture means you can set up your PC how you need it without having to also manage your desktop recording software.

I bought a ZuneHD 32GB as a replacement for my iPod Video. I still have the iPod but I don't particularly care for it (never really did) so I decided to search for a better MP3 player. After digging online for a while I decided on the ZuneHD which has proven to be far and away better. It is not a perfect device but it's excellent for my needs.

Looking a lot like a small smart phone, the ZuneHD is a sleek and attractive device with a nice touch screen and a brushed metal back. Having never before used one of these I was a little confused at first on how it worked but the learning curve is easy and it took little time to get used to it. It works a lot like a tablet, actually. The screen is very responsive and navigation is simple.

I confess that I never used the ear buds. Instead, I use a set of really nice noise-canceling head phones and the sound coming out of the Zune is excellent. My music of choice is usually techno-trance stuff so there is a lot of base and a lot of synthesizer, and by default the sound is well-balanced and clear.

So, my main use for an MP3 player is to connect it to my car. My car has voice-controlled everything and I wanted to be able to listen to my music collection in the car without fiddling with the player directly. When I used the iPod I found that the system frequently got confused and the player would often select the wrong song. If it got confused enough, it would hang the voice activation for controlling the MP3 player for weeks at a time, so I gave up and put my Zune in the car instead. So far, the Zune and the car work together nearly flawlessly. As a bonus, the car keeps the Zune charged up.

The only drawback I have found with the Zune is that there is no way to expand the storage capacity. It would be nice to have the ability to add a MicroSD card in to expand the capacity.

I am exceptionally satisfied with my Zune. I likely will never buy another iPod again, now that I know how much better an MP3 player can be.

Right out of the box, the switch was on and the keyboard had completely drained its battery so it had to be plugged in and charged overnight. This was a surprise but was not a big deal, just unusual.

When connected to a Windows 8 system the OS recognized it and immediately it was usable. It required no special drivers, no configuration changes or anything else – just plug it in and turn it on. It worked the same under Linux as well.

The real test for this keyboard/mouse was on a Raspberry Pi system. The keyboard connected and worked without a glitch – expected since it worked fine with Ubuntu Linux but not guaranteed as the kernel was known to work but the hardware was not yet tested. With a second external keyboard connected it was possible to type on both at the same time and also to use the other keyboard as a regular keyboard and the other just as a mouse.

There are a number of other SBC types and designs out there, and there is no reason that this device should not work with any of them that have a Linux-based kernel. Embedded Windows system should also support it as well.

Though I have not really tested the full range it is good to at least 10 feet. At that range the system still recognized input from the keyboard and touchpad without any issues.

So far I have found only one issue with this keyboard and that’s the space bar. I habitually press the space bar in the middle, and on this keyboard the press sensors are on the ends. The spacebar is not quite stiff enough and when pressed in the middle it bows instead of pressing down on the sensors, thereby not registering the press. To get it to recognize the press I have to press on the ends specifically. This is a minor irritant and is a very small price to pay for what this device offers.

This is a very small but fully functional keyboard/touchpad combination that works with multiple configurations. It connects easily and so far has given no real operational issues. Keep in mind that this thing is extremely small, though, which is great for portability, mobility and economy of space but less pleasant for systems that aren’t being transported anywhere.

If you're like me, you've done some research (extensively in my case) on comparing these two speakers, and have probably come out with a vague case for each of them. Some prefer the Miccas, some prefer the Pioneers. I decided to order both and find out what the deal is for myself. And although I haven't ordered many speakers, I've been a headphone enthusiast for many years.

FYI, I'm using these with a sub (Dayton 1200), so I can't comment on their performance by themselves.

The Miccas sound pretty good, with clear highs - solid performers for movies. But they never made me very impressed by their sound. They seem serviceable, good for the price but not particularly great. They are by no means a bad speaker, but they are a bit thin sounding, kind of one-note.

With the Miccas, if felt like I was listening to music, but with the Pioneers, I felt like I was feeling it. They have a lush tone that is very musical, and I noticed I was bobbing my head to some songs I wasn't before. Better dynamics, soundstage - they really allow you to get lost in the music. Even though the driver size is the same, everything sounds bigger, with more depth.

And even though they have less treble energy than the MB42X, they seem to retrieve a bit more detail. Certainly not "veiled", just darker in tone. I'd prefer there to be slightly less treble than too much - just make sure to remove the grill, as it can make them slightly too dark.

For $20 extra bucks currently I think it's a no-brainer to get the Pioneers, unless you can't particularly stand speakers on the warmer side. I have the center channel coming in today - I've heard mixed reports on it, but if it's anything like the bookshelves I'm sure I'll be satisfied.

My favorite camera (Canon Powershot G12) has been giving me a lot of trouble this year. I decided to look into another one. I was looking for a good strap and found one from this company, but it is leather. It is great to use when I need a sturdy strap, but for storing in my case, the strap is too stiff. I got this one as an alternative.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes wrapped in a cardboard stuck in a tube. I took photos to show you so you can get an idea. It is quite smart because you always know where it is.

COLOR
This is a really attractive light gray color.

HOW TO ATTACH
This has a great loop system which loops into the camera rings. The cord loops are attached to a snap on piece which locks into place on the strap. The strap comes with two of these so you can swap it between cameras.

PERFORMANCE
I really love to use my leather strap, but for storage, I prefer to have the nylon strap on the camera. If I need a quick change I can, but both straps easily interchange because they are from the same company.

BACK OF STRAP
The strap has silicone bars on the neck area to keep it from sliding around. Sometimes I like it and sometimes I am not as fond of it. It is great for use around the house as I take a lot of photos of products and jewelry.

IS IT ADJUSTABLE?
This is adjustable which is another feature I like. I am not locked into one length like with the leather one.

SECURE CONNECTION?
I find that so far the connectors snap in well and are secure. Over time, I am not sure how they will wear, but for now they are working well.

PLASTIC OR METAL?
When I looked at the photos for this listing, I thought the connectors were metal, but they are gray metallic colored plastic/nylon.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This neck strap fits my camera and I am glad to have it. It stores well in my camera case and is easy to disconnect and swap with my other strap from the same company.

MY RATING
I am giving this FOUR STARS. I think it is a bit pricey for what you get. The strap is nice, but I don't think it is worth quite as much as the price listed. I still prefer my leather strap as it has a wider neck band, but this is a good one to quickly use when I have to store my camera in the case and don't have time to swap.

Update!!: my review below was originally written 07/2019. I wanted to add an update THREE years later, 07/2022. This little laptop is still kicking. I use it every single day from comfort of my couch to write reviews, do basic doomscrolling (lol), write emails, etc. Camera still works. Speakers still good. No major issues. I never did do any adjustments to it. Just sort of kept using it as is. I;m maxed out for memory, so it isnt something I would rely on for loading pictures onto, but as mentioned.. if you just need something to get online with and do some shopping or searching, then this is fine. Has been worth it. I happen to be sniffing around for another laptop so I can go more photo work with it, but I havent been in a rush. I came back to this review so I could refresh my mind on the specs. It was then that I realized 3 whole years has gone by! OK.. back to orginal review:

It's a basic laptop. The price is right. You aren't paying a lot for a little. You are getting quite a bit of what you need for a couple hundred dollars. Cheaper than most tablets. If you just want something to get you online, to browse the internet, watch some videos, listen to some music, write some messages, play some basic games, do some video chatting, then this might be for you.I think most people want that. It doesn't have a lot of memory or speed, or a slew of storage- but it will get you far if you don't expect a lot from it.

I'm a gamer, so I won't be playing any MMOs on this (nor on most prefabs that are out there). But I will use it to play a variety of offline and online games such as those found on FB or POGO (ie; puzzles, word games, board games, hidden object, casino style, etc).

I use youtube to listen to music, watch videos, listen to podcasts etc.. the speakers are fine. I can hear what I need to, clearly and loudly, if I wish. Some of the sounds that come through are more dynamic than I expected, so that is a plus.

I do a little bit of office stuff, so I will continue to make use of Google docs but there is an option to activate a free 1 year trial of Office 365 which includes 1TB of storage (One Drive); after that there is a fee. The Microsoft website breaks down the pricing options, which include pay for the year, or by the month, if that is of interest to you.

This Windows 10 is in S mode, which is a special mode that essentially limits Windows 10 in a variety of ways to make it run faster, provide longer battery life, and be more secure and easier to manage. YOU DO NOT HAVE TO KEEP IT THIS WAY! The idea is that there is less security with non proprietary items (apps, browsers, internet security), and greater chance of phishing, slower processes, decreased PC health, etc. So "S Mode" isn't a different version, it is simply a different mode, with the usual Windows 10 home, underneath. From what I understand, you can take it out of S Mode, and you will have Windows 10 Home (and then you can use browsers of choice, apps of choice, security software of choice, etc) BUT you CAN NOT switch back to S Mode. It is a once and done deal. S Mode default browser is Microsoft Edge, the default search engine is Bing.

I'm used to using a different browser, and having more freedom of choice, but I am curious how this S Mode will do, as I have noticed in my time of using it that it never bogs down. It is likened to Chrome on Chromebook- it seeks to streamline all the while being as secure as possible. If at any point I just don't like it, at least I know I have the option of just using Windows 10 Home. But again, it is a ONE WAY DECISION.

The laptop itself is super light weight. It comes in at just 3.24 lbs according to description. Full keyboard, touch pad, USB 2.0, USB 3.1, headphone/microphone port, media card reader, web cam, 3 prong charge plug with long cord. Attractive black textured design. I've got some fingerprints on the lid/cover, but doesn't look bad.

No dvd/cd player. I bought a cheap external for those times I want to use it for storage, watching a video, or listening to a CD. Hey, I like options.

Set up is quick and easy. When Cortana (Microsoft virtual assistant) came on, I let her guide me through the start up process. I could answer a lot of her questions with speech. It did well with recognizing my words.

I still have quite a bit of learning to do about this laptop. One thing that I find interesting is that it has an option to use a phone app- where it will link your laptop and phone to each other, so you can (according to Microsoft website)
-Link your phone and PC to unlock a variety of cross-device experiences for Android and iPhone.
-See recent photos from your phone on your PC for Android only.
-View and send text messages from your PC for Android only.

Again, the price is right. This does come into play for me in terms of rating. For a couple hundred dollars, I am able to scroll through FB endlessly, add some comments without tapping them out on my phone or tablet, can access full webpages, can take pics, or video call with web cam, can play some lightweight games, etc..

At this point in time, I give it a full rating. I mean, I wouldn't go below a 4 for this anyway, and a 5 might be pushing it, but it is a nifty little machine, and I am happy so far. Once I realized that I am not stuck with S Mode, that boosted my opinion of it (not all PCs or laptops are given this S Mode option).

If I learn anything more that I think you will find useful, I will come back to update. I hope what I have provided thus far has been helpful to you. Take care :)

When it comes to radios, so many of them just don't have the reception that they used to. I came across this one and decided it was worth the try. Unfortunately, the battery choice is annoying, but let's take a look at the radio..

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This is a pretty straightforward radio. It has AM and FM. Each band has a horizontal dial on it. The volume button is large and turns the radio on and off as well. You can adjust the tone from high to low which will either focus on voice or on base tones for what you are listening to.

HANDLE
The handle on this is sturdy and easy to carry.

ANTENNA
The antenna on this is sturdy and easy to pull out and push in.

JACK
There is a standard headphone jack.

HOW DOES THIS PERFORM?
This performs beautifully. The reception is exceptional and I can pull in stations that most other newer radios do not pull in any more. The sound is fabulous with a lot of depth to it.

BATTERIES
I really dislike that this takes 4 D batteries. Those batteries are expensive and tend to run out quickly. I don't normally carry them in the house for emergencies, but it would be worth having some since this radio is great and easy to hear.

WHO MIGHT LIKE THIS RADIO?
Anyone who loves to listen to AM still would love this radio. Many of them don't have it anymore which is frustrating. I also found that it is great for older people to have one of these. I know an older gentleman who has been bed ridden and home bound and he loves this radio. It is easy to operate, see, and great sound.

THE BOTTOM LINE
I like this radio. It is good to have on hand for emergencies or for good listening when internet is down or I just am tired of the internet radio channels and prefer to be local. The sound is great and operation easy. Fabulous reception.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is a perfect gift for older people or those who really enjoy local radio and prefer an easy to use radio that has great reception. Just be sure to have D batteries for emergencies. If it had rechargeable features, it would be perfect!

I got this for my daughter who is involved in a business situation where a camera, laptop, and tripod (plus accessories) are required for product photos, posting, and keeping track of inventory. She is always misplacing things. I wanted this to be in one place for her. Let's take a look.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This is true to the photos with the listing. The case is padded, has a velcro flap on it which has a zipper in the front flap for flat things like our flat flash which we keep in a padded box, or cords, etc. The case itself has plenty of padding in it and non-abrasive soft fabrics.

CAMERA CASE
The camera storage has two adjustable velcro type walls in it so that you can make it bigger or smaller. The other two compartments are for storing lenses etc, and one of them has a flap, but the flap is not something you can fasten down. The camera that goes in here is a Fuji Finepix S1. The front lens sticks out quite a bit but it is stored on its back and is plenty protected by all of the padding.

ZIPPER ACCESS
There is a top zipper access so that if you have the flap down but need a quick access, you can quickly zip open the top and remove the camera.

LAPTOP POCKET
We have a laptop that I was sure would fit in there, but it is just about a 1/4 inch too long for the pocket. I thought it was a 14 inch, but it turned out to be 15 inch instead. A 14 inch laptop or tablet will fit in here perfectly. A 15 will not.

STRAPS
The straps on the bottom are adjustable to hold a tripod which is great to help keep all of this in order. When I want to make it easier to store, I remove the tripod and stand it next to this bag until it is time to use again.

SIDE MESH POCKET
This has a side pocket appropriate for a water bottle or can of coconut water, etc.

HANDLES
There is a single carry handle and a shoulder strap. The carry handle makes this a bit awkward, so we tend to use the shoulder strap except when we need to move the bag quickly.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Even though I wish this were slightly bigger to fit the laptop, it is my error, not the bag company, so I have to say other than that, this bag is well designed and does the job. It is a great way to keep all of the camera gear handy for the jewelry business it is needed for.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. It is not fair to remove a star for the misunderstood measurement, but this is not as handy for my needs as I had hoped. I am leaving this at five stars, because it is still handy to keep everything together for taking photos for the business it is intended for.
