I only purchased a smartphone about a year ago, previously being in the flip-phone-for-life crowd, due to the requirements of a job I was on. Since then I have slowly been picking up the various accouterments of such devices, the latest being this magnetic mount. I bought it mostly so I can use Google Maps for navigation.

It is remarkably effective. I have a Motorola Moto X4, in a slim silicon case, and an 05 Subaru Outback. The kit comes with the magnetic mount, two metal plates with adhesive (a rectangular one and a little circular one), a clear adhesive interposer, and, as a nice surprise, an alternate, black bezel.

What you do is attach the metal plate to the outside of your case, the inside of your case, or your phone. If you choose the lattermost option, then you don't attach it directly to the phone, but to the clear adhesive interposer (just a clear plastic sheet with adhesive on both sides), likely to prevent surface damage and dampen shock/reduce possible strain. If you have one of those pop-socket devices, you attach the little metal circle to the center of that instead. Then, you fit the magnetic mount to one of the grilles of your car's vent system, wherever it is most convenient. Now you can mount your phone to it, the magnet clinging to the metal plate.

I attached the metal plate to the inside of my case. It is very thin - I would say 1mm or less - and even on my slim silicon case it leaves only a very slight rise, hardly visible from the outside. I also attached it about 2/5ths of the way up from the bottom of the phone, as recommended (the Moto X4 does not have wireless charging). The magnet adheres quite well to the phone - the silicon case actually slightly pulls away when detaching the phone from the mount - not nearly enough to dislodge the case, but enough to let you know that the magnet is really sticking. As the mount has a rubber pad, and my case has a rubber texture, the phone does not slide at all in any lateral direction, the shear resistance is quite high. I am not concerned about the phone just falling off during normal operation of the car.

The tines of the mount grip the vents quite well - I have only had the mount pull off the vents once when detaching the phone after parking. There are two sizes of gaps - narrow and wide - and the narrow gap seems to fit pretty well on the Subaru. I like how you can pivot the mount a little to the left or right, and use the vent's own hinge to pivot it up and down.

There are some basic shortcomings of design. Obviously you can only attach this to the vents of the car, which limits your choice of positioning. I tried putting it on the left vent, but that caught too many outside reflections. I tried the right vent, but my hand was mostly blocking the screen. I tried the left passenger-side vent, but found that this took my eyes too far off the road while checking the navigation. In the end, I went with the driver's side right vent, since it required the lease eye-movement to check navigation and it was actually helpful to have my had block the screen, so as to avoid distraction. The tines hold, but they are not as secure as a hard mount would be. Likewise, the magnet could, in theory, be bumped out of position by kids/pets/carelessness and fall down into the foot well.

However, I would generally recommend this, at least as someone's first mount, to get a feel for what they are looking for if nothing else.

This is the first switch that I have owned that can be configured.  That's a big plus.  Once you determine the IP address of the switch, you simply enter it in your browser, enter the default password (which you can change) and you are into the setup program that is internal to the switch. There are two reasons why I didn't give this a 5 star rating.  1) The indicator lights showing active ports are on the same side as the cables.  Since I want cables to go out the back, I can't see the lights with the switch facing me.  My prior switch had lights on one side and cables went out the other.  In all honesty, I can't say that the lights ever provided much benefit and could be distracting, so this might be an advantage to some people to have both lights and cables on the back.  What's the point of the lights if you can't see them, unless you want the cables facing you?  2) In order to register the switch and get a program to determine the IP address of the switch (so that you can configure it), you have to use a mobile device (a smart phone) and install the Netgear Insight application and set up a Netgear account.  Strange that you need to use a device other than a computer to do this and it is rather a nuisance.  Apparently there is no Windows version of Netgear Insight.  You have to use your IOS or Android device.  Another problem I had is that you supposedly can change your password on your device, which I tried, but apparently the password did not meet the requirements, but was never informed of that by the program.  I was able to change the password on the device after getting into it via the IP address.  Netgear makes good products and I have purchased other Netgear products in the past with good results.  This is another quality product, so if the placement of the lights doesn't bother you, I would recommend it, especially if you need individually configurable ports.

Out of the box, you must charge it for at least 4 hours (the light will turn green on the back of the device when it is ready). Once it was charged I was able to pair it with my Google Nexus 7 with little difficulty.

The build quality is pretty good. It feels reasonably solid in hand, and the plastic shell is nicely made.

I found the manual to be easy to follow. You have to switch the button on the back to "on", then hold down the power button for 8 seconds to get it into "pairing" mode (not the usual 3 seconds to simply turn the device on). Then initiate pairing on your device (in this case, my Nexus 7) and it's ready to go.

Sound quality is good, and pressing the - and + buttons adjusts volume. The peak volume is impressive, which I like because my primary use for these speakers will be to hear over exercise machines. It also works well in the shower, and it's more than loud enough to hear over the shower spray.

The manual says the battery can provide about 25 hours of use when fully charged. I haven't timed it, but it does seem to last a good while. It lacks a battery gas gauge, so there's no way to determine how much battery life is left.

There is one issue I've been having with the speaker - stutters and skips. I determined streaming quality was not the issue and the speaker was correctly recognized by and paired with my tablet. I was able to fix it once by unpairing the speaker from my tablet, and then pairing it again. On another occasion I went into the Nexus 7 settings to disconnect and then reconnect the speaker (as opposed to fully unpairing/pairing it) to get the audio to play smoothly. It's a little annoying to have this extra step, which makes this a 4 star experience, but ultimately not a deal-breaker for me.

It's a capable speaker that provides the portability and audio volume I was looking for.

I own a DJI Ronin S which I use with my Sony A7 series cameras (an A7S and A7Rii). It worked well enough, but after trying this Crane 3 Lab, I'm blown away and ready to sell my Ronin for this.
For starters, I love the ergonomics of the extra handle. Being able to hold onto it with 2 hands and shift from the handle to the pistol grip makes using this thing far more stable than trying holding just the pistol with both hands. It also makes it easy to pass and shift to a low angle mode, as well as seamlessly pass it to another person easily for those really impossible looking tracking shots (thought a window, down a staircase, etc). I'm also really impressed with the buttons and controls- if you've got a USB cable controlling your camera, there's a lot more you can easily access right from the gimbal without touching the camera than you can with the DJI Ronin S. With the Sony cameras, unfortunately, you can't control the focus motor of an automatic lens with the follow focus wheel... that's a limitation of the camera since Sony doesn't have that protocol in their USB remote interface. Other features work perfectly, however, and I've been told that other cameras like Canon and Nikon work with the focus control as well (this is something I'm hoping Sony changes in the future, but for now I'll just rely on auto-focus during gimbal shots).
Another HUGE improvement over other stabilizers is the ability to LOCK the axis motors in place. This is a fantastic tool to help when balancing (you can lock the other 2 axis and work on balancing them one by one, rather than holding the other positions in place as you work backwards like on the Ronin), and its also great to lock it in place when you are powered down and carrying it around- I've found that when taking a break with my Ronin, it is always awkward to walk around with it since the camera can flop and swing around as I walk. The Crane 3 doesn't have that problem if you just lock the motors in place with a little red switch.
Honestly, I wish I would have waited just a little bit longer before buying my Ronin S so that I could see how much better this is. The app is honestly just OK, I've heard people say they like the DJI app better and I would probably have to agree with that, but this just does everything else so much better that it I'd still say it is worth it in the end. The crane 2 is easier to balance in my experience, more forgiving (less crazy vibrating when the gimbals shifts out of balance), has better features and ergonomics and overall just seems to do a better job.
I STRONGLY recommend it if you are shopping around between those two options.

So I decided to go for MSI after doing much research on Nvidia Pascal-Powered laptops. I do a lot of 3DS Max work, and I'm a gamer since the 80's, so I figured, this may be the best route. I didn't want to get a laptop which, in a few months, would already be obsolete, so I skipped some of the other current gen models from the likes of Alienware with 970/980 m cards. I didn't give Asus a shot because I've had a not-so-good experience with my current and previous desktops. My current desktop (which is quite powerful so no qualms there)... had a keyboard issue, and I was only 3 months into ownership. Asus refused to replace it as their one year warranty only covers the PC itself, not the keyboard which I'm sorry, but is part of the system.They said if I paid for shipping they would give me a new one at cost. How generous - after the price I paid for that system.The keyboard is backlit red which matches the red-lit system and impossible to find. My previous Asus had a cheap motherboard / power supply, which overheated only a few months after my one year warranty was up.

This is my first MSI computer, and I have to say, the laptop is stunner. The Steel Series keyboard is a pleasure to type on with its generously- spaced keys, and backlit configurable color spectrum while the non-reflective IPS screen is gorgeous, sporting good viewing angles with colors that truly pop. I love 17" screens for gaming when I'm sitting on a recliner, as I don't feel like being hunched over a desk all night. I haven't used it for VR yet, but I did run the Steam VR Speed Test to see where it stands. On my Asus G11CD Desktop (16GB i7-6700 3.40Ghz and Nvidia 970), the results showed my system just making it into the VR ready green band. The same test on my MSI Laptop had the VR Ready indicator near the very end of the green band, almost off the chart. As for Windows 10 itself -- it's up within seconds thanks to the 128 SSD. There's not much to comment on the touchpad. I never use them - they're the spawn of Satan. I always hook up a wireless mouse.

I haven't had a chance to test all of my games yet, as my laptop less than a week old as of this review, but the few I've tried ran smooth as glass. I downloaded the demo of the updated System Shock which has a 2017 release. Using FRAPS FPS counter, I was clocking in 92-120 FPS. Same download on my Asus was roughly 75-83. I've been heavily involved with the Planet Coaster (Alpha) which is more taxing than most high end first person shooters. I am running large simulated theme parks, with very advanced lighting effects and all graphic options maxed out. With Nvidia GSync (this monitor supports it) enabled, I'm getting a solid 60 FPS .98% of the time. In comparison, my Asus using the same dense parks using V-Sync gave me an average of 45-50 FPS

Thankfully, there is not too much on the bloatware end. Most of the included extras are MSI tune-up/tweaking programs and surprisingly, quite useful. Norton Security however, is bloatware in my opinion. It came with my Asus, it came with this MSI, and on both systems, it was the first thing I deleted. I don't need it. I never will. Stop it.

As far as the audio, the Nahimic 2 Virtual Surround is super impressive. I've had other laptops in the past, and they've always sounded like tin can alley. The sound that comes out of this unit is rich, and at times, the surround effect is quite effective. The max volume could use another notch or two, but it's still quite competent. Definitely game and epic movie-worthy sound.

The system remains fairly cool and quite capable of dispersing heat properly. Running the power hungry Planet Coaster Alpha no doubt generates a ton of heat, but it all seems to flow out of the back vents, so no keyboard hot-spots. One issue: I use a very thin, rigid laptop mat so the back vent heat winds up flowing to my knees which can be uncomfortable. The one way around this is pulling the laptop toward you, allowing for about an inch of the mat to stick out of the back as a kind of shield. A welcome addition is the turbo fan which you can easily access from a button on the left side of the laptop. I usually turn it on for about a minute and it diminishes the heat fairly well. One of the included MSI utilities gives you more access to the fan's options. Besides the fan, the MSI Dominator Pro has additional buttons that handle quick access functions like sleep mode, sample keyboard color layouts, and other options. Oh, and if you're thinking about lugging this around to your local coffee shop, forget it....unless you want to attract a crowd of wide-eyed onlookers. Also, It's pretty heavy, as in home gym bicep curl heavy. Unfortunately, the one area I haven't tested (my apologies) is the battery life as I am not one who travels with my laptop. I keep my laptop powered through AC in my living room.

Any regrets? None whatsoever - my jaw is still on the floor, but I have a very minor gripe.

The Laptop has a huge sticker on the base, in front of the keyboard. It's one of those highlighted specs stickers that all laptops generally boast. On the list it shows 120mhz display, yet, the on-line specs shows it being a 60mhz. At first glance, your heart will skip a beat and you'll be thinking... WOW even better than I imagined! That is, until you look close at the tiny word under that feature which says (optional). Really MSI - If you're going to slap a "Look what I have inside me" sticker on my laptop, at least leave out what is absolutely not included.

This is the no-BS line from Cisco. Enterprise features, but nothing proprietary, no forced contracts, no stupid power port that requires special power cords...

Once I signed into the box, I pretty much had to change my password, but then I had a world of options at my fingertips that I could change at my leisure. There were a few things I wanted to configure right away, and plenty of others I realized I wanted after doing some research. I still have plenty to learn and play with when I have time I want to spend on this.

I do believe you can use Cisco command line to configure these, but it also has a very familiar (to other consumer/business equipment) GUI that is intuitive to use. I will say, though, that the GUI it can be pretty cumbersome if you want to use it to go through and turn on a feature on every single port individually. Part of the problem is that you have to save each port individually and then use the drop-down to do the next port. This switch can be a little slow to respond and therefore frustrating when changing multiple features in a row. I also have a 350 series 10 port switch that does NOT have that problem. I am not sure if it has more resources available or just has less to keep track of because of having fewer ports., but that might be a consideration if choosing between the 250 and 350 series. And if you use command line, you might not care at all...

Oh, and you have to do the "save to running config" thing like you do with the Enterprise stuff. Seems strange, but I guess it more or less makes sense why. But at least in this case you can just click apply...and then go up and click the blinking disk to save (to running config).

I am using this in my telecomm closet, which manages to keep nearly all the ports in my house hot. I'm using ports 25-27 as a 3Gbps link to my Cisco 350 series switch in my external cabinet, which connects my servers with multi-Gb links. This is all new functionality for me, but something I've been looking for for a long time.

Here's some random stuff I figured out along the way:

-I am using 10Gbps copper DACs between the two devices. They do negotiate down to 1Gbps, they are cheaper than buying multiple SFPs, and I can use them later when I get 10Gbps ports (so the only reason you'd use fiber is if you needed a >100m link.

-Port trunking works between DAC and regular Cat6 (apparently it won't work with fiber SFPs mixed with Cat6.

-Not sure what I was doing wrong before port trunking on another switch, but I couldn't get anything better than high-error best effort to work as far as speed. On these 250/350 Cisco devices I'm using, all four of my trunks are working perfectly and clearly working at full speed without uncorrected errors (if any at all).

-There are "green features" included, but off by default. The one looks at link length and lowers power on those links if less than 50m. You can only use this if you turn off the Energy Efficient Ethernet standardized protocol, which you might do if the device you are using doesn't work, but I haven't found a case where it correctly reads my link length (and my testers do figure out the correct length, so I don't get this). The other green feature is Energy Detect, which I've turned on across the board, but it's hard to tell if that really saves energy or not, because it just is "on" when the link is down.

-The ports are counted strangely. Port 1 is the top left. Port 2 is bottom left. Port 3 is top second from left, etc. This caused me some brief confusion. The great thing is that you can name all your ports in the GUI so that can make things a lot more clear for you, especially if you keep all ports in your building hot or if you at least keep most of the devices static.

There are a ton of features here, and even more on the 350 series. If you're deciding between the 250 and 350 series, I suggest you do some serious homework to figure out if you actually need the 350 series. Here are just a few of the things I noticed the 350 series has that the 250 does not (not a comprehensive list):

On the 350, you can set link speeds lower on LAGS, use protected LAGS, more LAGS, UDLD, Ethernet tagging, VLAN mapping/private VLAN, lots of VLAN grouping options and more VLAN settings in general, and ISCSI status for QoS.

Oh...worth noting is that the 350 series apparently allows many more trunk groups than the 250 series, which only allows 4, so I would not necessarily want a 250 series for my 24 port switch if I didn't have my servers separate on the 350 (yet it seems unlikely you'd need more than 4 trunk groups on a 10 port 350).

One thing I don't like is that on some rack mounted equipment, you have one set of "wings/ears", but multiple positions/mounting options. These mounting brackets at least are included, but seem like they'd only work with this switch AND you can only put them on in one position, which means the switch will protrude about an inch forward in your cabinet (Well, you can also mount the switch backwards, if you consider that helpful). It would be better to have the option of recessing the switch an inch if you needed to. I also wish they could recess the power supply port on these things since - even with the heatsink on the back of this - the power cord is still the thing making this a tight fit in my closet.

Despite those two nitpicks, there's really nothing about this switch I don't love. Yes, I can absolutely imagine this to be a great line for a company to use, and I think I could even get a robust network up and running without too much stress or trouble. But there are plenty of other real-world applications for a home network as well: setting restrictions for kids or renters or whoever from getting to all areas of your network. There is all kinds of port security features here, protected ports, and VLAN features, so you should be able to do just about anything you want to do with these switches. Also QoS, traffic limiting, etc. I love having these features at my disposal, even at home!

I received these earphones from Amazon Vine in early January, 2018. I liked the over-the-ears design. It makes the earphones far less likely to fall off when exercising. The sound quality is also excellent. I found its wireless bluetooth function quite handy for listening to music on my smartphone while walking, biking, lifting weights or doing calisthenics.

But suddenly, a few weeks ago, after only 7 months of use, the battery simply would no longer take a charge. The manual says that the battery should last through up to 300 charges, and there is absolutely no way that in only seven months I charged this device 300 times. It holds a charge well while the battery is working, much better than the other bluetooth earbuds that I have owned. So I could use it for up to five days without charging the battery. This means that, in seven months, I only charged the battery about 42-50 times, at most. This means the life of the battery was a mere 16% of what the manufacturer promised!

This is not a device in which the battery can be replaced. Therefore, once the battery dies, the earphones are worthless. Since the warranty is only for 90 days, there is no recourse with the manufacturer for replacing this device after that length of time.

The way that this product works is a good idea, but until the design includes the possibility of replacing the battery, the high price is simply not worth it. I will have to stick to cheap earbuds which are not such a hit to my pocketbook when their non-replaceable battery dies.

Many cars on the market come with a rear-view camera that allows for seeing where the vehicle is moving when in reverse. Often the view appears on a dashboard screen. This is handy when parking and maneuvering while the vehicle is backing up. For vehicles that do not have a rear-view camera the alternative is to add on a kit that provides the same functionality. This is my first experience with such a kit and so far I am pleased with it. It does require doing a little work on the vehicle to set it up but the effort is worth it.

The package contains everything needed to set up this camera system. In addition to the camera and the screen, the kit includes the mounting screws for the actual camera as well as all of the wiring to connect everything together and to the power (reverse lights). There is also a mini-remote for interacting with the video screen though this is slightly inconvenient.

I spent a good deal of time reading and rereading the directions and concluded that the instructions could have been better. There are three pieces of documentation in the box; one shows a generalized set of four different configurations for connecting everything together (the fourth diagram on this sheet matches the configuration you want), one is a photocopied image of a wired system and the third is a “User’s Manual” which is one half-sheet of paper with a brief summarization of the product. There really needs to be a better documentation set than this.

If you are not skilled in working with electrical systems, either plan on this taking a good while or have someone you trust install the system. It’s not especially hard to set one of these up, but it does take some patience and a little bit of knowledge of the layout of the car’s wiring. I have worked on car electrical systems in the distant past so I had a vague familiarity, but it still took me a while to have everything set up and working.

Once wired the system is fairly straightforward to use. If it is wired up properly (meaning everything is connected to power on both ends and the two main components can see one another) it works nicely. The image when the camera is feeding to the monitor is bright and reasonably clear; the brightness can be adjusted as needed which helps when using this system at night. Another reviewer commented that he used a different camera connected to this system - while I am personally satisfied with the image quality, it’s reassuring to know that you can use another video camera if desired or necessary.

The addition of the remote will appeal to some, but for me it’s a component that can easily be lost. The menu system on the monitor provides the same functionality as the remote and this is good enough for me.

This is my first experience with rear-view video systems and though it gave me a little trouble setting up it was from lack of good documentation and inexperience, not from being a bad product. Once installed this is a nice and easy-to-use video system. Time will tell how long it works.

[[VIDEOID:1be91bfc02339bd396543d05da1fee38]] There are SO many things about the Angel's Horn turntable that impress me. But, first, you need to be a true audiophile to appreciate the way this turntable was designed and built.

Gone are the days of the automatic turntable, where you just drop on a stack of records and walk away. Those things were the WORST! Sure, you were free to do other things for longer periods of time. But, they were very harmful to your records. A true collector would NOT even consider having one of those things.

First, the body of the turntable is ONE SOLID PIECE OF OAK! No particle board, no hollow box, no cheap crap!

Then, there is the direct one-belt drive, no multiple gears or belts. And the motor has ONE job, the turntable. Changing the records and setting the tonearm are YOUR job, as is true with any turntable worth it's status as 'top of the line' with this one.

Now, the tonearm is another factor. As we all know, too much pressure on the record (or too little) can affect the quality of the sound, not to mention the wear on the vinyl. And, vinyl is a fragile medium, revered as one of the best sources of true stereophonic sound. We vinyl fans collect the best recordings and do everything we can to preserve that quality. When we play our records, we do so with love and care. The tonearm on this turntable is built just for us. It's counterweight is perfect, allowing us to adjust the balance to a microgram. I've not found a tonearm with a more accurate adjustment as this one.

The ability to switch between input types is a nice feature. Some of us prefer to provide our own preamps, allowing us further tweaking of the sound quality. I do. Thank you.

The dust cover is great for those that have their turntable out on top. I have mine contained within my entertainment center and opted to leave it off.

I am VERY happy with my Angel's Horn turntable and very happy to give it five stars.

I was trying to setup a studio for a multi-cam live Q&A web-broadcast, and this unit came highly recommended. Turns out this might not be the best choice, and the whole experience sort of leaves a bad taste in my mouth.
First the good:
The functionality of this device really impressed me! All I wanted was a live HDMI switch that would let me keep the audio separate (so it would be live regardless of camera active) and wouldn't blank the display when swapping inputs (which consumer hdmi switches do, as the connection re-negotiates). This unit goes far beyond that, using industry standard production controls for cuts and cross fades, title / graphic overlays, and even some basic Chroma Keying for doing live green screen (that was a surprise!). The little LCD is pretty neat too.
And now, THE BAD:
THERE IS NO HDMI OUTPUT. It only supports SDI, which no one mentioned to me when I said I wanted to toggle between HDMI sources. There is an HDMI preview which shows you multi-view (all the cameras in a grid), but no regular HDMI output. Only SDI, which is ridiculous to me. You have the HDMI port there, at least give us the option to choose whether it is multi-view or program out! Black Magic claims they didn't offer the HDMI out because the connection isn't reliable, so they want to push SDI as the output. But that isn't acceptable, the hardware is there, give us a choice! The result of this stream is going to an internet broadcaster which supports an HDMI input only! Now I'd need to purchase yet another accessory to convert the final product back into an HDMI signal so it can get where it needs to go.
Oh, and speaking of additional accessories that need to be purchased, THE BOX LACKS A POWER CORD. You have to source your own. That seems silly, its such an inexpensive thing that you expect to be there. Thankfully I have a cord from an old lighting accessory that I don't use anymore, but it seemed very odd that it was missing to me. Then, it did not come with a setup guide or instructions, only an SD card. That's fine, going green and all that, but I put it in my laptop and it came up blank. So now I have to find the software and manual myself. And at first, I found what I thought was the correct manual via Google only to realize it was for a different version of their ATEM products.
I know this is an inexpensive product for what it is, but let's be serious for a moment- it still costs nearly $1,000. For that amount of money, how much could it really cost to throw in a power cable and printed manual? $5? 10? Compared to the price of the unit, that's close to nothing. I also know that the buttons on front are because it is designed to be rack-mountable, but when you're setting this up on the fly and try to put on a tabletop, the controls are just awkward. It would have been a lot nicer ergonomically to have some controls on the top instead of the front side. But now that's just nitpicking. At the end of the day, I feel like this device is frustratingly close to what I was looking for, but the experience has been pretty crummy so far.

I have worked with a lot of ANC headphones, and I have a different pair of JVC phones that have served me well. I looked to these phones as a possible replacement for a dead pair of Bose QC-15 phones that finally just wore out. These are good phones that balance sound quality and ANC nicely.

The ANC function is what interested me most about these and I set about testing them. These work very well but they are not as aggressive as Bose or Sony when it comes to actively cancelling out low-frequency noise. This is a good thing in most cases as the aggressive ANC on Bose and Sony is actually uncomfortable when turned on. Where the two bigger players go all-out for maximum ANC function, these go for "good enough for most" and in terms of how they compare against other manufacturers such as Sennheiser, Philips, and other well-known brands they compare well. They cancel out the lion's share of low droning noises such as road noise and fans, enough so that turning on music at low volumes is still workable in noisy environments.

The sound profile is another important consideration and I have seen a wide variance in sound quality, particularly among ANC phones. These get the sound profile fairly close to right which is a refreshing change. The bass is present and strong but isn't pushed forward as with so many other headphones. The midrange is warm and gives music a decent depth. The highs are clear and bright without being shrill. These aren't audiophile quality phones by any means, but they are better than many I have used.

These are over-the-ear phones which is my preference. I also like that these fit snugly and don't slip off whern I look down which is also a personal preference but it's important to me. If you like a very light set of phones these probably are not quite the right fit for you; if you like a set that fits a bit more firmly, these are good in that regard.

These are comfortable too. The ear cups are padded nicely and I can wear them for a couple of hours before I need to take them off for a few minutes. Most headphones I have worn get uncomfortable after a while, and these do also but it is not as quick as with many.

My one complaint is the way these are powered on and off. Instead of a simple on/off button or switch, the cans swivel to power them on and off. I can see the potential for taking them off and leaving them powered on, resulting in reduced useful runtime.

I like these phones and have been working with them quite a bit of late. They're not a complete replacement for more aggressive ANC phones but they get the sound profile right and they are comfortable enough to wear for a long flight. These strike a nice balance between comfort, ANC capability and sound quality.

I'm a big fan of the Mi Band series of trackers, and this is the first device that finally got me to switch to something else. If you aren't familiar, Xiaomi and Huami aren't big brands in the US compared to other countries, but these are solid high quality products and not your standard fare Chinese junk. I've tried a LOT of different fitness trackers and smart watches- Everything from Google WearOS, Fitbit, Apple, and all the way down to the cheap trackers from Chinese throwaway brands with obscure apps. For a long time I've said I liked the features and quality of the expensive brands, but found they all had major flaws (battery life being a major one- I don't want another thing to charge as often as a phone!). The Mi band from Xiaomi was super affordable and high quality compared to others in that price range, and had a battery that only required being charged once a month.
This is basically the smarter older brother of that band. It is compatible with Mi Fit, so all my data transferred right over, but it is so much nicer than the band. For starters, the notification system is easier to read and keep up with messages, but the benefits go far beyond a larger screen. The music control is a nice touch, I like being able to pause and adjust the volume without taking my phone out of my pocket if playing on a BT speaker while I'm doing dishes, for example. The tracking is pretty accurate compared to other expensive brands, and while it doesn't support apps like Wear OS and Apple Watches, it has all the fitness functions you'd need built in already, including some fun widgets beyond the expected ones like a stopwatch, phone finder and even a compass! And unlike cheap brands, the UI is responsive and smooth. Not the smoothest out there for sure, but more than acceptably smooth considering how much a flagship smartwatch costs compared to this.
It has support for voice commands, but I honestly found that feature kind of gimmicky more than useful. The higher end version of this includes a speaker which might make the command function more useful as sort of a digital assistant, not to mention the ability to take phone calls from your wrist. But the model I got to try out lacks the speaker, which is a fine compromise for a cheaper price tag all things considered. The battery life at first was just OK, a few days on a charge if using lift-to-wake functions, but just as on my Mi Band tracker of old, I found if I turn off auto-wake and rely on using the button to wake the display, the battery life goes from counting in days to counting in weeks. That's the killer feature of this device- the ability to leave it on to track fitness and sleep habits without having to charge it so often. I'll have to charge it more than my old Mi Band's monthly top up for sure, probably at least 2x a month, but that's still very manageable.
So that's it, after years of loving my Mi Bands and considering it the standard by which all practical fitness trackers should be judged, I'm finally moving on to an Amazfit watch. This is a difficult value to beat.

Bluetooth... These are a pain in the backside on Win 7. When I want to use them I have to go and delete the previous pairing, pair them again and then go to the control panel and set these to be used for output. For movies on the computer, they get out of sync. I even set my movie player (Pot Player which I highly recommend) to use the Bluetooth headphones and they still get out of sync with the audio. I don't know if it's the player, the USB Bluetooth adapter, Windows 7 or some combination of them together.

I like that they can be used with a wire as well as with bluetooth. The controls are a little small, as mentioned by others but I don't have trouble working them.

I also tried the JBL EB45T Bluetooth headphones, which cost almost twice as much, at Target and these sound better overall. The JBL might have had better highs, a little punchier bass but these are more cohesive across the frequency range with nothing tweaked to make them sound 'better'.

Summary: I don't have any other Bluetooth headphones to compare these to but I think most people would be very satisfied with these at this price point for general use. If however, you are looking for audiophile on a budget, it's not here.

This is my review of the Opiheyoo Portable RGB Video Lights 3100mAh Rechargeable LED Camera Lights Mini. For a photo light the size of a thick cell phone, this little light is brighter than I expected and has useful features. First, you can use it while plugged in or if your battery is charged (and mine came fully charged), you can use it unplugged. And it's so portable!

If you use a lot of electronic gear, you'll probably find adjusting the various features very intuitive - I did. The dial for adjusting to colors is also the power button. Just push it in without turning it. You can adjust the color temperature with one of the dials, and you can adjust brightness with the third dial. All your settings show on a small screen that also shows your battery life. Since I'm tired of using a large, wired ring light for smaller items, this smaller light is great. And it's so portable!

The light has a tripod hole on a wide side and another on a narrow side. It fit my ball head and monopod without a problem. The light comes with a silicone soft box, a tripod adapter (I think that's what it is) and a charging cable/adapter.

A quick word about expectations. This light isn't going to replace my 4 500-watt photo floods on heavy duty stands. It's the size of a cell phone. But for close ups, fills for smaller subjects, macro photography and like that, I found it more than bright enough. I expect it would also be a good selfie light. For its size, it can be dialed up to be very bright.

One more thought. If you're one of those people who can see flicking in LEDs that other people can't see, you'll see the flickering here - I do. But it doesn't affect the pics at all.

I'm very happy with this light. It delivers everything I wanted - adjustable brightness, adjustable color temp, nice and bright, and it can be used plugged in if you forget to charge it. Add in the two tripod holes, and I'm very happy I chose the Opiheyoo Portable RGB Video Lights Mini . If anything changes, I'll update this review.

OK I admit it, I am leery of Linksys wireless routers. I have had four routers in my life (the E4200 being the fifth) and only the Linksys router gave me headaches. I vowed to never get another Linksys in my life, but I like Cisco so this was a dilemna and so far I am have been happy with it.

Design

This is a very slick device. I love the low profile that lets it hide on top of the cabinet it is on. A nice looking piece of hardware.

Setup

I have never had an easier set up on any wireless router. I installed the software onto my MacBook (mac friendly) and it self-discovered and prompted for the rest of the set up. Very nice setup, although a little long from beginning to end (7 minutes or so.) I loved that it prompted to personalize the SSID and password right up front. Software was slick and straight forward. Once set up I had all 7 wireless devices in the house on-line in about 20 minutes. Even my wireless printer worked instantly. - Five stars on Set-up

Functionality

I have only had the device installed for a weekend now, but I spent that time backing up my hard drive to a wireless SAN, watching streaming netflix and uploading a new website. No hiccups at all. About the only thing I did have an issue with is trying to set it up with my Ooma. I needed to rebooted the router and modem after removing the Ooma. No blame here, the Ooma doesn't seem to want to play nicely with any router or cable modem.

I really like the ability to have a guest network. It is easily turned off and on so I can easily provide a connection to visitors, but turn it off and totally deny the Brazilian students next door (actually it is password protected so it is not wide open, but less secure.)

Speed

I may not be the best to judge speed. I am not the type to watch the throughput numbers, but I can say that netflix streamed Mars Attacks wirelessly to my Wii without any issues. I have no issues with the speed at all.

Conclusion

I am very happy with the router. Who knows, two years down the line, I may be able to let my prejudice against Linksys go. If things continue to go well, or if they take a turn for the worse, I will update this review.

I have a set of Bose QC-15 headphones and I damaged the pads some time ago. I was able to find replacements, though the original Bose pads are quite expensive. I have been looking for good replacement pads that are less expensive and I have tried some off-brand pads in an effort to save money. So far I have found none that are an exact match though I have seen some that are quite close. These are a reasonable match though they are definitely different than the original pads, but at a fraction of the cost.

In appearance these are close to the originals though they are smaller and they do not fit exactly the same. When I put on the headphones with these pads in place, I have to fiddle with the phones a little bit to get them to fit right, more so than when these had the original pads. It’s a noticeable difference but it is not a real problem unless you have to have an exact match.

The pads are soft, but not as subtle and buttery as the original pads. They will soften over time with use, but brand new they are slightly more stiff.

The main difference I have found with these pads is that they do not do as good a job with passive noise canceling as the original pads. I replaced one pad with one of these new pads and put them on my head. With a fan on in the background I listened closely. The new pad allowed more ambient noise to reach my ear than did the original pad. As it softens I think it will fit a little better and will help with the noise isolation, but even new the Bose original pads did more for sound isolation. They still do a good job, just not as good.

So, why would you consider these? There are two good reasons to buy these. First, these are a LOT less expensive than the Bose replacements. At under $10 these represent a very significant savings over the manufacturer’s own replacement pads. Second, although these are different than Bose replacements, they do a good job of making the phones look new and they do the job well enough for most people. The phones are plenty comfortable with the new pads on and unless you are looking for difference you probably would not notice.

These are good pads to consider if you need replacement pads for your headphones and you don’t mind the small differences. If you have to have 100% identical pads, these aren’t what you’re looking for. If you are content with approximately 85% the same, these are a very inexpensive alternative to Bose replacement pads.

I wanted to build a relatively inexpensive computer to replace my 7-year old machine (also custom built), and after looking at various options I opted for this MSI mobo. The Bios flash is easy to do with the firmware file loaded onto a USB key. (I didn't try the funky flash button, did it from the interface.) I wish MSI provided a Windows app to download and update the Bios, as some other brands do, but this is a minor thing.

For the price paid, the value of this mobo is excellent. I highly recommend considering it for a mid-priced Ryzen build.

I don't think I could have gotten it exactly right had I not used this method: Before peeling any film, lay it where it needs to be and use scotch or masking tape (easily removable kind) to tape the long edge nearest the 'tab' to be pulled. (2 pieces positioned a couple inches from the ends should do it.) Then lift the film and start pulling the tab to remove the plastic a little bit at a time - with it up in the air a bit, adjust so it's straight (the tape keeps it aligned) and let the uncovered tabbed corner adhere to the screen. Slowly work your way diagonally pulling, adhering, and (I used a credit card) smoothing out. It just takes a bit of patience. I have zero air bubbles and just one tiny speck of dust I'd missed.

I have worked with a lot of different headphones, mostly active noise canceling (ANC) phones but also more traditional phones. Over the years I have had several Sennheiser phones and they typically have balanced sound and good build quality. This set is a step down from many of the others with which I have worked, though they’re still decent.

My preference on headphones is over-the-ear phones which for me are more comfortable. These particular phones are on-ear, and these pinch a little after extended wear. They’re better than some of the other on-ear phones with which I have worked, but I still prefer over-the-ear phones. One preference I have is a headphone that clamps down fairly tightly when worn so they’re less likely to slip off when I tilt my head down; these are a lighter fit.

These are Bluetooth-only phones and as such cannot be used with non-BT devices. This is unfortunate but isn’t a deal-breaker. These connect easily and quickly.

These are not ANC phones, but they have excellent passive noise canceling which is quite surprising for on-ear phones. They reduce ambient noise in my office considerably, which us especially noticeable when running a large fan that I use to generate white noise. I am pleased with that aspect of these phones. These are still not as effective as a set of ANC phones.

The sound profile is fairly typical of Sennheiser phones, though the bass is mildly beefed up.. The trend with phones these days is overdriven bass, and these do increase the bass response a little bit but not to a headache-inducing level. The midrange is full and warm, and that’s a good thing as many times the increased bass comes at the expense of the midrange. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. Overall, the sound is reasonably balanced, but certainly not audiophile quality.

Build-wise, these actually feel a bit on the cheaper side which is surprising. These aren’t exactly fragile, but they are definitely not of the same build quality as other Sennheisers I have used in the past.

These are probably best described as entry-level headphones. They’re not the highest quality, and they are not the most sturdy, but the sound quality is fine and the cost is right. The main thing I would change is the addition of an audio port so they could be used as wired phones.

This time I experimented to see if I could get Debian Linux distro running on the NVME on my older workstation.

It took a few tries. Getting the OS to boot directly from the NVME was a no-go. Since the NVME is mounted on an adapter card, I had hoped it would trick the system into thinking it was just an ordinary SATA drive and boot from it. But that didn't happen.

So what I did was installed all the Linux OS EXCEPT for the boot folder on the NVME, and put the boot folder on the SSD HDD. So it boots from the SSD but the entire OS is on the NVME and runs from it.

Step one:

The partition manager in the Debian installer didn't want to partition the NVME at first.

So I bailed out of it and used GParted (Gnome disks utility couldn't do this) to "create partition table" and selected msdos as type. That wiped everything and turned the whole drive into unallocated space. From that point the partition manager worked.

Step two:

From the linux bootable USB installer I partitioned the SSD (not the NVME) with a primary partition labeled (to be mounted) as /boot. (You can make this partition most any size from a few GB on up---the boot files don't require a lot of space.) The remaining space I manually labeled as /msc.

I partitioned the NVME so the installer would put everything else on it, starting with / (root). You can simply make the whole NVME / root and the installer will take care of putting everything else on that drive, or you can do what I did and set up size-defined partitions for /home, /usr, and so on.

After installing the system, the installer asks where you want the bootloader GRUB installed. I selected the SSD.

It worked. The SSD does the booting to the NVME, which then runs the OS. And it did improve speed.

The rooCASE Oragami Case seems to be currently at or near the top of the cases, the big advantage of this case being the number and variations of orientations, including both portrait and landscape, and at the price point, is hard to beat.  The oragami cover is ingenious, you can fold it up all sorts of ways, the iPad Air has a lot of applications that fairly beg for portrait orientation (reading a book, newspaper, etc.).  The conventional Apple case supports only landscape, as do a number of competitors (the CaseCrown Omni is one of the better conventional ones).  The Moshi and O!Case are also oragami cases, although the designs differ some.  The rooCASE has a more rubberized or grippy exterior, key because it's less likely to slip and get dropped.  Protection is generally pretty good, but the CaseCrown does a little better on edge protection, the openings on the rooCase tend to be U-shaped, the CaseCrown is more O-Shaped, but otherwise they are very similar.  The Moshi has one advantage, in that it has a back magnet, that lets it stay open better in book mode.  The rooCASE actually has magnets that keep it closed pretty well, but it lacks a back magnet.  The rooCase front cover of course folds up to support quite a number of variations or angles, which is a big advantage over conventional cases, and on a desk or table, is plenty stable.  The microfiber front interior is nice, it tends to help keep the screen clean, but it is worth noting that the orgami pattern tends to show up in the fingerprints and grease, so you do need to clean the screen from time to time.  rooCASE also shuts off the iPad Air screen when you close it, a very useful feature.  The end result is still pretty light and easy to carry, in keeping with the iPad Air design point.  Why not 5 stars?  rooCase is very close, but they could improve the edge coverage/protection, and add a back magnet (ala Moshi), and NuGuard KX probably has the better back protection (at the cost of some bulk), but at its price-point, front and back protection, oragami design that lets you pick multiple orientations and angles, the rooCASE is pretty much unbeatable, and worthy of consideration at any price.

I tried 2 other antennas at this location and was less than thrilled by the results. One was an amplified unit that I purchased years ago that had two vertical antennas that could be independently positioned forward or backward up to a ~45 degree angle from a straight, vertical position with a rotating base. I don't recall it's brand, but it worked fairly well most of the time, but I found myself going back to the old method of adding aluminum foil to get the best reception. The second antenna I tried was an RCA amplified bar antenna. It picked up most channels, but I had to change its direction back and forth depending on whether I wanted the CBS or the NBC affiliate; I could receive most all other channels with either direction. I returned that unit to WalMart.

According to AntennaWeb.org, I should receive 27 channels from 13 stations; the government site stated that I should receive 8 stations with a strong signal, 1 station with a weak signal, and that I would not be able to receive 1 station in the area. With this antenna, my TV found 49 channels this morning when I re-ran the scan, including all the channels listed on both sites that I mentioned previously. The first night that I ran the scan, I was able to pick up over 50 channels, including Channel 5 from Nashville! It was very cloudy that night, and I assume that reception was due to a propagation anomaly since I have not been able to receive that channel since then.

I highly recommend this antenna. For the record, I ran this test 11 floors up in a high-rise apartment building in downtown Louisville. As others have noted, very slight changes in the orientation of the antenna significantly affects reception of some stations. My antenna is currently attach to a window on one side and bends around the frame and attaches to the wall on the other side of the antenna. (I recommend getting some of the 3M replacement strips to attach the antenna so that you can re-arrange it as needed.)

I have a Fuji X-T3 and I have not shied away from third-party lenses at all. I have been looking for good wide-angle lenses and I have been aware of TTArtisan for a while. I was curious how well this lens would perform and I decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it though I am still working with it and learning that it can do.

This lens is a brick! Right out of the box I was startled at the overall weight. It has a lot of glass in it, but it also is all metal - very little (if any) plastic. Even the front lens cap is metal. In spite of the price, this is a solid little lens.

It is probably the tightest fit lens I have used. It requires a little pressure to get it to click into place and to remove it later when mounting on the camera body. I was a little concerned at first, thinking I could potentially damage the camera. However, it does fit and does not harm the camera in spite of how tightly it fits.

Optical quality seems to be good, though that varies a little with the aperture setting. At the widest settings (and f/1.4 in particular) there is a little softness in the corners and a slight vignetting. As the aperture is closed more the image gets sharper at the edges. This is not unusual or unexpected for wide-angle large-aperture lenses, and it is actually slightly better than I was expecting.

I have not yet had a chance to get out and determine the coma with this lens. I am waiting for a clear night so I can get a starry sky shot with the aperture wide open, which will highlight not only the coma but also the chromatic characteristics. If it is particularly bad I will come back and update.

As a portrait or landscape lens this one works very well. Initial exposures have worked out well, but I am still learning what this lens can do.

Are there better wide-angle lenses out there? Sure - and they cost a lot more too. For the price this lens is far better than expected and I am looking forward to working with it more. It is good enough that I am staring to look at other TTArtisan offerings.

Update: I really love this machine. You give a lot of things five stars if they're really good products, but this one deserves bonus. Original review:

Before this, I had two Sony receivers in my living room. My secondary is a much older model - about 12 or so years old - that does not have HDMI and I use it for my whole house audio system. My primary is (was - it just got replaced) a 3-5 year old Sony model that is admittedly in a lower class than this Yamaha receiver (the secondary was in a higher class in its time, I think).

While I usually have all Sony stuff, I was completely willing to try another well-known Japanese brand who specializes in receivers and amps. And - it's just awesome. Totally. Not a single regret about the switch. The RX-A880 gave me back everything I lost going from my older, higher-end Sony to my newer one, AND it gave me so many nice surprises on the way! As anyone can tell you that it sounds good and looks good, I'll concentrate on this little details that I discovered during setup:

1) Besides the seven HDMI inputs, it also has a composite video, a component video, two optical audio, one extra (second belongs to component) coax audio, and two composite audio inputs, not to mention phono.

The great thing is that you can assign different audio inputs to any of the video inputs. So, for example, I decided to keep my Wii around since I now have a component input (and it takes up almost no space), but the cable is component video with composite audio, but the component video input on this has coax for the audio. Bummer. But no, you can change it. Example number two is I have a computer in my telecom closet hooked up to this with both HDMI and line-out audio. For circumstances too complicated to define here, audio does not output via the HDMI. But because of this feature, I can make the audio appear when I select the HDMI input OR when I just want to listen to the audio directly (with no HDMI output). Perfect.

2) 9 Speaker outputs. First, I'm so happy to have the 2-zone thing back (my secondary receiver has it, but my other, newer Sony did not - it only had A/B speakers that shared an amp). But this one you can actually have 7.1 AND a second zone (although you can't play them at the same time. This is really cool if you want the best of both worlds. I don't know if I can find a place for two more speakers in my setup, but ...it's nice to have the option. Supposedly, this all works automatically. I imagine it could work fine, but I am unable to try it at the moment.

3) 2-zone done better. My older Sony had 2-zone, but the controls were - frankly - atrocious. It was always confusing, even for someone like me who can be a super A/V nerd and memorize anything. The way I use it now is just to keep the remote on Zone-2, and do Zone-1 on the unit itself.

This Yamaha, however, has a simple switch on the remote, and you're either controlling one zone or the other depending on that switch. Simple and effective. You can also control it from the unit, unlike the older Sony.

4) 8 custom presets, all controlled directly from the remote. Another 8 for Zone 2?!

The one complaint I read by a reviewer was that you have to scroll through all the inputs from the remote to get to what you want. But that doesn't matter for two reasons: first, you can change the settings to skip anything you don't want. But, second, with 8 custom presets - and each with their own remote button - you probably don't even ever need to scroll through the inputs anyway.

And the custom presets are great. You can turn on and off a bunch of features like whether or not it changes your HDMI out settings, if it uses your YPAO settings, extra bass, which speakers it uses, etc. And it even can link the second zone!

Two great examples:

I can't stand to watch regular background TV with the surround sound on because it makes the commercials that much more obnoxious. But of course I like big booming bass and surround for movies. And it's also annoying to switch the unit off and on all the time, especially if you want to use control for HDMI. So I have one preset for very flat TV sound using just the front speakers that is clearer than-, but no more annoying than-, my regular TV speakers. Then I have another preset for surround sound and big bass for movie watching.

I have one preset for straight music just in zone 1. Then I have another preset for straight music in both zones one and two. It turns on zone 2 automatically. I could not figure out how to make a preset just for zone 2, but it seems that when I am controlling zone 2 on the remote, I can make 8 more presets just for zone 2. You can not adjust these presets via menu, from what I can tell, though.

5) 14 character names on the front of the unit in dot matrix. My other receivers were all limited to 8 characters. You can see all 14 at once, which is great.

6) Much more robust networking. I haven't played with this too awful much yet, but it seems that if you start listening to a playlist or an album on your NAS, then the next time you go back to "server", it will start playing where you left off (well, the song you left off at will start over again, instead of at the exact moment you left at), but at least this way you don't have to turn the TV on just to play some music. I suppose you could create a playlist of all Death Metal, and then you just have a stream going whenever you want it. It also seems like you can actually sign into Pandora and all the other stations and listen to your own account. And all the Internet/Network stuff is a separate scroll-through than the other inputs. I really like how that is set up.

6) The "program up/down" buttons on the remote can be programmed to do about 10 different things. I picked to have the dialogue increased or decreased for when you can't hear what people are saying even though everything else is loud enough. To be clear, I think this depends on if the dialogue is known to the decoder. I haven't tried all the other options yet.

7) Remote is awesome. Besides what I mentioned above, you can also make some changes to the red/green/yellow/blue buttons, but I wish you could really program those completely to your liking. Everything is laid out nicely, and the second zone even makes sense, as I mentioned above.

8) I realize the second HDMI output would be great if you also have a projector or something like that. With it, you can have access to all your devices without having to rewire anything. Haven't used it yet, but am glad to have the extra functionality.

...

There's plenty more, but I'm forgetting some of the details right now. I've only played with this thing for a few days, but I like it more and more. The one thing that is missing is that you can't change all the options via the webpage. You can change some, but I liked with my newer Sony the fact that I could look at and change all my custom presets without having to turn the TV and go through all that. I'm only comparing this to my two Sony units so you get my frame of reference, but realize this Yamaha model is in a higher class than those. Regardless, I love this thing, and it has a lot of great functionality and no serious drawbacks that I've noticed yet. Recommended (obviously).

The sound is fine. It's what I would expect from quality tweeters and a reasonable size woofer with a decent driver. It does not compare to a decent set of bookshelf type monitors like the JBL LSR series but the price is far lower so I guess they're ok for PC speakers.

But the excellence ends at the sound. The speakers do not have an analog signal input from the computer (there is one at the puck for a MP3 player or whatever). Instead, the signal comes via USB. The problem is the speakers do not come with any drivers. Bose assumes you have the drivers already on your Windows installation. That's a very bad assumption as many people do not have the drivers (just do a google search on Bose Companion 5 drivers to see). There's no help from Bose here. The drivers cannot be downloaded from their web site. I called Bose's tech support and after half and hour they were not able to solve the problem. I eventually solved the problem myself on my Windows 7 Pro 64-bit install but I think it's terribly lame that Bose cannot provide the driver for their product. If I wasn't using the pre-load install of Windows they assume everyone uses, then I would be screwed.

So exactly what do I get for this odd USB input in lieu of a standard audio input? Nothing except incompatibility and the inability to use the speakers apart from a full blown PC. The audio quality and features are not improved by USB audio input. Period.

Room mode correction should be a straightforward feaure on speakers like these. It is not. Although my sound card supports it, the Bose speakers do not have the DSP to do it independently. The lack of sound-card independent RMC doesn't justify the high cost of these speakers. If it were included, the price would look a little better.

I installed the Companion 5 system on an Ergotron cart. The two speakers fit perfectly under the monitor the way I wanted (I removed the stands). The acoustimass is bulkier than I would have liked but I think it's fair to say a smaller module would not perform as well and for most under-desk installs it would be fine. What I do think it's fair to complain about is the poor design of the acoustimass module case. Despite being very heavy, it features a plastic rear end-cap that is fragile. Come-on. For the price, give me painted steel not brittle plastic. The case is also oddly shaped with curves that prevent anything but a bottom-down mount position. The case is not designed to be mounted in a down-firing position, up-firing or on it's side or upside down. The case is also not equipped or rated to be flown or ceiling mounted (it could fall apart and drop parts on people below). Bose should know these are all viable positions. Not everyone can have this thing on the floor with like six wires running out for people to trip over -- seriously, that is totally not acceptable in a public space.

Bose has a habit of not publishing Watts RMS specifications for their amplifiers or speaker handling abilities. I sort of understand not wanting to confuse consumers who don't understand driver efficiencies, but at least give us some max. 1 meter SPL's so we have some clue how loud these things are. As it is, the Companion 5 is loud enough for a PC system in a fairly live medium-sized residential room. It's much louder than my Wave system which proved way more anemic than it was made out to be. The Wave is useless except in the smallest bedroom. I use the Companion 5 primarily in my kitchen (on the Ergotron cart). The kitchen is fairly live but has some acoustic paneling to tame some of the reverberations. If I were putting this system in a small classroom, I would think twice. As a PC system for someone who sits right in front of it, it's obviously perfectly good. I probably wouldn't even use it at half-volume sitting that close.

I bought for my mother as a mother's day gift. I also bought a Vera Bradley cover and a $50 Amazon GC to go with it. My mom is not the gadget type. So, the Kindle only gets use when she travel, but she has figured it out somewhat. She can't quite figure out how to purchase books or how to change the settings, which she just gets me to do it for her, but it has gotten a lot of use because she does take it with her instead of a bunch of books. In my use of this Kindle, I find it somewhat clumsy, slow, and some of the icons are not self explanatory and takes a few tries going back and forth. What I do like is that the screen is the exact size of a paperback book, there is no glare whatsoever, which is a problem I have with my iPad, and the light in the screen is perfect for reading at night without a lamp on. However, you can download multiple books at a time so if you just can't stand not having something to do for 20-30 mins, I would suggest downloading more than one.

Battery life is out of control! I have never seen this go below 50% even after hours of use. One downside is that the plug to charge it is not included so you will have to also pay for that as well. It is also very lightweight, and if you have a little case it's like holding an actual paperback, unlike an iPad which is much heavier and cumbersome to read e-books on.

However, overall, I'm old school. I like paper books. The smell, the ability to write notes and see those notes on the margins, the feel of the paper between my fingers. I can go my references quicker and don't have to worry about running out of memory space because my books stay on a shelf until I need them. So, I recommend this for travel only for the sake making room in your carryon. It is easy to use once you learn all the little quirks. Otherwise, the geek/nerd in me just always goes back to actual black and white.

I was all set to return this because it would not recognize my Seagate 4TB SSHD. In disk management it showed up as GPT protective partition. After googling, I found that the only way to get past this was to use Diskpart and Clean the drive--that meant wiping out everything on the drive. Since I had already cloned it, I went ahead and used the Clean command and wiped it out. Still couldn't do anything with the drive in disk management. So using Diskpart again, I used the command, Create Partition Primary. At this point, Diskpart couldn't do anything else. It would not create a volume to format, so I had to use Disk Management to create the volume and format it to exFat. I should state that the drive was recognized by my computer internally when it was connected to a Sata port, but once it was put into the Sabrent, it's drive information was changed and made unusable until I performed the procedure above. Not sure why this happened, maybe because it's a SSHD, but I kinda doubt it since I had no problems with the drive when connected to a Sata Port.

I use messenger bags as book bags to take books and tools to and from work every day. I favor canvas bags because they are tougher than nylon and they are a bit more masculine-looking. This particular messenger bag is a little more stylish than some of the others I have seen and so far I am happy with it.

A messenger bag is characterized by the fold-over flap that snaps closed over the main compartment. This particular bag has a very colorful and decorative weave that makes up the entire flap and the result is a softer and more supple flap than if it had been made of the same canvas material as the rest of the bag. That is not a fault or imperfection by any means but needs to be mentioned as a difference. Compared to the flap, the rest of the bag is more coarse and rigid.

Everything about this bag suggests quality. The stitching is very tight and the materials are even and there are no imperfections (nicks and cuts) that I can find on this bag. The stitching used to attach the shoulder strap to the metal loops on the bag, as well as to attach the leather trim to the canvas, is visibly thicker and stronger than what was used to hold the canvas portions of material together. I like the fact that there is some manner of reinforcement on the bottom of the bag (stitched inside so it is hard to know exactly what kind of reinforcement was used).

Instead of actual snaps, the flap is attached to the front of the bag using magnets. These make it a lot easier to open and close the bag.

In the main compartment of this bag are three pockets, one zippered and two smaller pockets that are open on the top. The smaller pockets are ideal for cell phones, small note pads, a calculator and the like while the larger pocket is big enough to accommodate a checkbook or a small book; it is not quite wide enough to handle a DVD case. There is a front pocket that is just barely wide enough to handle a 10” tablet (though I would put a tablet in the main compartment instead). Finally, there is a zippered pocket on the back that is slightly more narrow than the front pocket because of the zipper and is good for papers and maps.

This is a nice messenger bag and I like it. It is made very well, it is spacious enough to handle a couple of technical books and it looks nice.

For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

UPDATE 10/31/2019:

I popped off the "P" key and looked at the mechanism underneath, since the keyboard was not otherwise useful. It does not appear to be broken, damaged or obstructed in any way. For this particular key, the plastic key cover needs a small bead in the center underneath to push down the silicone membrane to make contact. Using a very small piece of tape and a tiny ball (about the size of a pin head) I was able to add such to the key cover to get it working without damaging any parts, without changing the feel while typing, and without spending any money. However, this should not have been necessary as this should have been tested properly before pack-and-ship; my review and rating stand.

[[VIDEOID:121051b82f50880623cdf0499f74c575]] THE GOOD:
--------------
* 1080P native and extremely small, so it's very portable. The size is the whole reason I got this. It's for traveling and being able to project bigger screens in hotel walls.
* 300 ansi lumens, ALPD laser tech.
* 25000 hrs lamp life.
* Airplay, Miracast thru wi-fi.
* Aesthetically, very nice minimalist design.
* Picture quality is good, but I'm not a videophile. I do have a more serious Vava UST 4k projector in my living room, so all these portable projectors will never compare. They serve as a traveling device for me, and will not be the go-to video source at home.
* Very nice case is included to hold everything.

THE BAD:
------------
* Onboard 1W speakers are very weak to say the least. You will definitely want to hook up a portable speaker. It has a headphone jack, which is basically the same as an aux out jack. I hooked it up to a cheap little speaker and the sound improved drastically. Watch my video.
* No remote.
* No smart OS, so I have a chromecast connected in my video demo, and I just cast from my phone.
* No Bluetooth, so you must use aux if connecting a speaker.
* No mounting solution or tripod included. Depending on your situation, you might not even need it. Just set it on a coffee table and you're good.
* No built in battery.
* Lastly, the price. There are so many features lacking, so I do not understand the price point. If you're willing to spend $600, then check out the Nebula Capsule Max that's less than $500. It is also compact, the size of a coke can. It has a built in battery, 8w speakers, smart interface, bluetooth, and remote. The only thing it doesn't have is native 1080p, it is native 720p. But it's hard to even tell the difference with these little projectors anyway. So I am not sure that paying more money, and having less features is worth that 1080p. And if you have to also lug around an external speaker, a chromecast or fire TV, then it really defeats the purpose of being completely portable. With the Nebula, everything you need is inside a device the size of a coke can.

In conclusion, this is a neat little barebones projector, but the onboard speakers are so bad, you'll need to carry around a portable speaker as well, so it's no longer as portable as I anticipated. At its price point, I assume they're saying it's a premium to have a projector at this size that is 1080p.. But again, that size feature is almost negated by the need to bring along external speakers, and smart devices like a Fire TV stick. And if the Nebula Capsule products doesn't exist, then I guess this price point is justified, but the Nebula does exist, and it's a much better buy. I'm going 3-Stars.

There was an option on the bottom of their email to escalate the case to management if I was not happy with the response, and that they would get back to me within 24 hours. So I clicked it, and explained how I was not getting a response. But guess what? I never got a response. So five days later, I decided to return this because I'm still in the return window. Plus, there isn't much motion going on to drain the battery either. Sometimes, 3 or 4 days go by with no motion. The most number of times it has detected motion in one day is four times. So it's not like the battery is getting drained from the camera being triggered 10 times a day. I'm going to try one more time, and watch the battery life to see how quickly it drains before the return window closes.

**** Update **** The replacement camera will have a battery life of approximately 6 or 7 weeks, judging by the amount of battery used thus far. Since the return window is just 4 weeks, I have returned this camera again and will not try another one. 6-7 weeks battery life is better than 4 weeks, for sure. Also, the location of the camera does not get any direct sunlight, so even a solar panel would not have helped. If you are looking for just one camera that is wireless, and you aren't interested in having to take it down every month or two for recharging, this is not the camera for you.
