I bought a set of these skewers as I love to grill and I have found traditional skewers to be awkward and cumbersome.

First and foremost, these are flexible steel cable, not rigid stainless rods. The tips are pins, though, and that allows threading on food to be a simple and nearly effortless. This is a blessing in itself. The tips are a little wider than typical skewers though, so it does require a little bit of care when threading. Once threaded, though, the texture of the cable has a good tendency to hold food items steady in place. This is especially helpful when turning on the grill.

Because these are stainless steel these skewers will not react with food or with flavorings. This, paired with the fact that these are flexible, provide and opportunity not available with traditional skewers - the skewers and food can be soaked in marinade without ill effects. This is a great benefit as it is not necessary to cover one's hands in marinade while stringing food on the skewers.

These are longer than average skewers, too, so it is possible to string more food onto them. It is easy to optimize use of space too, by snaking the skewers on the grilling surface.

Finally, the tips stay cool when you hang them over the end of the grilling surface. The lid of the grill will even close with the ends hanging over the sides.

These are excellent skewers and make grilling with them instead of with traditional skewers eaiser and more pleasant.

Do keep in mind that because this is an LED-based light, the temperature band setting is quite narrow and presents a different light profile, one that the camera can see but the human eye cannot. Charging is done via a USB-C port, and the charging cable is included. I have not tried using this as a power source to charge my phone though the documentation doesn't say much about that. A full charge on this light lasts a while, though I have not drained it all the way down to find out how long it will last. Obviously the runtime is variable based on mode and brightness, and what is interesting about this light in particular is that it displays the estimated runtime on the screen based on current settings - this is a nice feature that I have not seen on a lot of these lights.

There are some creative modes for use with video or for special effects in a live setting, though the usefulness of these modes is dependent on the user. I personally will never use them. However, in the right hands these might be very useful for a project. There are several effects available, including police flashers, tube TV glow simulation, flickering candle and more.

The light comes with a nice canvas carrying pouch that provides basic storage and protection.

I do a LOT of work in front of a computer, and was getting these for when I work at home. At work, I use a Logitech 930 headset that I really like. I got these so I wouldn't yank my laptop off the desk when I get up. I got bluetooth, thinking they'd be easy to sync to my various devices. So, here's my breakdown:

Range
I can go upstairs and grab a few things or go two rooms away and I still get a signal. The range is pretty good on these.

Playback Sound
The playback sound quality is okay. Not blowing me away, but alright. I listen to music, no vocals, to block out the office noise and keep my head focused. The playback audio goes into tin-can mode when the mic is enabled. That's something I didn't realize as a limitation of how bluetooth handles the two signals. That took me a while to figure out.

Microphone
The mic is okay. It just flips me out that the playback goes into "phone mode" when the mic is enabled.

Battery
Well, I've only had these a couple of months. But, the battery seems to go at least as long as I can stand to keep them on my head. Max has been about 2 hours at a stretch before giving my head/ears a break.

Fit
I'm an adult and my head is average-sized, not large. After maybe three months these cans are still a bit tight. The cups don't quite fit entirely over my ears and get uncomfortable after maybe two hours --like, *ouch* uncomfortable.

Heat
These cans get pretty hot after maybe 45 minutes. Hot like I just got out of the shower and I need a towel in my ears hot. I don't think I've ever had sweaty ears like this before from a set of headphones.

Sync
I've easily sync'd these to Ubuntu 14.04 & 10, Windows 7, and OS X Mavericks.

Would I recommend these to a friend?
No. I like not having to carry a dongle around since bluetooth is in all of my computers (one has an $8 dongle that works just fine.) But, they get so hot, and are still not comfortable on my head and ears after maybe 100 hours of use. So, for the $50 price tag, I'd probably have to say no. If they were $25 and just to make the occasional phone call I might recommend them to a friend, but not to wear for any period of time. Even though I have always had an interest in astronomy I was never able to work a course in this subject in my college schedule or afterwards. When I saw this telescope offered I realized that now I had both the time and the means to explore my interest a bit further. I had very little difficulty setting the scope up, and spent some time familiarizing myself with the various components. I practiced using this by checking out objects in my neighborhood, and managed to get an 'up close and personal' view of some birds in a neighbor's yard and quickly realized that this scope was powerful.

That evening I took the scope to an upstairs window to see what I could see, and despite the pesky street light was able to get a great view of the full moon (btw did you know that it sparkles a bit?). I saw details that I had only seen in photos before which was fascinating. Then I decided to take a look at Mars, which was near the Moon that evening. That is when things got complicated. The finder scope and the main scope need to be synced, and I don't know how to do this (yet). With some fiddling, and aided by Mars' close proximity to the Moon I was able to find Mars, which was exciting but for some reason it was distorted (it had a starburst appearance). My husband and I fiddled with various lenses and combinations to try to eliminate this but were unsuccessful. The experimentation was further complicated by the touchiness of the stand....it was difficult to make small, smooth adjustments and to keep the scope locked in position. Some of this is no doubt due to our in expertise, some I think is due to the equipment.

My enjoyment of this scope would have been much greater if more instructions had been provided. We discovered, more or less by accident how to lock, at least partially, the scope into place. We managed to make some focusing adjustments by trial and error. Even some rudimentary instructions in a small booklet or even a sheet or two describing how to adjust, focus and lock the scope as well as an illustration of the scope with all the components clearly labeled with a brief description of their function would have been greatly appreciated. This is a basic instrument, one that will primarily be used by beginners or novices who will not necessarily be familiar with this equipment. Basic instructions should have been included. As it is my unfamiliarity with the various aspects of the telescope make following many of the instructions I do find on-line difficult to follow.

Despite this problems I am enjoying my new toy. I found the stand to be steady, and the tray located on the stand to be a handy place to put lenses and covers. As I mentioned earlier this is a surprisingly (at least to this beginning user) powerful scope. I'm going to play around with this some more, and will probably upgrade some of the lenses and add some accessories based on my experiences. Besides star gazing I think this will be a great item to watch birds or wild life, and it is certainly portable and forgiving enough to take on a camping trip.

I have purchased this for a small office, I run mail and a file server so I need to have the network up at all times.
The device is nice and easy to setup, concept is good and the price is not bad. This is where the good ends. I received the unit pulled it out of the box and started playing with it everything works well, then I turn off the stereo and I hear a very faint buzz coming from the unit. Since I work with electronics almost daily (component level repairs) I knew that the power supply will die soon, (it was a sign of a cheap ps).
I decided at only $130 im not going to send it back I will fix it myself (i don't really care about warranty).
Under the cover there are 3 boards. 1 relay outlet board, 2 power supply, 3 controller. The controller board (the one with the display) was ok, it didn't look bad at all. The relay outlet board I have found 2 cold solder spots, that would cause malfunctions with an outlet down the line. After fixing it I pull out the power supply and OMG, that this looks like someone was first learning how to solder, the board had a ton of faults, remaining flux and cotton from swabs. I decided to throw the power supply out instead I installed 12v to 5v converter for the controlls and connected 12v for relays. Installed external plug for a 12v ps and it works great with no problems.

This unit is ok.
It should have a good power supply (a $5 ps from china is 100 times better than what it came with)
It should be using solid state relays (it would be silent, and it would last much longer, also you would only need 5v to supply it)

Good Luck

I had my concerns because I've researched Powerline Adapters before, and there is talk about how your home's electrical wiring may cause your adapters to work or not work depending on where you plug in your adapters. For me, the process was pretty painless. I plugged the main adapter (GPL-2000PT) to a wall outlet next to my Frontier Gateway. Then an ethernet cable connects my Gateway to this adapter. BTW, the GPL-2000PT is the smaller of the two adapters. For some reason, my brain correlates MAIN as being BIGGER. So without looking at the model numbers on the device, I connected the bigger adapter next to my router initially and got it wrong, and had to start over. Anyway, so remember the smaller one is the one that gets tethered to your router. Next you plug the bigger adapter (GPL-2000WAC) to wherever you want to have the new wi-fi network. Press the Security button on the main adapter, then press the Security button on the other adapter.. wait for them to pair, and voila, you have a new wi-fi network. In my case, I was pleasantly surprised that everything worked because I needed better wi-fi in the garage, and there weren't any wall outlets available. Manual specifically recommends using wall outlets. I have these outlet boxes that the previous homeowner had installed along exposed 2x4 beams. I plugged the adapter into one of these and crossed my fingers, and amazingly, everything linked up. Speeds are super fast and snappy too.

The hiccup I run into, which is the same hiccup I run into every time I play around with gadgets of this kind whether it be powerline, meshes, or wi-fi extenders.... is the part where I would like to change the SSID and password. The default they give you is always something that's hard to remember, so you always want to change this. I can never get to their user interface with their provided IP's. The idea is that once you're on the adapter's network, you should be able to go to the provided address to access the user interface. It never works for me, no matter the brand. Either there is something about my network that I'm not understanding, or there are many consumers in the same boat as as I am. In any case, I will tell you what does work for me every time.. I simply go to my own router ADMIN. So if you're Spectrum, go to your Spectrum admin, if you're Frontier, Verizon, etc., go to their router admin. Then look for your new Nexuslink adapter. Your router would have assigned it an IP address. Type that ip address into the browser, and it will take you to the Nexuslink user interface. So whenever you can't get to a user interface provided the manufacturer of a powerline adapter, wifi extender, etc., just go to your own router admin and get the IP address that it was assigned. BTW, when you're browsing your router admin for the IP address of the adapter, you might not know what you're looking for since it may not be labeled by your router properly. So you'll need to find it through a process of elimination. All the IP addresses listed will show whether the device is connected by wi-fi, moca, or ethernet. So you can ignore all the wi-fi and mocas. Look for the ethernet connection that is unfamiliar to you. Mine showed up as "UNKNOWN." I have several devices connected to my network as UNKNOWN. I simply tried them all out, and one of the addresses eventually took me to the Nexuslink user interface.

If any network expert is reading this, I'd love for you to chime in below in the comment section and explain when it comes to this part regarding accessing the user interface of an adapter whether it be powerline, wifi extenders, etc., why the default given address in the manual never works for some of us. This hiccup doesn't deserve a star subtraction since I've experienced this with every other brand I've tried. Anyway, I can now access my garage camera blazingly fast, versus the 50/50 hit or miss connections before. This is 5 stars!

I ordered the iHome Alexa Built-in Bluetooth Speaker Portable Wireless Waterproof Rechargeable Lights Up to Music, with Speakerphone, Passive Subwoofer, Carry Strap, Durable Shockproof Floatable Design (IBT158) to replace an old sub par portable speaker that I’ve had for years. The iHome is quite the upgrade with the built in Alexa, better sound and being waterproof. I’ve had this product now for several weeks and would like to share my thoughts.

I must say that the sound is pretty good and packs a punch in such a small size. It’s much better than the much smaller and several years old portable wireless speaker that I have been using. In fact there really is no comparison at all. Let’s just say that it is the best sounding portable wireless speaker that I personally have ever owned. My daughter who “borrowed” the older speaker some time ago (and she never gave it back) keeps asking to "borrow" the new iHome as she says, “it’s louder and sounds WAY better”. I absolutely agree with her. Plus the lights on this thing are a nice touch, and there are options (via a button on top) to cycle through and change the color options or turn them off.

Setting up the iHome for Bluetooth and Alexa was easy and very straight forward, and there has been no issues whatsoever. We are mainly an Android household however my oldest daughter uses an iPhone and everyone has had the same great experience. So far my only complaint is that the Bluetooth connectivity distance isn’t the greatest but with that said, none of my Bluetooth devices really have much range in our home so I am not going to knock points off for that. The sound out of this little guy makes up for the Bluetooth short comings and the bonus of Alexa being packed into this as well as the waterproof features make this a great value for the selling price.

One thing worth mentioning is that to use Alexa, you can’t just say “Alexa” to activate her. You do have to physically press a button on the iHome speaker to access her, which isn’t a huge deal breaker, but because of this, you can’t use other Alexa devices to make an announcement and have it broadcast to the iHome speaker. Being fairly new to the Alexa and smart home world, I am not going to hold this shortcoming against the iHome device. It actually makes sense that with this being portable, you wouldn’t want to have Alexa always listening and drain the battery while on the go. Speaking of Battery life, it's decent but not spectacular by any means. This is pretty subjective however as usually when I use the iHome, I'm listening to it at a pretty high volume ;)

Another observation is that this uses micro USB to charge, and I really would like to see more devices using the newer and better USB C charging capabilities.

As far as the “waterproof” capabilities go, I must report that I have yet to float the device in a pool or let the kids play with it outside while running through the sprinklers. I know that it says it’s waterproof and it absolutely looks like it would hold up to getting wet as it is very well built, rugged and quite solid, but I don't want to risk ruining this new toy that the whole family has been enjoying so much.

This small, silent, unmanaged 1000 Mbps Ethernet switch has 8 super fast ports that not only provide high speed internet but automatically detect if the plugged in device needs power and, if so, how much!

I did thorough testing on this unit over the last couple of months and I am thoroughly impressed by the performance.

By utilizing the built in PSE Chip this switch will provide up to 30 watts to every Ethernet device connected but will not provide any power to devices that do not require power. I found that this switch works absolutely flawlessly.

Having the capability to provide super fast internet speed and power at the same time makes this switch perfect for both business environments and as a hub for security systems.

At the current Amazon price, this set of two universal remotes is a great buy.

However, I'm not clear about why anyone would need to buy TWO remotes at a time when the purpose of getting a universal remote is to reduce clutter and the number of remotes you own. One remote handles 3 devices, while the other handles the 3 PLUS 3 other ones. So why wouldn't I use the 6 device remote alone, since it includes everything?

My guess is that this product is aimed at households with at least 2 TVs. However, the price is so cheap that you're basically getting an extra remote for almost nothing. It's wasteful but hard to turn down because of the price.

The packaging and the instructions are confusing. RCA claims that one remote controls 3 devices while the other one controls 6. However, the 3-device one actually controls MORE than 3 - it just uses one button to control the DVD/VCR (it treats 2 devices as 1), one button for the TV, and another for the combination Satellite/Cable/digital TV converter. The second device is even more comprehensive -it offers buttons for all of the above PLUS one for the DVR/Aux 1, VCR/Aux 2, and Audio.

The two remotes also look different cosmetically - the 6 device one is shiny and glossy while the other is a matte black. Not sure why this is.

Having one VCR, one DVD, one TV, one cable box and an audio deck with a set of speakers, I used the "6 device" remote. My audio deck with attached speakers, which are circa 1988, would not work with the codes. However, switching from DVD to VCR went smoothly, as did from TV to cable.

In conclusion, the universal remote functioned well overall and cleared up the clutter of remotes beneath my coffee table. I liked the battery saver function - if you by chance lost your remote between your sofa cushions, the battery turns off after awhile.

Now if I could only find a way to use my 3-device remote...

Let me start off by saying I've owned Kindles and other e-readers so I can say I'm already somewhat familiar with the concept. I really like what I'm seeing here for the price of this product! This is a small / affordable e-ink device that makes it ideal for all kinds of things.
Personally, I'm a big fan of Overdrive to take books out of our local libraries for free on readers. My biggest complaint on Kindle readers is that this was always a hassle - I needed to do it ON A DIFFERENT DEVICE. A laptop or phone with a browser was necessary because you could not access Overdrive to explore content directly. On the Kobo, like other non-Amazon devices, you are free to browse directly on the reader, find a title you like and click borrow, all for FREE and 100% legal! This is a huge selling point to me. My kids can browse the YA and children's' section and find all kinds of content right on the device using an account they made with their local library card.
The screen is great for little hands as well as big hands, it even looks great displaying some graphic novel pages (albeit in greyscale obviously). I found that I had zero problems connecting to my Wifi, and downloading books is fast and easy. Battery life is excellent as well! The only caveat is that when you DO need to charge it, it's the slightly-older micro-USB charging plug. I wish it would have been a USB-C as most of our micro USB cables are being replaced with the new standard, and in 2021 its a little weird to still have a new product use an old standard... but this is a minor issue at best.

Some really cool mentions:
1) There IS an experimental web browser function. It's very limited, mostly due to the limitations of using E-ink instead of a display that can be updated faster like LCD/OLED, but super cool for browsing websites for text articles!
2) You can manually load a document to use as a screensaver!! This was a very cool find for me. There's a folder on the device when you plug it into your computer called .screensaver , and if you place a document in there (jpg, pdf, whatever) it will display it when the device is powered off / sleep. I actually put our weekend calendar information on there so we can refer to times / reminders, and stuck some magnetic strips to the back of the reader. Now it sits on our fridge when no one is reading, displaying our calendar and saving us at least one sheet of paper to print per month! Then whenever someone wants to read, my kids (or me!) can take it off the fridge, read a few pages, then put it back there for the next person. Because the Nia is a small and light tablet, it stays on really easily! My old Kindle was too large and fragile for that.

Way to go, Kobo!

[[VIDEOID:77a3ec20470319659bbfe251184b088d]] [[VIDEOID:2fd4b5f04957762b48a4d5abc3581407]] [[VIDEOID:7403cf057d2f5a59a8e99dce132cfb9c]] This is a really well made and nice looking messenger bag that's large enough to fit my 10" iPad plus water bottles and plenty of other gear without being too big or bulky. The remote is quite limited (it's not programmable for your tv, for instance), and there are few meaningful adjustments you can make to the settings. One big objection I had is that all pictures are stretched into 16:9, there is no option (that I found) to force a 4:3 display for the standard format recordings.

So if all you want is a decent dvd player that will do a pretty good job doing what a dvd player should do, then for the money this is a pretty good option. One thing to consider: given the move to BluRay (and the fact that BluRay players will play old format dvds), it might not make sense to spend a lot on a dvd player right now.

This past weekend I got to use both the SN600N and the Yongnuo YN568EX with the YN622 triggers. Basically both function completely with the YN622 triggers in both manual and iTTL modes. The only thing that I noticed with the SN600N was that manual power 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 all seem to be about the same output using the YN622 triggers - you have to lower it to 1/8 or less to start seeing lower outputs. Not a huge deal, but I'd like more output options. More on this below:

Here are a few details that a pretty important about these two alternatives to the Nikon SB series:

a) The 568 light is much higher quality - and I really mean the LIGHT quality. It is even, consistent, and clear. On the other hand, the SN600N is very scattered - what I mean by this is there are lines of brightness and darkness from the flash burst. This must be an internal flash "lens" issue - whatever the light is bouncing around and through within the flash is creating texture and light inconsistencies. This is not the case with the 568.

b) Yes, the SN600N is a more powerful flash, but in my opinion, it needs to have more levels of output on the lower end (1/256) because it's TOO bright for some situations. I use grids and modifiers during wedding receptions, and I like balancing the natural light with the flash output. 1/128 with the SN600N is equal to about 1/64 on the 568. I use the 568 at 1/128 quite a bit for details - so this was kinda a bummer to me.

c) The AF beam on the SN600N is better and more centered than the 568 - but they both need to improve designs. The ONLY reason I'm holding onto my Nikon SB900 at this point is the AF beam - which makes accurate AF possible in pitch black - no joke. The AF beam on the Yongnuo is a joke - they need to fix it on the 622 triggers too - it's basically worthless and too bright/annoying to the subject.

d) In my experience using the 568EX, the batteries get warm and stay warm, whether you're using the flash or not. If the flash is on, the batteries will get warm. It also EATS through batteries. I used to be able to photograph 2 weddings without recharging my Nikon SB setup (using SB600 previously) - now I have to recharge between weddings. I've upgraded to 2800mah EBL AA rechargeable (previously using Amazon 2000mah) and it has helped quite a bit.

So this is my current setup: SB900 on camera, 2x 568EX off camera group A+B for reception lighting, and then SN600N as group C for periodic fill. Rather than commit to a single brand, I'm using them all as tools for different situations, because they all work differently. I also am really enjoying the SN600N as on-camera if I don't need the AF beam - the quality of light is bright, crisp and rich - and the SN600N "brain" (basically how it works using iTTL mode) just works really well with Nikon - it's a very consistent flash, sometimes even better than my SB900. I like that it can zoom all the way to 200mm, too. If the SN600N had a better AF beam and better quality of light, I would ditch my SB900 and use it all the time. But I switch between the SB900 and the SN600N for different effects. I actually like the previously mentioned internal lens flash inconsistencies at times - it creates a grittiness that I like.

However the (10 x) zoom lens is NEW. Not only to me, but to all (point and shoot) cameras I have ever seen. Now, the 10 x zoom lens that I am talking about is NOT digital zoom. But rather, purely optical. There is a digital zoom offered in the menus of this camera. But I simply turned this feature off. If I want to do any digital zoom, I'll do it in Photoshop on my own time.
Other perks include; a battery and charger. The battery is lithium. And knowing that a lithium battery must be conditioned before its true capacity can ever be obtained. And even before the battery had been `conditioned' it was still able to take approximately 400 shots. And of course four or five HRS of me playing around in the menus with the features. And I know from past experience this can be one of the biggest power drains on a camera battery. And this is only the first cycle. I don't foresee a need in my future to buy a spear battery.
While I am on the subject of batteries, I need to mention. The battery charger is a cute little thing. The part of the plug that actually goes into the wall will fold into the plastic housing. So it is not a burdensome piece of machinery to store. And the whole thing is extremely small. It is only 3"x2"x1". To me that sounds ridiculously small, and if it were not right here in front of me I might not even believe. But it is true. It will fit in my small camera case, instead of the drawer. I already have enough mess around my room.
Also about batteries, there is a handy little gauge, on the LCD screen, that reports the amount of battery left by a four bar indicator (like a cell phone).
I spoke earlier about the massive zoom lens. But I didn't even tell how this camera can also take a macro picture up to about 8" away at full wide angle (zoom out). The 8" I just spoke could be off a little by + or - an inch. The manual that could tell me for sure is over there in that box, and I am over here. And I'm a lazy person.
I'm really impressed at how small this camera is. It will fit very nicely, with lots of room to spare, in my chest pocket. I do wear a 2X shirt, but there is so much room left over, I bet you could fit this camera in a large size pocket. I haven't had a chance to test it; I'm just using my best estimate. On outings, being able to tuck this camera away in my pocket will be way awesome. And it is so light weight.
And it weighs very, very little for such a nice camera. I have a cordless optical mouse hooked up to this computer. So by comparing weight, the mouse is the more heavy of the two.
I think I have touched on the biggest topics I can think of at this sitting, but to sum this up. This is the best camera I (personally) have ever owned. I do wish you could combine it with device music groups in Alexa (so I could say, for example, play this song on the everywhere group and it will play inside on our Echo and out on the porch with the Ecobee), but sadly only echo devices can be grouped. That's OK, I knew that before getting this as other devices in our home can't be grouped either (Facebook Portal or Kindles, for example).
If you want to spring for the subscription service, there's a TON of goodies and advanced features beyond even the cloud storage things. I also wondered if my wi-fi router interfered with it, wouldn't others also interfere with it?  The tech support person said no, because I wouldn't be that close to them.  Makes no sense to me. I had the device charged up 100% last night and it still seemed to be charged 100% this morning, but in trying to use it today, it has already dropped to 90% and that's probably from only a few minutes of use.  If I ever get this working, I'll update the review.  At the moment I really don't feel that this is ready for prime time. Our AV department bought a BDP-300 so we could release our HD video content on Blu-ray. We bought the expensive Blu-ray burner for the computer, we bought the expensive authoring software, we bought a bunch of expensive BD-R and BD-RW recordable disks and we bought the expensive Sony BDP-300 player, with an eye toward buying a bunch more for our conference rooms if the system worked. It didn't.

We found that the BDP-300 will not play back BD-R or BD-RW discs. Though it might have been possible to be upgraded via a firmware update (like its REALLY expensive big brother can be firmware upgraded) it most likely never will. Thanks a lot, Sony. Way to make an integrated system. No wonder Blu-ray has been so slow to catch on. Thus we as a very large company cannot commit to Blu-ray because we can't play the recorded Blu-ray disks back on even a $400 player. Sigh.

Secondly, if you connect to a digital display that only has DVI-in via an HDMI/DVI adapter or an HDMI/DVI cable adapter, the player doesn't work. I suspect the problem is connected to copy protection schemes built into the multiple HDMI standards.

So, if you have an older HD display that only has DVI-in, forget this "reasonably priced" Blu-ray player. You'll most likely need to use the analog YRB (component) outputs, which is an inferior signal to the digital HDMI output. I did a component/HDMI comparison for my wife and she definitely picked the HDMI as the superior output picture.

There is a workaround that allows the HDMI/DVI to work, but it's a pain: First, connect both the HDMI and component cables to their respective inputs on the display. Now, before powering the player on, manually disconnect the HDMI cable from the back of the player while leaving the component cables connected to the display. Then power up the player and switch the display to the analog "component" input. You can now see the menus and the Blu-ray disk will be able to be played. After you get the movie running, manually plug the HDMI/DVI cable into the back of the player and switch the display to the digital DVI input. The Blu-ray disk now works and allows the menus and other overlaid controls to function normally. As different HDMI copy protection schemes get adopted this trick might fail.

If you have HDMI-in on your display, the player might work, but no guarantees. Bear in mind that the HDMI standard is constantly changing. I think they're up to at least HDMI 1.3 so far, and counting. And a totally new plug protocol is on its way for computer monitors, too, called DisplayPort, which might make it to TV sets, but who knows?

After this little problem was overcome, I finally got to see the picture. It was very nice, especially after I got to see it via my HDMI-DVI workaround. Definitely better than the analog component feed.

The overlaid menus allow you to access the menu anytime, without leaving the movie. Pretty cool. The menus are also more animated and better integrated.

Audio quality is fabulous. Both Dolby and DTS sound great because with all the storage capacity on the disk, the signals don't have to be compressed as much as they are for a standard DVD.

If you want the very, very best audio, though, you can select "uncompressed" and route the RCA audio outputs directly into your amp's dedicated preamp inputs. This takes the Dolby and DTS compression systems out of the picture altogether. So you are hearing multiple uncompressed audio tracks sent directly to your amp.

The worst part of the Blu-ray player is the time it takes to "boot" up. It's really a dedicated computer running an operating system. Java, at least, and maybe more. Thus it takes a full two minutes to fire up. You press the power button and nothing happens. After about ten seconds, you get a display that says "power on." After about 90 seconds, the machine is finally ready to play your disk. Give it a lot of time to fire up, especially the very first time you plug it in. After the initial plug-in/power-on sequence, the manual says it will be subsequently faster. But not by much. And the system can "crash," requiring you to turn it off and reboot. It happened several times to me as I moved too quickly between menu selections.

Overall, this player can put out a great picture, eventually, and after learning a bunch of quirks. I don't think it's ready for prime time, though. For the price it should be much better: faster boot up and with the ability to play back recorded Blu-ray disks.

Buy the BDP-300 knowing you will be replacing it for some reason in a year or two.

I wanted to find a cheaper alternative to my wife's wireless Bose headset, something with decent noise cancelling for flights and work. So far I've used Bose, the MPOW H5, Treblab, and Woltix with ANC.

Nothing will compare to Bose noise cancellation - but these Woltix are actually really nice for the money. The MPOW H5 don't have as good audio clarity as the Treblab, but at the end of the day I got noise cancelling headphones for the noise canceling. I ended up returning the Treblab and the MPOW H5 and I kept the Woltix because they are more comfortable than the MPOW and had the best low-price ANC. The MPOW also had some sound interference issues randomly when the ANC was on, and the Treblab had a slight hiss to them when ANC was on.

I ended up keeping the Woltix brand. They just work, they're very light, and they are not too tight on the ears. The Active Noise Cancellation isn't as good as Bose, but they actually work pretty well for a $65 set of wireless ANC headphones. For the price, I'm very happy.

The ONLY thing I don't like about these is that there is no battery meter display on my iPhone when these are connected via bluetooth. With the other brands there is a small battery meter. I have no idea when these are low, so I just charge them like once a week.

So, quick breakdown of my experience with these wireless ANC headsets:

Bose: Best noise cancellation, good audio, comfortable, but definitely expensive!
Treblab: Best audio, worst noise cancellation (you can hear a slight hiss when turned on), comfortable, but large and they don't fold down too small.
MPOW: Good audio, good noise cancellation, but was getting some weird sound interference with the ANC on sometimes. Tight on ears.
Woltix: Good audio, good noise cancellation, most comfortable (way lighter and less tight on the ears than the MPOW), and fold down the smallest. No battery meter displayed on phone.

I want to preface this review with a quick note; I returned mine shortly after receiving. This had everything to do with the feature set that I was looking for and not with the quality or performance of the item.

Within the price range that this dashcam is offered, this is a fully-featured and functional dashcam. I did a considerable amount of research about several of the more affordable offerings and determined that the LEVIN dash cam seemed to satisfy and could be a solid investment.

The product pictures appear to be taken at an angle that make the item appear to be much bigger and bulkier than in hand. In reality, the LEVIN Dash Cam is slender, small, and discrete. The installation is not dissimilar to other models and is very quick and easy.

I don't want to comment on the actual performance because I had a very limited experience with the item. But according to the research I did while shopping for a dashcam, the image quality and video performance was satisfactory if not very good. Nevertheless, consider this just a vicarious assessment.

The physical buttons and layout are good. The button click action is substantial and assured and the buttons themselves are easy to find and depress. Unlike the dashcam I upgraded to, finding a button doesn't necessarily require direct sight as the button layout allows for easy tactile navigation of the control panel. My upgrade item however has a touchscreen with no physical queues as to where specific controls are located.

Lastly, the reason why I returned it... no wifi. My primary reason for investing in a dashcam was an incident that my cousin had. His dashcam had captured a traffic accident in which he was not at fault. The other driver of course dishonestly tried to establish fault by my cousin, who promptly downloaded the related video content to his phone, showed it to the responding traffic officer and sent copies to both the reporting officer and his insurance company. While the content can easily be obtained from the onboard storage, the ability to share and view that content on the fly allowed my cousin to establish non-fault and include it as part of the LEO's official incident report. Wifi is the feature that made this possible and because of my cousin's experience, it's one that I didn't want to miss. I do wish however that my new dashcam had the capacitor feature that the LEVIN has.

Aside from lacking the wifi feature, this dashcam is everything I would need it to be. It's also more affordable that most given its feature set. Even if you were to upgrade at a later point, I don't think you can go wrong with this one. Unless price is not an object, if so look to this model as a good pattern for the kinds of features you'll want in a more expensive model.

I love that this surge protector and plug strip has two USB ports for charging my Kindle and cell phone, but the placement of the USB ports, which is a major selling point for this unit, is hindered by the position of the cord wrap feature as well as the areas to plug in your larger electronics that have the big boxy plug. The USB ports are tucked right in between the cord wrap spot and the place to plug in larger plugs, so if one isn't blocking your USB ports, the other is.

In addition, I kind of wish that the majority of the plugs were spaced farther apart. I have a few electronics that have very small boxy plugs, and those don't fit right next to one another on the main area of the plug strip. The only thing that will fit on those plugs without overlapping are the traditional small plugs that are on lamps and other uncomplicated items. I don't have too many of those, and I'm guessing that most people buy plug strips because they have a bunch of electronics, almost all of which would have those bigger boxy plugs.

That said, the surge protector feature is absolutely effective, and I know this because we had PG&E replacing some poles in our neighborhood recently and we had many incidences of brownouts, surges, and spotty power, and this unit kept any harm from coming to any of my electronics that were plugged into it.

And while it is easy to make design suggestions, I have to say that I haven't found the perfect plug strip yet. Almost all of them seem to have some design characteristics that make them not quite ideal. While this unit is not perfectly designed with regards to the placement of the USB ports and the spacing of the regular plugs, it is certainly a high-quality, very functional unit that does what it says it does, and I trust the Belkin brand that it's going to function for some time. This plug strip is also nice in that it has a space so that you can mount it on the wall or on the back of your desk if you so desire.

When I saw this I thought it would be a great addition to my camera gear. The description says it's good for DSLRs and up to six pounds. After opening and inspecting this monopod system I reluctantly tried my ultra-compact Sony WX9 camera on this mounting system. My conclusion is I can't and won't trust this rig with my WX9 let alone my much heavier mirrorless Fuji gear.

The padded extendable main monopod shaft consists of three sections that are secured with a twist. It's easy to not torque the sections hard enough for them to unexpectedly collapse while you're trying to take a picture.

The ball-head mounts, this system comes with two, are fairly smooth metal on metal construction. Alarmingly these have no secure locking system. You simply use your thumb to engage a friction locking system. All it takes is a tap to cause the ball-head to be completely free moving. I would never trust a camera I liked on these mounts.

There are two feet that come with this set. A rubber edged magnetic mount and a suction cup -
The magnet is too small for a secure mount. With the monopod vertical and not extended it was reasonably stable. Horizontally it felt unsafe set up in any configuration. Extending the monopod drastically increases the ease with which this tips over. The magnet is just not wide enough to be stable.
The suction cup mount was surprisingly strong but like every other securing point in this rig the slide to release the mount does not lock in place. It's just too easy to hit the release while trying to set things up. I had thought I could mount this low on the car to get some interesting video but after trying this out I'd be worried road vibration would cause this to release and drop the camera.

In conclusion: While the materials are of decent quality this system lacks security. I won't risk my cameras on it.

Okay, I realize that everyone's definition of "easy to set up" comes from a different place. For me, I've worked around computers for over 25 years now, so pretty comfortable, BUT - I am more comfortable with software than hardware. So although this should not have been intimidating, it was a little bit. I formerly was using a Linksys router on our home network. It did a fine job, and was very easy to maintain. However, it didn't give much of a boost to the downstairs connections. The computer was always slow, and would drop the connection from time to time, and require a reboot to get the connection back.

This router is truly great looking. It is white, sleek and has nice blue lights. It sits vertically, rather than horizontally like my old one. I wasn't sure I'd like it, but I do. It comes with three screw-on antennas that can be pointed in any direction to boost your signal in that direction. The metal frame is very sturdy and would take a LOT of pressure to bend. I currently have mine on a separate little shelf because my current desk is too small.

There is only a quick set-up sheet included with this item. Ironically, if you need help, it tells you to go to the company's WEBSITE! Ha! So, if you can't get it to work, go ahead and get online. Yeah, No. But, if you are willing to disconnect and reset up a single-user home network using your old router, it could work! The sheet does give you very plain graphic instructions that tells you which item to plug in where, which many will find very helpful It came with a very short ethernet cord, so you either need to keep the router close to you or buy a longer cord. (The one I had was just purchased last year and was six feet long, so I was in good shape.)

Now, I couldn't get it to connect right away. The short troubleshooter on the insert says to reboot your modem, then to reboot the router. I did. Several times. The computer refused to acknowledge the new router! I was ready to just reconnect my Linksys when I decided to go against all logic and swap the ethernet and modem cords. For many years, computers and peripherals have been fairly color-coded to make it easier for non-tekkies to hook things up. In this case for the TP Link, the ethernet ports (there are four) are yellow and the modem port is blue. I even had previously bought color-coded wires so I didn't accidentally pull the wrong one. After 45 minutes of not being able to connect, I take another look at the back. Everything is in the right spot. But, since I wasn't connecting anyway, I decided to swap out the modem cord and ethernet cord, plugging yellow into the blue slot and the blue cord into the yellow slot. Totally backwards. As you might guess, it took off immediately! So apparently, our unit was either labeled backwards or connected backwards on the inside. Seriously strange. But as long as it works, I don't much care.

The default setting of this router is PUBLIC, so be sure to change your settings to PRIVATE NETWORK, if you don't want everyone in the neighborhood to try and tap into your network. Yes, they would need your password, but there are a lot of smart hackers out there, so you just never know. Better safe than sorry. There are default settings for the account name, network name (your SSID) and passwords, so you will need to change those as soon as you can. (If you forget to write them down, there is a reset button on the back to rol it back to the default passwords.) I also had to change the other settings to WPA2 for our area for the home network. No big deal, just different from before.

The TP Link C9 runs two parallel bands - 2.4Ghz, which is what most home routers use for regular internet access and browsing, and a 5.0 Ghz band, which is for streaming videos and movies. The nice thing about this router, is that if you name BOTH the 2.4 and the 5.0 the same name, it will AUTOMATICALLY switches to the strongest network for your use. I love that! The on/off switch is on the back of the router, so it won't easily get bumped. While my photos show the antennas straight up (we haven't had to move any of them to get a better reception), they rotate and bend towards whatever area you might need a little boost.

Has our reception improved? Yes! The downstairs computer now cruises like it was directly connected to a wired access point. The kids can watch movies and I can browse the net without anyone slowing down. The reception range is fabulous - we live in a multi-unit building, and could probably provide internet connection to all four units. It offers connection speeds of 1.3Gbps over the clearer 5GHz bandwidth and 600Mbps on the 2.4GHz bandwidth. We have not yet found a dead spot in our place - even outside picks up the signal.

In addition to the fabulous signal and great connection speeds, this router can also handle your USB 2.0 and 3.0 devices. There are ports on the side of the router, so you can easily transfer files, photos or data from an external drive to your own computer, or even hook up your printer to print wirelessly. (I haven't tried that yet, but the possibilities are there.)

It also offers a "tether" function for your smartphones. I have not used that, and won't be using that, but it would be great for parents who want to monitor network access/usage from work for their older kids. It is nice to know that option is there.

I am so very pleased with this router! I probably would not have looked at this brand, since I tend to stick with the equipment companies I've had previous success with, but I cannot state enough that this would be an asset to anyone's home network setup.

I travel quite a bit and many of the trips I take are short in duration- often only two or three nights. I don’t need a lot of luggage space for these short trips and I like taking backpacks because I can often avoid carry- on and baggage fees if my backpack can fit under my seat. This desire for economical travel led me to get the Case Logic BRYBPR116 Bryker Backpack Roller.

With this Case Logic Backpack, you get a two-in-one backpack and piece of luggage well suited for travel or business. The wheels make it perfect for traversing an airport and with the added straps, you can carry it on your back, like a traditional backpack. There is an outside pocket where you can tuck the straps so they are not hanging out, flopping around when you don’t need them. And the handle can be completely pushed inside the backpack and sealed off with a zipper so that no one sees it. I like these qualities because it means I can make this look like a backpack when I want it to and I can make it look more like a piece of luggage when I want it to.

Inside the backpack, there is a separate compartment for a laptop and I like that you can unsnap this if you like, making for a larger interior space that is just right for stuffing your two- day supply of clothing and personal items. Like I said, my primary usage with this backpack is for travel and I usually don’t take my laptop with me when I’m on a two- day trip, so I would rather have the open space, to make it more like a piece of luggage.

There is one thing to keep in mind if you take this backpack on a plane, and that is the size of pack makes it only barely able to fit under your seat. It will stick out some, so be prepared to have a snug space where your feet normally go. And unlike other backpacks, it’s too rigid- thanks to the handle- to make it collapsible and flexible. To save having to pay carry- on fees on certain airlines, I am willing to place it under the airline seat in front of me regardless, even if it does stick out some. If your flying on an airline that doesn’t charge extra for carry-ons, then this won’t be an issue since you can easily place the backpack in the overhead, which is what I recommend doing. For everyone else, just bear in mind that the length of the backpack makes it a challenge to fit under a seat.

I have a wide assortment of backpacks and luggage in my home to accommodate different needs. This Case Logic rolling backpack is a nice addition to my collection and I like that it performs a dual role. It has suited me well so far and it makes a good choice of luggage/backpack for business people and others who are constantly on the go for short spans of time.

I'm going to sew a few stitches next to the strap as a precaution in case the snaps come undone. You can use any type of strap to secure the cover to the camera. I read a newspaper review that recommended NOT buying this excellent EA6900 router, because of testers' problems with the second band and with nonfunctioning USB ports. I absolutely love this EA6900 router, which I've been using for more than a month now. As befits its price tag, the Sony has the look of a budget receiver with its old-school silver chassis. Build quality is decent enough: the fascia has a mixture of polished buttons and knobs including an input selector and volume control. The unit's remote control will be familiar to some - it features styling similar to the remotes that come with Sony's W Series of LCD TVs.

Before we get stuck into how the SRT-DG820 sounds, it's worth noting that Sony went back to the drawing board for its whole 2008 receiver range. And the Japanese giant has introduced various new features that, it claims, help improve performance.

For starters, the chassis of the STR-DG820 has been strengthened and embossed in certain places to help control any nuisance vibrations and minimize their effect on the key video/audio components found at the rear of the receiver.

High-definition audio decoding

Sony has even used custom-made brackets to secure the front panel and chassis and improve rigidity. The key video circuitry has been positioned as close as possible to the receiver's HDMI inputs for a shorter signal path and minimal interference.

The STR-DG820 offers 7.1 channels of surround sound (100w per channel) and can decode all major high-definition audio formats, including Dolby Digital TrueHD and DTS-HD Master Audio.

An inquisitive look around the rear of the receiver reveals a good selection of sockets. These include four HDMI inputs, (including a dedicated Blu-ray input), one HDMI output and three sets of component video inputs. The receiver also includes one coaxial and three optical digital inputs.

However, there is one notable omission: multichannel analogue inputs. So, your player has to be able to stream the HD data through HDMI for everything to work properly. In addition - not that you'd really expect them at this price - there are no pre-outs.

At this point it's also worth pointing out that the STR-DG820 can't upscale (Sony's step-up 'ES' range can upscale to 1080p), nor can it upconvert (again, the 'ES' range can). These features aren't vital, but upconversion would have been a welcome addition.

Sky HD usability issues

It also has to be noted that early versions of this receiver have had compatibility issues with Sky HD, which does not carry surround sound via its HDMI connection.

When you hook the Sky HD box's HDMI feed into the Sony and the Sky HD surround sound in via an optical input, the receiver over-rides the optical so you only hear the stereo feed supplied via HDMI.

Sony is working on a fix that will be applied to all existing and future STR-DG820 models. In the meantime, you can get round the issue by connecting your Sky HD via HDMI directly to your TV or projector, and via optical through the receiver - in this way you'll get both HD pictures and full surround sound.

Silky sound, dynamic dialogue

But back to the receiver in action. Set-up is done through Sony's Digital Cinema Auto Calibration system. It's ridiculously quick, easy to use and accurate - the receiver takes just a few seconds to set up.

And, hooked up to a Blu-ray player such as the Panasonic DMP-BD30, the Sony sounds sensational. Fed the Dolby TrueHD soundtrack from Batman Begins, the STR-DG820 impresses with its solid, controlled sound.

When Batman's Tumbler causes havoc on the streets of Gotham City, the Sony delivers explosions with a fine sense of immediacy and impact. Bass notes don't wallow or linger. In fact, you soon forget you're listening to a `budget' receiver.

The Sony is a dab hand at dialogue, too. Voices sound full-bodied and boast exceptional clarity, even during the most boisterous action scenes. There's no trace of brashness or harshness in the sound that could prove tiresome over prolonged listening.

Sure, more expensive receivers can give you a greater spread of sound and greater scale but, for this sort of money, the STR-DG820 is an absolute star.

It's equally adept at music

Dare we say it, the Sony also sounds adept when it comes to CD playback. Press the Analog Direct button to turn off all unnecessary internal processing and the receiver's clear, composed sound once again comes to the fore.

It exhibits a fine sense of rhythm for an AV receiver and dishes out decent bass weight during Eminem's Without Me.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

I have tested and reviewed many wireless doorbell systems. Typically I always advise to avoid any wireless cameras due to the inherent security vulnerabilities but this is often not possible with doorbell cameras. That being said there are key components I look for in wireless doorbell cameras: clear picture that provides a wide viewing angle, it either be hard wired or have excellent battery life, when chime button is pressed alert is sent and app can be opened and responsive in a quick time, 2 way audio communication is clear on both ends, motion sensitivity is adjustable and accurate.

I have thoroughly tested this product over the last 4 months and in comparison to the others on the market around this price point this product has proven to be clearly the best.

In terms of what is excellent - the internal battery is long lasting and dependable - I have found that it will last nearly 2 months on a single charge. The vast majority of wireless doorbells use proprietary batteries which forces users to purchase secondary batteries typically costing $30-$50. This factor is a huge bonus.

The camera is quite good. Images are clear and the wide angle provides a full view of the area in front of the doorbell. The AI Smart Human detection is without question the best I have found. This is a huge feature that helps prevent constant false alerts.

The base station holds up to a 128GB SD card for video storage. This is awesome for multiple reasons. If the camera was stolen the evidence will be saved on the base station within your home and all of your recordings are stored locally. This is an outstanding system.

Unfortunately, as with many similar products, while the hardware is good the software needs some work. As is typical, I can not find any way to force this doorbell to work with better software. It is obvious this was designed on the Tuya platform though I have not found any way of integrating it. I would much rather use the Tuya app where I have the bulk of my automation set but this will not migrate.

The lag from the time the doorbell button is pressed until you can see who is there is mediocre. The FASTEST I’ve been able to get this to work is 18 seconds - and I’m using an iPhone 13 Pro Max with 512GB on a super fast 1G mesh WiFi with a node located within feet of the doorbell inside the door.

The 2 way audio is spotty. It sounds like ordering through a drive through where every 3rd word is audible. Since I don’t use these to have in depth conversations it isn’t a huge deal but should be noted.

This is definitely among the best wireless doorbells I have tested for a while. It is not perfect, the sound leaves room for improvement as does response times but overall this is a quality unit.

While the vast majority of the doorbells I tested I advised to avoid all together this one is one worth using.

I have had good success with Kingston products (in particular their SSD storage) so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this encrypted thumb drive. It has a lot of promise and it works better than other encrypted drives I have used. There is one drawback, at least for me - it does not support Linux (if it does, I haven't figured out how yet).

I have the 16GB version, and the thing is built like a tank. It has a metal casing around the inner workings and it can handle some abuse. That's good news if you keep these things in a briefcase or loose in a bookbag.

Setup is easy. When it is plugged into a Windows machine (I do not have access to a Mac so I cannot speak to that use case), the software is available and can be used to set up the drive with a password. That's pretty straightforward. If you forget your password, you can wipe the drive and start over but you cannot recover your data. So, choose your password wisely.

Copy rates seem to be decent - a little slower than similar-sized drives I have that aren't encrypted but not prohibitively so. It's a trade-off, and a small one at that.

When I popped this drive into my Linux machine, the kernel saw it immediately. However, all it could see was the setup partition which is approximately 100mb, a far cry from 16 GB. The drive is smart enough to hide its data from foreign OS-based systems so your data is safe. Linux is gaining users though, and being able to access the data from a Linux system would be good, even if there was a tedious process to get to the partition but still requiring a password. This is better than other encrypted drives I have used in the past which made the data scrambled but was still accessible. However, not being able to use this drive under Linux is a problem for me.

To be fair, it is not advertised as compatible with Linux.

This is a good drive and from what testing I have done it works well. That said, it does not support Linux and that is a negative for me. Hopefully Kingston will release a Linux-based version (or a software layer) for it in the future; for now it's only usable for me under Windows.

I've been obsessed with fully wireless earbuds for years and have tried out at least a dozen different ones throughout.

I fully support some in the $30 range, I had a pair of old soundcores that worked great. I've also tried the more expensive Samsung Galaxy Buds (2018 version), which worked well enough. I've also tried some mid-range ear buds in the $70 range. Earbuds have gone through some growing pains with drop off issues between the left and right buds and battery life. In my experience, I believe the $30 buds are great value and >$100 buds are worth it only if they have good sound and good app support. For me every one of the $70 buds that I have purchased have broken down in less than three months, so I'd say stay away from those.

Now on to the review:
The Cleer Audio, Ally Plus II True Wireless Noise Cancelling Earbuds are in the >$100 range (although just barely) but in the last few weeks that I've used them, I truly believe they are worth their asking price. I will of course update this review if they break down in a few months.

There are so many wireless earbuds being produced these days, which most imitating the airbuds with their ugly stalks in one form or another, Cleer has gone with a tear-drop shape and capacitive controls that I appreciate. I purchased the tan-colored buds and they don't stand out like a pair of white or black buds would. There is only a single dim light on the earbuds to indicate charging status and they are the in-ear-canal style of earbuds.

Features:
- Light-weight.
- Charging/carrying case supports type-c connection as well as wireless charging. Interoperable with products designed for airbuds wireless charging.
- Long battery life. I listen to audiobooks and they have lasted for hours while I worked on chores around the house.
- Passthrough with good app support (more on it later)
- Active Noise cancellation
- Can be used as a single earbud without having to pair each separately
- Touch controls: Only tap, double tap, and triple tap are supported. Configurable through the app.

The App:
When I first received the Cleer earbuds, the app was unimpressive. There was a single slide bar that changed the balance between noise cancellation and passthrough, a equalizer with no presets (and no reset for that matter), and there was limited control over what the tap functions did.

Since then, the app has been updated and the earbuds had a firmware upgrade. While the app still has room for more improvement, they did separate the passthrough, normal, and noise cancellation modes into separate controls. Passthrough now has a slider to control the strength of the surrounding noise and the noise cancelling has a "smart noise cancel" mode. In addition, a new personalized audio feature was added. The app takes you through a hearing test and adjusts the sound to your hearing levels. Quite cool.

The limited controls over the touch function is still there and the barely passable equalizer is still there but I'm hoping that they will be improved in future updates.

Other reviewers will probably cover the wi-fi setup, but I got this for another reason. I hate wi-fi because it can be slow, too many things can interfere with the signal (such as microwaves) and there is always a security concern. In addition to being a wi-fi extender, this works great for extending the range of your router's wired connections, which is how I am using it. There are two parts to this; one is the sending end, which you plug into your router via included ethernet cable and then into an electrical outlet. The receiving end of this has 3 ethernet ports and you can connect up to 3 devices by ethernet cable. If you use it this way, there is no setup at all. It truly is plug and play and worked immediately for me. The setup sheet doesn't make it clear that it can function this way, but there is a picture on the box showing it. Also, I was very pleased with the fact that both pieces included a pass-through outlet, which is a great feature. It would seem that this would keep you from losing an outlet. Maybe and maybe not. Here's why. Both pieces are quite long. If you plug them into the top outlet of a typical 2 part outlet, the devices will cover the second outlet. So just plug them into the bottom outlet, right?; then the top outlet is free. Maybe. The problem is that the devices are just a little too tall and you cannot fit a 3-prong gounded plug above them. You can use a 2-pronged plug and it will mostly likely fit. You would think someone would have tested this when they designed the product. It's that slight design flaw that caused me to knock one star off my rating. Other extenders of this type that I have seen are small enough to fit with another 3-prong cord above them when plugged in to the bottom of a 2-part outlet.

If you have a large house, it is possible you might have more than one main electrical circuit running through your house. This only works if you plug both devices into the same master circuit. Of course that is not the fault of the device; that will be true of any range extender of this type.

These power plug range extenders have been on the market for a while, but nice someone finally decided to include a pass-through outlet, but too bad that the device isn't just a little smaller so that it doesn't partially block the second plug in a 2-plug outlet when plugged in at the bottom. Note these do need to be plugged directly into a wall outlet; can't be used off a power strip. That could be an issue if you are short of outlets, as I am.

The connection speed wasn't quite as good as I expected, but it is adequate. The units heated up a little, which I didn't like, but not uncomfortable to the touch. I also have experience with standalone extenders that don't use the powerlines in your home; they work just about as well and some of them also have ethernet ports; the only difference being that you are going Wi-Fi to the extender and then going back to ethernet if you want to use a cable, whereas with a powerline extender, you are going through wires all the way. Those standalone extenders only require one outlet too.

I have used other TP-Link products and generally they seem to be of good quality, so I don't hesitate in any way to use their brand. Made in China, which is common for electronics products.

I paired this up with a Onkyo TX-NR809 home theater receiver and i'm extremely pleased. Its a bigger improvement sound wise from my RSW-15 sub from klipsch . I've owned the Klipsch Reference line since around 2002ish and they sound just as good today as they did after a few hours of break in. The reason why this middle brand 12 inch improved the sound quality in my room is purely my hearing style preference. I love front firing subwoofers my old one had a passive 15 inch behind and front firing but air flowed behind so the sound felt strange, In this unit, the bass is very deep for a 12 inch and has 3 options. Movie, music and flat settings . Each one can be customized. My room is large or slightly under a large. It fills everything with tight bass.

I have to run it on +3 volume on the subwoofer with my receiver set to reference (dead center) if I want extra bass.. Even if the sub itself set to 0 (dead center reference) it still produces tons of large bass. Especially with bass tracks and movies. For me to listen to bass music like drumming bass, Deadmau5, DJ baby Anne I have to set the subs volume to -8 so it doesn't disturb neighbors and I STILL GET BASS! One of the reason I went with this 12 inch was to control the deep bass from extending and having cops called on me. It didn't help. I have absolutely no problem with this.If anything it reinforces its a good subwoofer.

TIP: for many of those using receivers that do auto calibration. Its better to do yours subwoofer settings by hand and personal hearing preference. Many auto-calibration systems like Audyssey have a tendency to ask you to lower the subs volume on the unit and mutes the bass sound. This is normally done to adjust the speakers hertz frequency and measure the room but system like Audyssey do not take bass into account. So your speakers will probably get shifted to see itself as "large speakers" even if you have towers. This reduces overall bass tracks your subwoofer plays because it thinks the other speakers can reproduce low bass. To fix any lack of bass, change the hertz settings of each speaker at a starting point of 80hrz. This will feed the subwoofer bass tracks that the others speakers can not reproduce. Satellites speakers crank it up to 120hrz or more.

-LFE (low frequency effects) in your receiver settings to 120hrz. Sub crossover or LFE settings are in the receiver itself.
-all speaker herz settings to 80 or test by going higher. Some have a setting for small and large Set them small even if you have towers unless they have powered subs built into them.(this is normally in the settings of the speakers in the receiver) Not the sub itself.

This allows your receiver to control where bass gets redirected. If you set the receiver to control every speaker, you would disable similar settings on the subwoofer itself, That way you don't get the sub and receiver having a double filter effect. The only thing you raise up and down would be the subs volume control and equalizer settings IN THE SUB. I avoid lowering and increase sub volume from the receiver , instead ,do it by hand on the unit.

I'm a big fan of Kindle e-Readers. We own two of the older generation ones (the last Kindles with keyboard) and for x-mas I bought my mother a Kindle Fire HD 8.9 for x-mas. But, alas, she doesn't seem to have fine enough motor control to hit the small buttons on that device (see my review for that device). So the Fire has been sitting unused on the coffee table for a few months now.

But this is not a review of the Fire HD 8.9. I want to describe my very short experience with the basic Kindle and the Kindle Paperwhite - as they relate to the intended user: my mom. She recently suffered a stroke and one of the side effects is that she now has a constant tremble in her left hand. As she had trouble with the Fire HD 8.9 we went to Staples to see if the more purpose-built Kindles were easier to operate. We were not surprised when she often made mistakes selecting books on the Paperwhite's touch screen. But we were surprised to find that she couldn't even handle the physical buttons on the basic Kindle! From what I could tell, the problems were: the side-buttons (page forward/backward) are much smaller and narrower than they were on our old Kindles (which my mom had no trouble with), so basic navigation among pages became iffy. Similarly, the D-pad is smaller too - and that made selection of books difficult for her. Finally, while I could easily hold my old Kindle with one hand AND operate the page forward button, this is a bit more difficult with the new basic Kindle. My mom could not manage it at all. And since she can't hold the Kindle with her trembling left hand, neither e-Reader was for her. [She is now making do with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9 by laying it on a flat surface and only operating it with her right hand].

I'm still giving the Kindle 4 stars because none of these shortcomings are of interest to the majority of people, but I wanted folks to be aware of the newer devices' potential limitations with those suffering from limited motor skills.

I've been using desktop PCs since the 1980s. In the old days we always bought the biggest PC cases so we could add more components like multiple disc drives, CD drives, extra I/O and networking ports, a bigger power supply, etc. These days, computers come packed with features and interfaces, internal storage is smaller and cheaper, USB3 is fast enough for external peripherals if we need them, and more and more computing is done in the cloud instead of on the desktop.

This little 5 inch x 5 inch x 2 inch box is all I really need for my desktop computing needs. The Intel i5 CPU is the same as what most mid-range laptops use. The built-in SSD and 16gb of RAM are faster than the hard drive and 8gb in our old PC that we replaced with this one. There is space to add a 2.5" SSD to increase the local storage space (I'm planning to add a 2TB SSD). The computer has plenty of ports; even a microSD flash card slot. The PC comes with Windows 11 pre-installed and it launched flawlessly when I turned the PC on.

There are 2 limitations for me. First is that there is only one memory card slot which currently contains a 16GB memory card. This is enough for most people (especially considering the mid-range i5 CPU) but if you want to add more memory, you must discard the 16GB card and replace it with a bigger card. Most PCs have 2 memory card slots so you can simply add a second memory card that adds to the first one. The second limitation is that the built-in graphics processor is not suitable for high-end gaming and there is no room to add a high-performance graphics card. If you are a hard core gamer, you should probably look elsewhere.

Considering the size and price of this mini-PC, I think it is fine as an everyday desktop computer for home or for the office. Students will probably want a laptop that they can carry to school, but a lot of adults prefer having a full-sized keyboard and screen and this mini-PC is cheaper than a comparable laptop if you have to buy a separate monitor in either case. If I want more power than my phone when I'm traveling, I bring a tablet instead of a more bulky and more fragile laptop.

My only real complaint about this mini-PC is that the fan is not super quiet and it runs a lot when I am multi-tasking with more than one program running.

The prices on big-screen smart tvs are in free-fall these days; projectors are always a bit of a project. But you're sure you want a projector, right? If so this is a great choice. Easy set up, great image, amazing keystoning (more on THAT in a moment), powerful internal speakers, and a decent price point (under $900 currently.)

Setup could scarcely be easier - provided you have your screen and the (not included) input cables/stick - or a wireless dongle. As I already had a projection screen and an HDMI cable for my laptop, all I had to do was switch on the projector, adjust the lens, run the start utility to keystone for the projector being offset from the center of the screen, connect the cable from laptop to projector, then allow the device to find the video source - the device finds the input in a few seconds and is soon streaming video and audio.

The projector's own audio is surprisingly good - and loud. Response to the remote is... a little slow, depending how close you are to the projector. The projector's own audio is great, and as we have it closer to the screen than we sit, I haven't felt the need to connect speakers. Persons with more demanding tastes in audio will of course differ, but the device's own speakers do a solid job.

Video quality is OUTSTANDING. Colors are vibrant and although a light source placed near the screen washes them out, the image is still clearly visible. With a light source more than 10 feet away and even with natural light through windows (at the opposite end of a 25-foot room) the image is perfectly clear; even though as I'm using a white screen the blacks are clear and dark. There was one strange exception to this with a streaming video (Extant) where the darks were warmer in the projection than on the laptop, but we have run other video and also had a DVR player (hooked up via the triple cables), and run DVRS with perfect light levels. I recently got an Amazon Fire Stick, and actually set it up on the projector - setup was easy and there have been no adjustments needed for the streaming video.

The keystoning is an amazing, but somewhat tedious, feature; you can offset the device and still get an excellent image. Using the keystoning feature on the remote, some tweaking gives you a near-perfect image. I say near perfect because when we had the projector placed eight feet back and some feet down to the left of the screen, the upper right-hand corner of the image frame bent inwards - although the cast image itself was clear and undistorted. This was apparently because the projector was not on a perfectly horizontal surface. The real issue was that when the projector was moved back in front of the screen, I had to redo the keystoning manually; holding down the OK key was supposed to reset it, but this didn't work for me.

The projector is relatively light and easy to move around. The feet are easy to unscrew to manipulate the image, but for the afore-mentioned keystoning issue, it was necessary to adjust the surface the projector was resting on; this would obviously be a whole different matter if ceiling-mounted.

I think it's a great projector. So really it all boils down to whether you WANT a projector - the VERY big picture and/or the portability, eh? You don't care about having to control light levels, positioning the device itself (and the associated transmitting device,) maintaining a screen, dealing with multiple interfaces... You're not the complete couch potato, surfing the channels via remote... Not to go on and on - this is a projector, not a tv. You can hook it up to a tv, or a laptop, streaming stick, etc, but - a projector is always going to be more complicated. This, however, is an amazingly uncomplicated projector!
