As with the original Fire, the out of box experience is very nicely done. Very straightforward process of just turning it on and letting the tablet register and update itself. It took about 10 minutes (with the majority of the time waiting for an update to download) and it was ready to go. It picked up all my original Fire music and books from the cloud and most of my Fire apps. I was disappointed to see that a couple of my favorite apps (TED Talks and Play Music Videos Free) were judged not compatible with my new Fire. Hopefully updates will be coming soon.

The screen is delightful! Crisp and clear, and a marked increase in resolution versus the original Fire. Videos on the HD Fire are simply amazing.

The sound quality is also a marked improvement. While it was pretty much mandatory to hook up an external speaker for the original Fire, the new Fire puts out pretty decent sound quality all on its own. I still hook it up to external speakers (I'm partial to the Bose Companion 20) for movies and music when I'm at my desk, but it puts out more than adequate sound all on its own.

Response time is more snappy than the original Fire, and the carousel is easier to navigate (smoother scrolling). Picking up a WiFi signal seems to be better with the new fire - I'm getting all signal strength bars displayed in areas of the house where I could only get 2 or 3 bars with the original Fire.

The form factor is great for video watching. The extra screen size makes a big difference. The other huge advantage to the size is typing. It's MUCH easier to see and use the onscreen keyboard than on the original Fire. I had no problems typing without a stylus; on the original Fire a stylus is a must.

So far I don't see many misses other than a hard-to-find power button. The casing and build quality is not at the same level as an iPad, but neither is the price. I'm very pleased with the price-performance level of the HD Fire.

This is not replacing my original Fire - I'll continue to use that for most of my book reading and when I need portability. For everything else, the larger screen is well worth the additional cost.

I have a Nexus 7, the iPad 2 and an HP Touchpad and the Fire is my favorite by far. Not because either the original or this new Fire are the best in terms of build quality or speed or tech specs, but for one simple reason: the Fire makes it so incredibly easy to avail myself of entertainment and content. The tight link to the Amazon ecosystem is, for me, a huge plus - it keeps my entertainment pipeline full of things I want to read, listen to or watch with little or no effort on my part. Most of the USB cables I have are either 3' cables or are really short ones that come with electronic devices. Sometimes a longer cable is really handy, especially when the immediate area surrounding a work space is cramped. I looked to these 10' cables to help alleviate one such issue and I learned a few things. One of those things is that a cable can be too long in some cases, though this is a failure in organization, not in the cable.

These are flat USB cables. Flat cables are less likely to tangle than their round counterparts, but I will confess to preferring round cables anyway (it’s a personal preference, not a technical preference). These are shielded in woven nylon which is great; the nylon is stronger than soft plastic shielding and gives the cable a little more stiffness but does not make the cable so stiff that it’s awkward to run. The connectors are interesting - two-tone plastic that is different than anything else on my desk which makes it a lot easier to determine where both ends of the cable are plugged in. I tried stressing the cable ends at the connectors by trying to pull out the shielding from the plugs and they held firm.

I tried one of these with my phone and it worked just fine, I was able to charge the phone and move data between it and my laptop. I did not attempt a speed test.

There is a big difference between 3' cables, 6' cables and 10' cables. If you need a 6' cable, a 10' cable will leave you trying to figure out what to do with the extra 4' of cable. In my case this meant having to use a twist tie to bunch the cable up in the middle. This is not a criticism but rather a suggestion - get a cable that’s the right length for the job. If you need a 10' cable, these have worked great for me.

First, let me preface that I in NO way count myself a photog. I am just a shutter bug who has been firing frames almost non-stop since the age of 18. I learned on my dad's 'old' Nikon SLR with an f/1.2 lens. The Nikon SLRs/DSLRs I have owned are: N50, N60, N55, N80 and D50. My N50 ad N80 had the best lenses. The N60 and N55 were not as great and the D50 was a fabulous entry-level digital. The only medium format camera I own is my Holga. But hey, unlike the photographer at Portrait Innovations, at least I know 'medium format' does not refer to the number of megapixels at which I am shooting. As for my working knowledge, I had three semesters of photography in college. I can process/print both B&W and color film. (Not that that does me any good these days LOL) I can shoot completely 'manual' and I have stood among many pro photographers on the bridge at sunset, waiting for the color to be just right on Half Dome. (My Bogen tripod was way too heavy to be practical for an amateur but it gave me street credit.) So, in a nut shell, I shoot by the 'Sunny 16' rule. I know that opening my f-stop should increase my shutter speed give me a shorter depth of field; and, per the great Ansel Adams, f/8 is a proper exposure for all pictures.

That said, I hate my D3100.

I have had metering issues since I opened the box. I bought the camera so I could take 'even better' pictures of my infant son than I was getting from my D50. Ha. Joke was on me.

The contrast was BLINDING on the factory settings and every shot was over exposed. I have tried every metering option in the menu but the only changes I can achieve are under-exposure, blurred focus and missed shots. It's go high or go without.

I always lower my ISO to 100 when I'm outside because I crave rich color but it's just not there. I have tried Aperture Priority, Shutter Priority and Manual. Nothing. f/16 over my film speed on a sunny day. That's supposed to work! I have used it on many a 'less complicated' camera and achieved photos that make jaws drop. Well, there's no jaw dropping with this camera.

The metering overrides my manual choices every time. It's like I'm having a battle of wits with my camera. :( It reminds me of the days when Kodak was marketing 800-speed film as a universal, never-miss-a-shot solution to all your photo woes. Bleh. Just because there's always an image doesn't mean it's the RIGHT exposure.

I get that being an entry-level/made-for-the-masses DSLR really does mean it's a glorified point-and-shoot but it should preform at least as well as it's predecessors. Honestly, I got far more reliable results from my Canon SureShot and a roll of Kodak 100.

My expectation for a camera is that the image should be very close to perfect when the shutter closes. I know there's always room for improvement before printing but that's the art of photography. The hours I spend working on my photos after the shot should be to make them pop. Instead, my time is spent trying to rescue precious memories.

If you are considering this camera as your first DSLR because you think it will improve your skills, skip it. Invest in an equally expensive point-and-shoot that will give you all the same manual controls and preform much better in low-light situations. The D3100 does not live up to the standards of a Nikon SLR.

I've had problems with Pixmas in the past, mostly having to do with wireless networks and having to reinstall the software over and over to try to get them to hang on to network settings. I can't guarantee that this printer is going to be any better in the long run, but the set-up actually works pretty well if you use the standard version, not the WPS... and I'm getting way ahead of myself on this one.

To begin with, the printer requires a lot of time for set-up. You're not going to be doing this on the fly, so set aside an hour or so to: 1) remove all the tape of which there is much, 2) read over the instructions 3) install the ink, 4) run a print alignment 5) set up your wireless connection (about which more in a moment) 6) install the software (which takes a good 15 minutes or more), and 7) put the machine (and yourself) through its paces. Yeah, it's going to take a while.

Now I know you can read about the features on your own, so I'm here to tell you about the things that work for me and those that don't. First off, the wireless set-up is confusing. Choose Standard instead of WPS and save yourself some headaches unless you're a computer whiz kid. After the third error message in the WPS set-up I went to standard, entered my pass code and had the connection up and running in about a minute.

Once that was done and the software was installed I fired up the Canon Image Garden. First I scanned an image and attempted to rotate, crop and fix any deficiencies I found. The scan was over sharp and looked a bit jagged, but a little fiddling with the Canon software fixed that. Canon software also rotated and cropped perfectly. One really nice feature is that they remind you to put the printing side of the paper down in the paper cassette. How many pieces of paper will that save?

The biggest complaint I had was that it didn't give me a choice of which paper cassette to use for printing, so I got a ridiculously truncated image on the first try. I believe it chooses the paper based on the size of the image, which I get, but at the same time that limits flexibility in printing. I opened another photo processing program and it allowed me to print from whatever cassette I liked. Coupled with a better suite of applications for correction and enhancement, I think it's safe to say that I'll be using the Canon software almost never.

Printing on plain paper is clearly not going to be as satisfactory as it is on glossy, but in some cases I found it surprisingly good, good enough to give you an idea of what sort of image you're going to end up with when you switch to photo paper. It's also more than good enough for printing out emails and web pages.

Scanning and printing are both pretty fast, another plus. And the copy function works pretty seamlessly without any sort of computer interface. Just punch a couple of buttons and Bob's your uncle! It does take a bit of time to warm up and is a little noisy but no more so than any Canon printer I've ever used. It's not bothersome, in my opinion. You might feel otherwise.

Inks are easy to install, but you'll find refills pricey, no question. I suspect off-brand ones are available or will be soon enough.

In short, it's a good, inexpensive printer for a home or home office. Use photo paper and settings and get the full quality the MG5420 is capable of producing; I think it's pretty remarkable. The photos I printed out are as good as or in one case, better than the original. That's a powerful recommendation in my book.

I really like the "ZeroTouch" voice-command app that comes with this ZEROTOUCH DASHBOARD CELL PHONE HOLDER (With Voice-Command App for Android Phones). It was easy to set up on my Galaxy S7 Edge, and it seems to work very well "on the road".

I haven't tested it a whole lot (because of physical installation issues, more on that later), but it seems to have an excellent, up-to-date GPS Navigator, and a terrific Text Message Handler. To send or reply to a text, you wave a hand to wake the app, tell it to "Send a message to (name a contact)", dictate the message, listen to the readback, and answer "yes" to the query "Should I send it". If you have the Samsung "S Voice", it's quite similar, except that "ZeroTouch" notifies you of incoming text messages, and lets you reply to them strictly with voice commands.

The "ZeroTouch" app only works when your cellphone is docked with the cellphone car mount base. Docking and mounting are where I ran into problems. First, there aren't many places in a Honda Civic that are suitable for a suction-cup-base cellphone holder--at least not if you worry about the suction cup losing its grip and dumping your expensive smartphone on the car floor.

Second, the cellphone docks with the car mount base via a thin, adhesive-backed magnetic plate that you're supposed to attach directly to your cellphone or cellphone case. (Tip: If you're having trouble pairing during setup, place the thin metal plate that attaches to your phone directly atop the round part of the base until the magnet grips.) Attaching the plate was an issue, because I didn't want to apply it directly to my new phone (and maybe mar the finish). Applying the plate to my cellphone case worked for a short time, but the adhesive wasn't strong enough to hold the cellphone case through repeated dockings and undockings. Now the adhesive is worn out and won't adhere to anything.

However, there is a workaround. If only the magnetic plate is docked on the base, the "Zero Touch" app will work whenever your cellphone is NEAR the base--within Bluetooth range, I guess. So my hands-free calling/messaging arrangement uses the Honda Civic's two cupholders. The base with the docking strip goes in one cupholder, and the cellphone with the "Zero Touch" app goes in the other.

With this setup, I can use all of the "Zero Touch" features. Of course, if I want to use the handy "parking location finder" feature, I need to undock the magnetic strip from the base when I leave the car, just as I would if the strip were still attached to my cellphone.

The magnetic plate did NOT interfere with my S7 Edge's wireless charging feature, when I had the plate attached to the lower quarter of the cellphone case. (The "ZeroTouch" app setup has a diagram showing you where to attach the plate, if you use wireless charging.)

Because I love the easy-to-use "ZeroTouch" app, but am dissatisfied with the holder mounting arrangement (suction cup and adhesive may not adequately secure the cellphone), I rate this product at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

This item is one version of the OSSC, and turns out it is not case-compatible with the official one, having several different components populated on the board, so it will not fit in the normal OSSC cases.

It is not at all confidence-inspiring that the manufacturer here deviated from the official board layout and component selection. The PSU is extremely cheap, and some things are just incorrect.

Some of the components I noticed were different are:

- the screen: The height of the screen is quite a bit lower than what's shown in pictures of the official OSSC, and on closer examination, it appears the screen was soldered to the wrong side of the board because of layout issues.
- the buttons: the buttons here have yellow nubs on top, but the official one has low profile tactile buttons. This is another point where 3D printed cases made for this (such as those sold by Laser Bear) will interfere with this OSSC, preventing the case from closing.
- The audio select switch: the switch is mounted to the bottom of the PCB instead of the top. There appear to be traces for the switch on the top of the PCB, but it's not clear why they were mounted to the bottom of the board. Again, this is an issue because cases will have allowance for this switch, and expect the switch to be located on the top of the PCB.

Given that these components were swapped or moved, I can't be certain about the rest of the component choices, and given how cheap the power supply is, I'm not confident at all that the manufacturers here prioritized quality over price in any way whatsoever.

I'm a huge Lensbaby fan. I've been using them with my Canon SLRs almost since they first came out, and have assembled a pretty extensive collection of them over the past few years. Yes, I am a lover of blur. It's one of those creative effects that you either love or don't (although I certainly will admit it can be overused with some horrible results). I've recently been playing around with Micro Four Thirds cameras and was thrilled to see that Lensbaby came out with a model specifically designed for the MFT format.

Quick primer for those not familiar with a Lensbaby: it's a very simple device that allows you to tilt the focal plane of the lens to shift focus to any area of the frame and produce a smooth blur effect. It can be in a small or large part of your photo depending on which of the several aperture rings you choose from (all supplied with this Lensbaby) and how much tilt you apply.

This particular version of the lens, called the "Composer" is part of Lensbaby's new Optic Swap System, which allows you to use any one of several optics (plastic, glass, double glass, pinhole/zoneplate) that you can easily swap out of the main body. This comes with the double glass optic - the other optics have to be purchased separately.

The new Composer design allows you to lock the tilt into place for some level of repeatability in your shots. A lot more convenient than earlier versions of Lensbabies, which required you hold the tilt with your fingers. Now it's just pick your aperture and your optic, tilt, and snap away!

This lens comes with an extra you can't get with other Lensbabies for other camera formats - the "tilt transformer." This is an attachment that will allow you to use any Nikon-mount lens as a close approximation of a tilt/shift lens (only close, since you really only get the benefit of tilt and not shift). With this attachment and a "regular" lens, you get a movable sliver, a line of focus, as opposed to the movable point of focus you get with a Lensbaby Optic. Same basic principle, but it produces a slightly different look.

Build quality is good. There's a lot of plastic in it, but my other Lensbabies have performed very well over the years with zero problems. The product comes nicely packaged, but only has minimal instructions. That's not really a problem since the company website has a lot of resources on how to use Lensbabies, plus has photo galleries, forums, instructional videos, and a lot more. Very nice resource if you own one. If you're not sure if a Lensbaby is for you, that should be your first stop to see what type of effects their products can produce. I've spent a lot of time there, and it has been time well spent. The company itself is excellent when it comes to customer service. I've contacted them a couple of times with questions, and they answer emails promptly.

This lens is versatile, and is more convenient to carry (both the Lensbaby as well as a MFT camera itself). I've found with all my gear that convenience of toting it means I'll carry it more often, and thus have more opportunity for taking great shots. The tilt transformer is a wonderful addition - you can play around with a tilt lens at a fraction it would cost you to buy a real tilt/shift lens.

While pricy for a Lensbaby, when you add up all the features it brings to the table, I find it to be a real winner. Highly recommend if you have a MFT camera.

Having recently dug my music collection (odd how we go back into hobbies after years of stagnation), I took time to curate my setup (and by setup I mean my Note8 with a USB DAC) for optimal listening. Until recently, but "best" headphones were my Shure Aonic 4, which are excellent for the price range. The cable it comes with is okay, but preferably replaceable. It comes with an inline mic and makes a lot of feedback-noise when moved. I know cables are a mixed bag when it comes to audio equipment, so I shied away for years. But rather than place the emphasis on audio-quality improvement when looking at cables, I realized I'd rather get a cable if it looks and feels good. This one fit the ticket.

This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way.

Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. They are easy to tangle, even if I use the "roadie wrap." Putting them on while on the go proved to be suboptimal; I have to be sitting or standing to put them on.

Sometimes I get some feedback noise, but rarely. Definitely not the same as the stock cable that comes with the Aonic 4.

The biggest problem I have is that the end connection disconnects nearly every time I use the cable. Having a modular cable is awesome, but the connection from the cable to the audio jack doesn't lock. I expected there to be a click, indicating it's on and snug, but no such thing. Since I use this cable while on the go, it's connected to my phone, which rests in my pocket. At least once the cable end will come loose. It's easy to press back in (just a little nudge will do), but it is rather annoying.

Now for the good.

The cable feels awesome. I get now why people prefer to upgrade certain cables. I care very little for how much the audio quality is "improved" (there's too much immeasurable subjectivity in that area), but having a cable that doesn't tangle easily and is very light makes enough of a difference to justify the upgrade. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. The metal ends and Y-splitter are very nice and definitely attribute the cable with a premium look.

This cable has sold me on the reasons to upgrade headphone cables.

I happen to use a D-Link DIR 1360 as my internet router at home, and while it does a decent job broadcasting signal around me, it is located at one corner of our home which means the opposite corner of the house has too many barriers for a fast signal. And if I want to take my laptop out to the porch? No reliability at all!
But with this placed a few rooms over from the router, it has greatly extended my network and the speed of things nearby it. It was super simple to set up, too! I'm not sure if that's just because I happen to have a D-Link router, but all I had to do was press the setup button on the router and extender while plugged in next to it, then once setup I could unplug and move it wherever I wanted to extend to. No app or IT knowledge required! Literally press the button, wait a few minutes for the lights to turn green, and good to go! The access point matches the original name of my router, so it is all completely invisible to the user. The device picks whichever device is closer / stronger and automatically connects to it without any user intervention, much like a cell phone. Now, this is only possible because my router supports this mesh-style setup. Otherwise you'll have to do one of those alternative SSID things where the device sees two networks and has to decide which one to connect to. The first was is preferable obviously, and just works better in addition to being cleaner.

With my laptop in my living room (on the other side of the house from my router), I used to get somewhere between 20-40mbps in my speed tests downloading. That's not terrible, but I'm paying for 300mbps service! But with this plugged in the middle of my home, that jumped to 80-90mbps reliably! Still not the 200+ speeds I get if only a room or two away from the router, but definitely an improvement by almost 2x... and spots outside on the porch that rarely had coverage before now do.

HOWEVER, like any extender, this WILL introduce some lag to your network. This is the part I was warning about in the headline, as most people think extenders will improve your performance across the board, which isn't true. While my download and upload speed improved, my Ping time degraded from 8ms to 14 (lower is better). That extra hop from the extender back to the router has a cost. Now, that difference shouldn't make a huge difference in most things, 14ms is still pretty respectable, however a larger ping lag can effect real-time performance like lag in multiplayer games and video call performance. Arguably, in those cases, a lower ping is more important than higher speeds. So if I'm having trouble with gaming lag or video call echo, I'd probably unplug this and go with the original weaker signal to the router directly. But if I'm going outside, or just streaming Netflix etc, than the download performance is more important than the ping. So, make your decisions wisely... I've seen too many people running multiple zoom devices over lockdown and think a wireless extender is going to solve their problems, but in fact just made everyone's zoom calls worse! But this isn't the fault of the device, that's inherent of how all extenders work. So, I'm still giving this 5 stars for being an excellent instance of what it should be: a way to boost transfer speeds and extend range that's dead simple to set up.

I was so excited to finally have a separate GPS again, as my Garmin one was from 2009 (OLD maps) and using my phone was unsafe because even with stuff disabled during driving, I was still getting messages and interruptions that would pop up, plus I like listening to something on the drive, and using it as a GPS makes that tricky. Having tried several Garmin models, Apple Maps, and Google Maps, I was excited to try TomTom. And I was disappointed.

Problems:
•Screen is VERY dim in the sunlight, and living in Florida, this is most of the time. It is NOT easy to see the map, which even in my ancient Garmin is much more visible and automatically switches from day mode to night mode. Likewise, my iPhone screen automatically changes brightness for the amount of sun coming in. And this? It looks horribly dim and takes a lot of effort to see.
•Routes don’t always make sense. I’m used to some amount of this in the other systems I’ve tried, but they’re really wacky on this thing, taking a REALLY scenic route that sometimes involves making a full circle for something that was literally as easy as just turning left in the correct place.
•Point of interest search is slow and ineffective. Even with my ancient Garmin (and obviously with my phone), it would never find most places, even ones that have been there many years. This after waiting an interminable amount of time for the list to compile. Did I get the long update on my computer and add it to the GPS? Yep. I thought that was the problem, did the update, and then discovered it was Not the problem.
•Doesn’t appear to take traffic into account. Neither does my old Garmin, but it should do better than a piece of tech that’s 10 years old and at least be comparable to a current smartphone’s GPS; otherwise, what’s the point?
•Hard to stop. You want to sometimes say, “OK SHUT UP. I know the rest of the way!”, and in all other GPS systems I’ve tried, getting to the “end route/stop” place is usually two steps, max. It is long and complicated, and I don’t want to die in a car accident, so I end up having to suffer through unnecessary and often over-complicated routes that make no sense.
•Doesn’t default to turn-by-turn. Sometimes it shows an aerial view, which is zero helpful, has no detail, and requires me to think a lot about “is this to MY right or left if my car is facing this way and the map is oriented North Up and I *think* I am moving East maybe, but I can’t tell because this stupid thing is both dim and also has an unbelievably zoomed out map view where I’m not sure Where my little dot is going?!?!”

So yes. Unless I sit in the parking lot and fiddle with it for a good while, nothing is quite right, and everything takes a long time to find or set up. I tried it for a month now, and my opinion has not changed. This is frustrating.

Good things:
•nice size screen
•fun voices

Overall rating: 2 stars. I like Garmin more, and I am quite unhappy with this. It is slightly better than my now failing 10-year-old Garmin GPS. *slightly*. I would not buy this or recommend it. The interface is cumbersome, the visibility is bad in the sun, and finding places is a pain and basically 100% of the time requires me to just search for an address on my phone and plug it in. Nope.

I prefer a good messenger bag to a backpack most of the time. I prefer the way a messenger bag looks, how it is organized and how it provides protection to the contents of the bag most of the time, the trade-off being reduced space when compared to a regular-sized backpack. This is a nice bag and I am pleased with it. It recently came in very handy when we were traveling.

This is a large, canvas messenger bag. The canvas used is not the heaviest grade canvas I have seen but it is not the lightest or softest either. It seems to be the right balance of durability and softness as the bag is durable and holds up to abuse but is still soft and pliable enough to be workable in most spaces (like crammed behind a car seat).

Most messenger bags I have seen of late have used magnets as the closing mechanism and this one does so too. There are two leather straps on the flap that have buckles, but these buckles are strictly decorative. Attached to the main body of the bag and to the buckles are magnets and plates that work to close the back with little effort. They hold as well as metal snaps in most cases, the exception being if you overstuff the bag. There is a zipper to supplement the flap, so if you can zip the bag then you can snap it shut too.

The bag has a large main compartment that has a padded divider in the middle. This compartment is large enough to handle a smaller laptop (and I have a 10” tablet and keyboard that fits it very well) and it also is large enough to handle a couple of books. It also has a zippered pocket in the main compartment that is a good size for a phone, a calculator or a small note pad. On the front of the bag on the outside there are two small pockets that are also good for small items. This bag is about the right side for a school bag or a “go bag” with essential tools in it.

This is a good bag and I like it. It is well-made, roomy and has a good layout for the space and pockets. It’s a good choice if you need a durable and useful daily bag or even an emergency tool bag.

Some people have had battery problems with this camera. I bought 2 extra Vivitar batteries with higher mA-h ratings than the stock Canon batteries. If you do the math, this camera can put a huge load on the microprocessor when you ask it to take high-rate, high-resolution videos, or multiple shots. Zoom a lot at the same time, and these little batteries aren't going to hack it. In addition, Canon has something wrong (I suspect) with the battery life sensor/indicator. (My guess is the 1.0.2.0 firmware update that's available from Canon is to help that.) On the good side, that's depressed the price of this camera. Since I don't intend to take a lot of videos with this camera, I'm OK with that. :)

I may have also gotten a good one. Over 2 days of playing with it, I've yet to change the battery. It's showing 2/3 charge. It has however, flashed "charge the battery" warnings a
couple of times.

For calibration, this is replacing a Canon A1100IS we bought about 4 years ago as a second camera.

Pro (for me):
Really good, clear pictures
Good image stabilization (hand-holding at 1/15th of a second or slower!)
Low noise, as low as ISO 1600
Large zoom range
Manual focus
DIGIC 6 processor (latest generation)
Very nice screen
P, Av, Tv & M exposure modes
Canon's basically good control layout
Small and light; carrying around a DSLR can be wearying
Wi-Fi is handy
Fits in the same case as my A1100, which was originally bought for a tiny 35 mm Vivitar I carried as a 2nd camera for years. It's marked "Samsonite World Sport, Model #20" if that helps.

Cons:
Not as good a macro capability as the A1100 (which is sterling at that one thing. I'll be keeping it for that.)
No viewfinder (unlike the A1100. It's not needed all the time, but it is handy)
Slow GPS lock in (my Nexus shows 18 or so satellites in view, and took maybe 30 sec. to lock in. The camera took several times that)
GPS power hog. (It appears to suck up a lot of power, turning it on and off a few times did seem to affect battery charge indication)
No auto bracket (To be fair, that's not common on cameras, but it should be. Canon puts it on the similar S110.)
No hyperfocal distance setting (You can do it manually, of course, but, Canon, why not add another click on the focus bar? There's a computer in there, you know)
Lithium batteries (I prefer the A1100's NiMH AAs so you can get a new set at any Staples for cheap or use alkaline AAs in a pinch)

So, with all of 2 days of experience under my belt:
1) Nice easily-portable camera at a low-ish price
2) Power hog, due to inefficient GPS, big zoom, and powerful microprocessor being pushed by video, etc.
I'll update this review someday when I have some durability information.

Update: 4/27/2014 Took a nice long walk, shot 6 min. of 720p x 30fps video and took 101 L-superfine .jpg (4k x 3k pixel) photos. This used up most of a fully-charged Vivitar 1700 mA-h battery. I got a battery warn and shutdown after my walk while reviewing the video at home. The 1000 mA-h stock Canon battery would give proportionately less life. Canon says that the stock battery is good for 210 photos. A 1700 mA-h Vivitar battery should be good for 147 more than that, or 357 photos. That means that 6 min. of 720p video is worth 256 photos! I don't think anyone will be shooting at 1080p x 60fps much.

Another way to look at it is the number of pixels processed per second by any of the 11 modes of the camera. The normal L .jpg picture takes 12.0E+6 pixels/sec (12 megapixels/sec). The least hungry mode S, takes only 0.307E+6 pixels per second. The hungriest mode is the 14 frames per second L multiple shot mode, which takes 168.E+6 pixels/sec. Since this is only in use for a few frames, it's not bad on battery life. The second worst mode 1080p x 60fps takes 124.E+6 pixels per second, 1037% of the normal L photo processing power! The 720p x 30fps mode I used is only 230% of the normal L mode. Remember, though, the single shot modes are on now and then, maybe a second out of every minute at most. The video modes are on continuously.

NB: Good cameras with a lot of features have historically eaten batteries. I carry around a handful for the A1100.

Misc.: I'm sorry to see the little A1100 get superseded; it was a trouper. Its biggest problem was auto-focusing at long zoom, which isn't a problem if you're taking snapshots in your yard, but it can be a problem if you see a magnificent vista before you. The SX280 shouldn't have a problem with that (manual zoom). YMMV

Update 7/13/2014: My one significant complaint with the SX280 was the macro focusing. As I've gotten more experience with it, some of that has gone away. The SX280's autofocus seems to work differently from the A1100's. I tend to use the macro setting less, and let the normal mode carry the freight, except in extreme cases. In many cases, that's plenty good enough. It's still not as good as the A1100, though. In all other ways, this is an amazing still camera. It also still has too small a battery. Canon seems to be phasing this one out. If you need a still camera and can find one of these cheap, you might consider it.
August, 2017 Update: 3 & a bit years after purchase, the camera is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 (lens) errors more & more frequently. That's not a bad lifespan for a point & shoot, especially with a wide-range zoom lens. The error appears to be focus related.
Sept. 2018 Update: I replaced this with a 720. Much better. I actually cured the lens error with some strong blasts into the lens gaps from canned air. That's risky, blowing dust into the camera, but in this case, it worked. The 280 is now my office camera.

I’ve tested a few similar sets of ear buds with mixed results but I was really impressed with this set.

I read the instruction manual - removed the tiny stickers on each ear bud and plugged in the case. It achieved a full charge in just over an hour.

I removed the ear buds from the case, the right one first and then the left and they paired with each other immediately. I went to my Bluetooth settings in my iPhone and found Haylou-GT1_R and my phone paired with the set with no issue.

I was surprised at the sound quality these tiny ear buds deliver. They can definitely be turned up as loud as you’d want to listen. The bass, midtones and treble is on par for ear buds - even those that are much larger.

I did figure out that the initial way I had them in my ears was upside down when I went to test the calling features. The microphone needs to be pointed towards your mouth for best audio reception and sound quality improves a bit in this position.

Call quality was excellent for both hearing the other person and them hearing you.

In my testing the earbuds had no problem receiving within the 33’ stated range (actually making it to around 40’) and even received clearly through multiple walls - 2 rooms away with the doors closed and many obstacles in between.

The only issue I struggled with was tapping the ear bud to stop / start the music and answer / end calls / activate voice assistant and skip tracks. There is no button, you just tap an area of the exterior of the ear bud but you have to tap a very exact area which isn’t necessary easy to locate as it is not differentiated from the rest. It would have been helpful if the manufacturer put a different texture in that area so you could feel it with your finger to locate it.

While the manufacturers claims these last for 12 hours I found it was closer to 8 under normal use - still excellent. And the case will charge them without it having to be plugged back in which is always a nice feature.

These earbuds excelled in all of my tests showing that they are a high quality, dependable product.

This is a set I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend.

We have an old DVD player in our basement that tries to up convert but it is not always that great. It has some nice features that were great when we got it, but we wanted another one to replace it that did not take up so much room.

WHAT THIS WAS USED TO REPLACE
The DVD machine this replaced was a really old Philips. It played all regions. No fancy settings, except a sleep timer setting that shut it off after so long. The menu was ancient and very clumsy to navigate.

DID THIS PLAY AS WELL AS THE OLDER ONE?
This DVD player played DVDs as well as the older one. So far we have not had any issues with it. It was only hooked up to the HDMI and the used a mini USB to USB cord the plugged into the outlet. We made sure that it was powerful enough to run the player.

PICTURE
The picture was comparable to the old DVD player- perhaps a bit nicer in some cases. I am actually surprised that it has performed as well as it has.

TRAVEL
I have to say that traveling to a cabin we go to occasionally was nice. We are able to bring this DVD player with us to plug into any TV and watch some DVDs if we want to. It is without TV service so DVD is the only way to really have entertainment if we want it.

DOES IT PLAY BLURAY?
This is not designed to play BluRay.

ANY ISSUES?
This is not a top of the line DVD player with super high definition. If you are looking for that, this isn't it. Is it good DVD quality? Yes. I think so. If you have the right set up, it is a great way to take up little room and still be able to play DVDs. I am not sure I would have this as my permanent player in my bedroom or anything. But it is great to use once in a while at home or travel.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Although this is not fancy or super high quality, it plays DVDs as well or better than our old player so we are happy with it. The footprint is small and it is portable.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is a decent player and so far has been good in a pinch to use for playing DVDs. I like the small footprint and portability especially when we have to go somewhere for a while. It is nice to be able to tuck it into our luggage/bags to take with us. The remote is a bonus.

I first heard about Cobo Vault on twitter from a few of the various people I follow on there. The thought of a new hardware wallet that was open source (something I really like about Trezor) but also air gapped (no Internet connectivity or USB, bluetooth, etc.) was also super appealing to my ultra paranoid side. I figure as Bitcoin and perhaps other cryptos go up in value, security will become even more paramount so the ultra-paranoia is justified.

Anyway, I started with the Essentials version of the product and I was first impressed with the way the product was packaged nicely; nothing loose in the box, everything protected well. Upon removing it from the packaging, the build quality of the device itself was impressive, setup was straightforward as well.

I really like the fact that the Cobo Vault hardware has a sync to the mobile app. Setting this up is part of the initial setup wizard. Doing this allows you to view the balance in BTC, ETH, etc. or fiat equivalent on the mobile app without actually having the hardware wallet. You can also receive via the mobile app through a QR code. It's likely better to use the QR code off the hardware wallet display itself if you're ultra paranoid but, again, it's an option to use the mobile app only. Keep in mind, you can't view the fiat balance on the hardware wallet since it's air gapped.

For sending, you initiate it through the mobile app but you will need the hardware wallet to complete the actual transaction. This is accomplished through a back and forth process of scanning of QR codes between the hardware wallet and your smartphone.

Because I liked the Essential one so much, I bought another Cobo Vault but this time the Pro version. The reason I bought the Pro version is because it has a fingerprint scanner and I found it to be easier to unlock and perform other operations using that method. Without that feature, you have to either type alphanumeric passwords on the tiny keyboard on the touch screen display or draw a pattern on a display (similar to smart phones). Both seem to be difficult for me as it is a little difficult to type the password correctly on the small touch screen display or draw the pattern correctly without going slowly; especially if you have bigger fingers.

To address this, perhaps having an random ordered numeric dial pad for a password might also be a good alternative.

Battery life: Another reason why the Pro version is superior to the Essentials version is that it includes a rechargeable battery as well as the AAA option. The AAA option seems to have inconsistent battery life and seems to drain really fast for me. I brought this up to the Cobo team and they were really responsive to me and explained why the AAA battery life was hard to calculate and inconsistent at times. Still, it'd be nice if there was some way to bring consistency to AAA battery percentage displayed. That being said, the rechargeable battery is the way to go for consistent use but the AAA battery option is great for long term assurance of the device should it outlive the rechargeable battery.
Suggestion would be to allow the device to be powered and/or charged while in use. Right now the rechargeable battery requires the battery to be detached from the device itself in order to be charged.

firmware updates: I'm really impressed with the frequency of the firmware updates as well as the new features being introduced. A+ on that. Performing the updates has been a mixed bag for me. I've found that for some updates, using the rechargeable battery (charging it to full) and then performing the update works best. Other times, most noticeably the update to 1.40 multicoin, I had to use the AAA battery pack with fresh batteries to update both my Pro and Essential; a fully charged rechargeable pack did not work. I'm confident they will work through this as the product continues to mature.

Which brings me to my last point, the thing that impresses me the most about this product is the response from the Cobo team. They are open to feedback and suggestions and both acknowledge it, respond with great detailed answers and work hastily to incorporate new features. I'm really impressed with the support.

I use a mix of different hardware wallets to store my crypto offline and Cobo Vault is probably my favorite to use right now. I'm super excited to see and be a part of this product line as it matures.

By the time you have them loaded with a good power supply and several hard drives they begin to feel like a tank when you need to move them.

The cutouts and gaps to make routing cables easy are nice, they not only improve the appearance but also help air flow freely through the case. I was a little worried about sharp edges but have not found any, which is good because knowing me if there was even one I would have cut myself on it.

At first I was a little confused about how the hard drives are meant to be installed but once I understood it, it makes perfect sense and is no problem to work with. Another thing that both surprised and pleased me was when I was installing the power supply I noticed there were two extra holes which makes it possible to mount the ps either right side up or upside down. I am not a huge fan of bottom mount for power supplies and as others have said, it can cause problems if the leads for motherboard power are not long enough. Mine just barely reached to the cpu power connector after running it up the rear of the case, resting as it is on the motherboard and running under the video card. I have extensions on order though I'm sure I could get by for the life of the ps as it is now.

I like the long, thin blue light on the front for power on though the green light for hard drive activity is a bit hard to see. Most of all though, I love the paint. No more of that ugly, dingy looking gray metal with thoughts of how I want to paint it black. I am not an expert on such things but I believe the paint is baked on giving it a very nice texture and appearance.

This is a case I would not have been disappointed by if I had paid 60 dollars. Getting it from amazon for 36 with free prime shipping is one of the best deals I've ever found.

My three year old i7 tower with its still impressive Geforce decided to freak out and shut down due to the Northbridge turning into an oven. I couldn't get my Asus to stay on more than 3 minutes before it would abruptly shut down. When turning it back on, I would get a NB temperature warning, so I knew it was hopeless. I opened it up and saw the results of the bake off: My passive heatsink was resting on the floor of my tower, instead of its designated spot on the MB. Come to think of it, I did hear this clang sound at one point. I ordered this product in hopes that it would solve the problem and eliminate the need to purchase a new motherboard (I'm not THAT technically good). Turns out - it was fairly easy to put in. I just used some 90% isopropyl alcohol to clean the left over goo from the previous thermal paste, applied the included thermal paste, placed the adjustable metal rods with spring anchors into the heatsink's base, and snapped this baby down. Finally, I plugged the fan into a nearby free power cord, waited about 20 minutes, then turned it on. Drum roll .... perfect! The temperature levels are now safe and I got my main computer back (so long for now backup laptop). Oh, and the fan is super quiet.

Just one note: My heat sink popped off on its own from the drastic heat, so popping in this replacement NB cooling fan was a breeze. If you are removing a faulty heatsink/fan that still happens to be in place, you may need to take the entire mother board out,.You see, those two screw like things (I called them anchors), snap down into holes through the motherboard in order to clamp down the fan. Once they snap down, the bottoms expand so there's no way get them back out except by squeezing the bottom end (under the motherboard) to get them through.

Once setup on the main router was complete adding the satellite units was as simple as pushing two buttons, and now you have a new MESH wifi network where your devices automatically transfer connectivity to the unit with the most powerful signal.

For speed the primary unit is pretty good. if my main router wifi speed is around 450mbs, the primary wifi is around 300mbs which is pretty good. Now the satellite units speeds drop down to around 45mbs which is good for an extender setup, and is somewhat dependent on how far from the primary unit they are, but the speed is never above 50 mbs. That gets us to range. if this was a wide open building with no interior walls I could see where two units would cover 2000 sq feet, but in reality 2 units are good for a around 1400 sq ft. This still isn't bad considering the install footprint.

What I do like these for is the network is always up no matter the main WIFI router condition. In other words if my main cable modem WIFI goes down, but I have my PC and Printer on this mesh system I can still print while the primary cable modem is down. I've used several compact speakers over the years and they all were decent performers. Nothing to compare, however, with my favorite desktop speakers, the Bose Companion 20. While this speaker doesn't hit that mark either, it is absolutely, hands-down the best compact mono speaker I've used.

It's tiny. And I mean TINY - just a bit over 2 inches in height, width and depth. As per the name, it's a cube. About as unobtrusive as you can get.

The build quality is excellent. It feels solid and well-made. It also comes very attractively packaged in a clear, thick plastic box. While I would normally scold a company for what could appear to be wasteful packaging, in this case the packaging is useful: one of my primary uses for this speaker is as a take-along for my laptop, and the plastic case makes for excellent protection against the bangs and dings suffered by my laptop bag. So, in addition to making it look upscale, the packaging has an actual use down the road.

Setup is simple - plug and go. It has three outputs - 3.5mm cord for something such as a tablet, a USB port for a computer, and a 3.5mm cord for headphones. Covers all the bases as to potential uses.

I did most of my testing and playing with this attached to my laptop. Outstanding sound quality that is crisp, clear but still has decent bass. I used it mainly for listening to podcasts and webinars (some of them actually work related!) and the sound quality was miles beyond what I was getting from my laptop speaker, and significantly better than the lower-end portable speakers I was using.

Now, the Cube doesn't sound as good as the Bose Companion 20. That didn't come as a surprise since the entire speaker is about the same size as just the power converter for the Bose. The size of the Bose make them non-transportable; the Cube is a very easy device to take along with a laptop.

It does not have a volume control. I don't miss it when using it with my PC since it's easier to fiddle with the sound level from the PC rather than have to use the speaker. I can see that as a negative, however, for other uses. On the other hand, a volume control device, be it a knob, wheel or button, would detract from the clean, simple design lines of the Cube. So, an equitable trade-off in my opinion.

This is one of those products that I really can't come up with a single negative other than the fact that it is pricy. But, if you value good quality sound but have to keep the speaker as small as possible, it is worth the cost. This is about the same size as the small take-along speakers that run in the $20 range, but provides sound quality that is miles beyond what they offer. Highly recommend.

I like tech. I've had a computer since the commodore Vic-20 came out. That being said I'm not into competing with or against other computers and computer users. I don't run testing or speed diagnostics on my hardware. If it works and feels or seems to be working as advertised and expected I'm completely happy. I just don't care to sit here are see how many micro-seconds faster my new drive is than my older ones.
All that being said I use external drives exclusively for maintaining backups of my personal files, photos, documents, music, eBooks, Etc. Everything else I can simply reinstall in a couple hours. I don't have that many things installed. My computing needs are simple. But I have lost files due to a drive crash so I meticulously make weekly backups of my important files. This new Samsung solid state drive is remarkably faster at copying files to than my mechanical drives and easily a quarter the size and weight of the Seagate drives. Now I have three complete backups of my files and feel that much safer and secure with three copies of my files and I love that there's no moving parts. I've been using a clip-on light for my Kindle Touch when reading at night. It works, but I don't like that there's a separate piece of equipment I need to keep track of. This all-in-one solution has proven to be an effective way to light up the Kindle without having a separate light.

The case itself is nicely made. The cover is soft and cushy; the interior is a nice "suede" type material that wont harm the screen. All the stitching is even and tight. The Kindle fits in easily and is held securely. The cover has what I assume is a magnetic closure. It works well, and keeps the case closed in transit, but opens without having to undo any snaps or zippers.

The light is attached on the back of the case. When needed, you undo a protective flap (has a snap button), flip the light over the top and secure it in place with a "hook" that's built into the top of the case. The on/off switch is on the side of the light housing. Takes only a couple of seconds to get it into position.

The light is more than adequate for reading is a dark room. It uses 2 button batteries (CR 2032).

IMPORTANT: my case came with a plastic protector on the batteries to ensure the batteries remained fresh in transit. This must be removed before use or it will appear that the light is non-functional. Unfortunately, there are no instructions about this (I guessed it was the issue when the light would not turn on).

While it's great to always have the light as part of the case, the downside is that the light housing creates a bulge on the back side of the case. That makes this more cumbersome to toss into a briefcase since it increases the width. But, for me, it's a fair trade-off since I don't have to remember to bring the light with me.

I'll give this 5 stars, but 4.5 is a more accurate rating since it should come with instructions with regard to the battery. I also think the battery cover should be thicker (no problems so far, but it's a thin plastic) as well as the lens cover (very thin plastic that bends easily). Those quirks aside, I'm finding this to be an excellent case for my Touch.

I've been a Magellan user for several years - have owned four of their GPS systems, and always appreciate how they have improved their products. This unit is my 5th, and replaces a Magellan 4040. After using it for a while I've confident in saying this is the best one yet!

The most visible change is the actual size of the unit. The screen size has been increased, but the unit is thinner and lighter. Very sleek appearance, and the screen is a real joy -- sharp, clear graphics even in the sun, and bigger on-screen buttons for easy use. The mounting system has also been streamlined, and looks and works well. It mounts very easily on a NavMat holder (basically a bean-bag system that I got on Amazon. I'm a huge Navmat fan - makes it a snap to hide the GPS with narry a trace. Best accessory by far for any GPS).

The power connector was not well thought out, however. You have to connect it to the GPS unit AFTER you mount it in the holder. They should have moved the connector it a wee bit to the side to avoid that.

The only button is a slide-type power button on the top. Boot-up time is OK -- not speedy, but not a huge delay either. It does not have a "sleep" mode, so you have to do a cold boot every time. Not a problem in real world use - by the time you get situated in your car, the unit is ready to go.

Voice is clear and easy to understand. Not as natural sounding as a TomTom, but understandable.

Pretty much any recent GPS unit will get you where you want to go. I've found the routing on the Magellans to be very similar to Garmins - could be because they both use the same mapping set (Navteq). The Magellan shines, however, in features that I find helpful. The direction of the next turn is always visible regardless of how far away the next turn will be. Up until recently, Garmin did not offer this (they do now on some of their units). Sounds like a small issue, but I find it very helpful. The Magellan also allows you to very easily exclude a route (or portion). That's a fairly standard feature nowadays, but Magellan allows you to do it in a snap.

In terms of routing, Magellan offers four options (fastest, shortest, most use of freeways and least use). You can see all four options on the map (as a summary) at the same time so you can pick the best one for your needs. Perfect!!

Love the AAA Guidebook, which is a unique Magellan feature. Lets you get details about restaurants and other points of interest just like the paper version from AAA. I used it a lot in my 4040, especially when traveling out of town.

Other unique Magellan features I appreciate is the "ding dong" sound right before a turn (incredibly accurate!) and the fact that the software reminds you to "stay on the current road" when you encounter major exits. Some find that to be nagging, but it has saved me from inadvertently exiting on more than one occasion.

A new feature for Magellan is the lane guidance. Very nicely done. I've used this feature on Navigon units, and found it rather unhelpful. Magellan's implementation is far more useful, with better, clearer graphics. However, lane guidance is not available for every road.

The software is also nicely done - very logical to use. If you're a past Magellan user you can pick this up and use it in a second. If not, there's a short printed user's guide in the box (plus a CD-ROM with more in-depth info) that gets you up to speed quickly. The box also includes the mount, power connector for the car, and a USB cable. It does not include an AC adapter.

OK, now for the bad news. When it comes to customer service, Magellan has been horrid. We're talking so bad it's almost funny. I'm hoping this situation will change - the company was bought by Mitac late last year, and perhaps this will signal a change for the better in terms of customer support. Lord knows, they couldn't get any worse.

The leader, in my opinion, for customer support is Garmin. They are nice to deal with on the phone, answer emails promptly, and offer regular firmware updates. Whenever I buy a GPS as a gift I always buy Garmin since I don't want to saddle the recipient with the miserable service that Magellan offers. It's a shame, since Magellan offers some real benefits over Garmin, and more value for the money. Tom Tom is also decent when it comes to support, but they use TeleAtlas maps which are less complete than NavTeq (sp?).

Bottom line -- if you're looking for a straightforward GPS at a good price, this should be on your short list. It lacks features such as Bluetooth and an MP3 player, but for me, I want a GPS to offer guidance and not entertainment. This has a very robust feature set, great screen, and well-designed software. It also has traffic capabilities -- did not test that feature out, so I can't comment on it.

The "safe" bet continues to be Garmin. You'll pay a bit more, and get less features, but you can be assured of solid support. Whether Magellan's new owners will put them back on the right track (if you'll excuse the horrid, but unavoidable pun) in terms of customer service is not yet clear. I hope so -- they make a great product!

UPDATE: 5/21/09 There's a firmware update on the Magellan site. No new functionality (in terms of new features) but, according to the release notes it improves overall performance. Easy to install - just follow the included step-by-step instructions. It seems like it makes the unit a bit faster, but that could just be my imagination.

Bose headphones are noise suppression first, sound fidelity second. If it’s sound fidelity you want, buy a comparably priced studio monitor headphone without noise suppression.

I’ve owned and worn out every iteration of the Bose noise-canceling headphones over the last 20 years for jet cabin noise suppression. Commercial airplane cabin noise is a proven travel fatigue-inducing component. A 2-17 hour flight with noise reduction headphones delivers noticeably less flight fatigue.

They’ve been beaten about, dinged, I’ve replaced the ear and head cushions twice. I suspect I have a wiring failure that’s about to reveal itself fully. I use the Bose most frequently without music for just the noise suppression. They work great as a sleep aid in hotels with and without music. Noise suppression is my #1 priority in this category. I have tested 2 of the latest Bose noise suppression headphone competitors. The ambient noise suppression that these new 700 headphones provide is a significant improvement over the QC-35’s. The bass quality of Bose has always been a question mark easily revealed in a sales counter testing for comparison. Honestly, after an hour, the bass issue disappears in the Bose sound ambiance.

As to music reproduction, Bose does not represent the product as a monitor grade headphone. I happen to have a pair of Blue Ella monitor grade headphones. It is an error to compare the Bose work-horse noise suppression headphones that the 700 series represent with studio monitor grade fidelity. There is no question that studio monitor grade headphones deliver superior fidelity for the time they are worn.

Can I comfortably wear the Blue Ella’s on a trans-con flight? No (plus they are prone to a five-finger discount). They simply aren’t designed for hours of head comfort. The Blue Ella’s are fantastic for a couple of hours but are no way suitably head comfortable for a 17-hour flight to Australia.

The Bose 700’s are a clear step up for the QC-35 users. These are lighter on the head, and though they don’t have hingey elements of the QC-35, I’ve not experienced a flexibility problem from this lighter weight and flexible design. They are an improvement in the Bose reputation for the best designed, long-wear consideration.

Ok, to be fair I work with cameras for a living. I wasn't expecting this to compete with my cinema cameras or even popular DSLRs for video, but I was expecting it to at least hold up to the standards people are expecting from cell phone cameras these days. It doesn't. Aside from filling a 4K frame, there aren't a lot of positives to say about the video quality.
To be fair, this has a LOT of advantages over using a cell phone. Recording for long lengths of time onto an SD card is a big plus, not the mention the ability to mount it to a standard tripod and have accessories like a mic and light attached to the body (which are all included!). It comes with a wide angle lens (that is oddly called "macro", but no- it's not for macro shots, its for going wider) which screws on to the front, as well as a handle mounting bracket, an LED light and a microphone. It even comes with a 64GB card, a spare battery, and not one but TWO useful carrying cases (a large one for everything, and a smaller one for just the camera solo). But that's about all the positives I can say about it. If you are outside with a lot of light, you can get decent shots, but this isn't a zoom lens, the zoom is digital only. You can go wide with the external lens or just stay at a fixed medium without it. So no closeup shots for soccer moms. The dynamic range when using it indoors was pretty bad, worse than your average mid-range cell phone. Forget about low light. But that's ok, because the ergonomics of a camera make it better than a cell phone, right?
Well, sorta. Holding it with the strap and the flip out screen is nice. But the UI is confusing, it's hard to go back and watch clips you took because everything is kind of sluggish and not intuitive- once we went past the first page of recorded clips, it was really difficult to move to the next page without accidentally clicking and opening a clip for playback. It just feels really laggy to navigate. Then there's the mic input... it's actually a proprietary plug that goes into the charging/USB plug, and gives you a pigtail for USB on one side and a mic input jack on the other. Odd, considering it COMES with a mic, you'd think it would have an input directly on the body. But no, just this weird mess of wires. Everything about this feels like jumping through a hoop to make it do what you want, and at the end of the day you have to wonder if you couldn't just be better off getting a mic adapter for the cellphone you already own and putting it in one of those holster cages.
Speaking of cell phones, this does have an app which supposedly lets you remotely control and perhaps even copy files from it, but I didn't get that far. I tried to install the app but then gave up when I decided I didn't want to grant this all the permissions it wanted from my personal phone. And I didn't think the video quality was worth it either.
Oddly enough, I kind of like the accessories it comes with. The LED light is pretty nice, the mic isn't terrible either. But for the money, I feel like I would have rather skipped those accessories and just gotten a better camera for a little bit more. It feels almost like they realized this camera was a hard sell so they beefed it up with lots of a accessories for the price.
In conclusion, you DO get a lot of accessories for the money. It's not the worst camera I've ever used, and you can't really get a set with everything you need for any less so I'd say it's worth at least 3 stars for being a functional kit. But I can't really imagine a scenario that I would recommend it.

I was going to wait until I actually had truly tested and used this before I wrote a review.  I got this free as a review unit.  The problem is that I can't use it without spending some money for cables, as it does not come with cables.  StarTech says that's on purpose since people have different cable needs, especially different lengths. The cables that StarTech has available for it are over $21 each, which comes up to well over $60 for my 3 computers, almost the price of the switch.  With 4 computers connected, the price would be even more.  Okay, so they don't provide cables, but for the price of the switch, maybe they should at least give you a coupon or a voucher for one or two cables or a discount on the cables.  Interestingly the 2-port version does include cables; the 4-port does not.  StarTech's cables are nice, as they combine the needed USB with the VGA cable; otherwise you have to run two completely separate cables (one VGA cable for monitor and a USB cable for keyboard and mouse).  If you have USB cables as most people do, you can easily purchase the needed VGA cables inexpensively.  This brings me to the first real issue I have with this switch.  The master monitor connection is a female connector, which is standard.  Unfortunately the 4 computer monitor connectors are all male connections, so you can't use a standard male to male VGA cable that you would normally use from a computer to a monitor.  You have to get male to female VGA cables (which are typically called extension cables).  Why they would use this non-standard method of connecting monitors is puzzling.  A couple of reviewers were also concerned that this switch does not come with a power supply.  That's usually not a big deal as I found out that a power supply is not necessary, as the switch gets it's power from the USB connections.  There is no explanation as to why it has a place to plug in a power supply, although in some cases if you have a lot of USB devices connected to your PC, you might need additional power that a power supply would provide, so I assume it is for supplemental power.  It's good that they provide a way to add additional power, if you need it, even if not the actual power supply.  The next issue I encountered was trying to determine whether or not you could switch between computers with a hotkey sequence on your keyboard or whether you actually had to reach over to the switch and press the button for the computer you wanted.  Apparently there is no keyboard switching or if there is, no one seems to know what keys are used.  I read the manual for the setup and was concerned that it states that for PC to get the switch to work properly, a couple of BIOS settings for PC need to be changed.  I am not even sure that my computers have those particular settings, especially my older computers that sometimes have more limited BIOS settings available.  I have had 3 other KVM switches and none of them needed a change to BIOS settings.  Given the problems that others have had with this switch in that it doesn't always work flawlessly, I am not sure that I want to take time to test it right, since I already have a nicely working KVM switch.  I still have to buy cables.  On the plus side, this switch appears to be well built with a metal case; not cheap plastic.  It appears to be nice and solid and just heavy enough.  If the issues I mentioned are not a deal-breaker for you, I think this is worth trying.  I will update my review and add or subtract stars once I have a chance to test this in actual operation.

Had a 45 inch Sharp Aquos in the living room for over three years, and always thought it delivered wonderful HD output. On my PC, I own a Nvidia 3D Vision Set for the past two years for my PC gaming. The 3D Vision uses shutter technology, and definitely works beautifully with a 120HZ Monitor. Being a huge fan of all things tech, I've been watching the 3DTV market for the past few years, and finally it happened: Passive 3D! An affordable option which can feed 3D to a group of four+ without making you bankrupt.

I transferred the Sharp to the bedroom, and plugged all peripherals (PS3, 360, HDDVR and Roku) into the LG. Fired it up and immediately noticed how the colors popped. It actually ran rings around my Sharp Aquos! I transferred some 3D tech demos I saved on my PC to a USB drive, then ran them on the LG and was blown away by the 3D quality. Clean, bright and wonderful depth! Next, I popped in a BluRay movie (Monsters vs. Aliens) and again, my jaw dropped. I understood that the passive tech on the LG is suppose to have one drawback: horizontal resolution is decreased in 3D mode, but I'll be damned if I can see any difference. The TV arrived the day after Thanksgiving, so we still had the Thanksgiving Day Parade saved on our DVR. We used this to test the 2D to 3D on the fly conversation and it worked out pretty nicely. It definitely adds depth to any 2D broadcast, but nothing compared to true 3D.

As for gaming, the PS3 recognized I had a 3D TV from the start, and the few games I quickly tried (Wipeout, Uncharted 3 & Super Stardust) were mind-numbinlgy gorgeous. I didn't get a chance to try any 3D gaming on my 360 yet, but that's next!

Overall, I couldn't be happier with my decision to go for this LG!

Some quick notes:
- Unlike my 3D Vision PC shutter set up, the LG Passive does not darken the screen; colors remain bright and vibrant!

- My eyes were able to handle much longer periods of 3D viewing with the passive glasses. The 3D vision shutter would screw me up for the night if I played a long gaming session wearing them.

- The LG uses the same glasses they give out in theaters; go see Hugo and keep the glasses! :-)

- Get access to YouTube on your TV, and search YT3D! The LG Passive supports a number of different 3D formats which work brilliantly with most of YouTube's 3D showings'; there's TONS to see on there!

- The only ghosting I noticed was when you were not watching the TV from a normal viewing angle. For instance, if you stand up and move a bit close, you'll see overlapping images, but who watches TV like that?

- The two negatives: LG supplies a set of two orange and two white glasses. Orange and White? Really? What happened to the black glasses shown on the box and in a zillion ads? No big deal though, glasses are cheap. I found an eBay vendor selling a lot of 10 Movie glasses for $15.00! Try doing that with shutter technology. The USB input does not support DTS sound, so if you have a movie stored on a USB drive, it has to be converted or you will have no sound.

I use this to connect my MP3 player to a 3.5mm jack I installed in my car's center console. The low-profile 3.5mm connector was very important to me because I wanted to make the connection as slim as possible to avoid accidentally torquing it, catching things on it, or applying pressure to the jack when moving things in and out of the console.

It works quite well for this purpose. the connector is slim - about as slim as they come, such that it basically clamps right up against the side of the player and the wall of the console. The plug itself feels solid and has a small snap when connecting to things. The cable is soft and almost as flexible as a woven cord, even if it does prefer some orientations to others. Sound quality is typical - which is to say, as good as every other cable I've owned.

The only thing I didn't like about the cable was the colors - it really doesn't go with the car interior and stuck out as a result, a bit distracting. So I used a Sharpie Pro - the big chisel-tip type - to turn it black. It is cotton sheathing, so this is quite viable. I was careful - after inking the entire cable and letting it dry, I washed it in warm water, then dried it and ran a soft, clean rag over it about a hundred times, until it came away basically clean. After the fact, while you could tell the original black bits from the inked threads, it's just different shades of black, rather than looking blotchy. I imagine using something like RIT black dye would be about equally effective, if you heated it and let it soak for a good long while.

So I would recommend it. The braided cable looks premium and is much easier to work with than its equally-thick rubber counterparts. This makes it easy to handle the MP3 player while it is still plugged in.
